guides.title: Abstract Strategy Games and Their Families
guides.summary: A survey of the games of pure skill played on boards — what defines them, the mathematics underneath them, and the great families they fall into, from chess and go through mancala, connection games and hunt games to the modern designed abstracts.

sections.heading: What Makes a Game Abstract
sections.body:
An abstract strategy game is one in which chance plays no part, both players see the entire position at all times, and the game carries no simulated subject matter that the rules depend on. Chess is the canonical example in the Western world, go in the East, but the category is far larger than those two and stretches from scratched lines in Neolithic stone to games designed and published in the last decade.

Three properties do most of the defining work. The first is the absence of randomness: no dice, no shuffled deck, no hidden draw. Whatever happens on the board is a consequence of decisions. Backgammon, whatever its depth, is therefore not an abstract in the strict sense, and neither is poker, though for a different reason. The second is perfect information, the technical term for a position in which nothing is concealed from either player. Stratego has no randomness once set up but hides the identity of pieces, which places it in a different mathematical category entirely. The third is thematic independence: the rules of chess do not actually model medieval warfare, and if you renamed every piece the game would be unchanged. The theme is a mnemonic layer over a mathematical object.

Two further characteristics are common without being definitional. Most abstracts are for exactly two players, because zero-sum reasoning becomes tangled with three or more, where a losing player can decide who wins by choosing whom to attack — the kingmaking problem. And most are finite, with rules that guarantee termination, though several important games needed explicit repetition rules bolted on later precisely because they did not terminate naturally.

Why does the category matter? Partly because it isolates skill. In a game with no luck and no hidden information, the outcome of a single game is a statement about the players, which is why chess and go have supported serious competitive cultures for centuries and why rating systems were developed for them first. Partly because these games are mathematically tractable in a way that few human activities are: they are finite objects with definite values, and the effort to compute those values built much of modern artificial intelligence. And partly because their reduced palette makes design lessons unusually visible. An abstract has nowhere to hide. Remove the theme, the dice and the cards, and a flaw in the rules shows up immediately as a boring, drawish or degenerate game.

Finally, abstracts are the most portable games humans have. A grid drawn in dust and two kinds of pebble reproduce a substantial fraction of them. This is not incidental to their history — it is precisely why they appear independently in nearly every settled culture on earth, and why the archaeological record of gaming is dominated by scratched grids whose rules we no longer know.

sections.heading: The Formal Skeleton: Perfect Information and Zero Sum
sections.body:
Underneath the wooden pieces there is a precise mathematical object, and understanding it explains a surprising amount about why these games feel the way they do.

A two-player abstract is formally a finite, deterministic, sequential game of perfect information. Every position is a node; every legal move is an edge to another node; the whole game is a tree, or more accurately a directed graph, since positions can recur by different move orders. Terminal nodes carry an outcome. Most abstracts are also zero-sum: what one player gains, the other loses, so there is no possibility of cooperation and no ambiguity about what each side is trying to do. Games with a draw are not literally zero-sum in a strict numeric reading unless a draw is scored as one half to each, which is the usual convention.

Perfect information is the property that does the most work. Because nothing is hidden, there is no benefit to randomising your choices — no need for the mixed strategies that dominate poker or rock-paper-scissors. In a perfect-information game there is always an optimal deterministic strategy. This is the practical content of a result usually credited to Ernst Zermelo in 1913 and refined by others afterwards: in a finite two-player game of perfect information with no chance, exactly one of three things is true. Either the first player can force a win, or the second player can force a win, or both can force at least a draw. There is no fourth option and no dependence on who is cleverer. The value of the starting position is a fixed fact about the rules.

This is a strange and slightly deflating result the first time one meets it. Chess has a definite value. Either White wins with perfect play, or Black does, or it is drawn — and nobody knows which, though the overwhelming professional intuition and all computational evidence points to a draw. The value exists whether or not anyone can compute it. Human play, then, consists entirely of navigating a tree that is too large to see, and skill is the practical business of steering toward positions where the opponent is more likely to err.

The sizes involved explain why this is a permanent condition rather than a temporary one. Claude Shannon estimated in 1950 that the number of possible chess games is on the order of 10 to the power 120, a figure now known as the Shannon number, against roughly 10 to the 80 atoms in the observable universe. The number of legal go positions on a 19 by 19 board was computed exactly in 2016 as approximately 2.08 times 10 to the 170. These are not numbers that better hardware will eventually overcome; they are beyond any physical computation. Depth in these games is not an illusion produced by human limitation — it is structural.

sections.heading: Solved Games and the Limits of Solving
sections.body:
A game is said to be solved when its value under perfect play is known, but the word covers three quite different achievements and conflating them causes endless confusion.

Ultra-weak solution means the value of the initial position is known without any explicit strategy being available. This can happen through pure argument. The most elegant example is the strategy-stealing argument, which shows that in certain games the second player cannot have a winning strategy: if they did, the first player could make an arbitrary move, then simply adopt the second player's winning strategy, treating their extra piece as harmless. Since the extra piece cannot hurt in games where more material never hurts, this produces a contradiction. The argument proves that Hex is a first-player win — combined with the fact that Hex cannot be drawn, this shows the first player wins — without revealing a single move of how.

Weak solution means an actual strategy is known that achieves the game's value from the standard starting position. Checkers, on the standard 8 by 8 board, was weakly solved in 2007 by Jonathan Schaeffer's team at the University of Alberta after roughly eighteen years of computation; the result is that perfect play by both sides is a draw. Connect Four was weakly solved independently by James Allen and Victor Allis in 1988: the first player wins by opening in the centre column. Nine Men's Morris was solved by Ralph Gasser in 1993 as a draw. Awari, a mancala variant, was solved in 2002, also a draw.

Strong solution means the value is known for every legal position, not merely the starting one. This has been achieved for small games and, partially, for chess endgames: the Lomonosov and Syzygy tablebases give perfect play for all positions with up to seven pieces on the board, comprising hundreds of trillions of positions, and have revealed forced wins requiring over 500 moves that no human would ever find and that violate the fifty-move drawing rule.

What solving does not do is end interest in a game. Checkers being a draw did not make it unplayable between humans, any more than knowing that noughts and crosses is a draw stops children playing it — although in that case the game is small enough for a person to hold the whole solution, which is exactly why adults stop. The practical threshold is whether a human can internalise the solution. Chess and go are protected by size in a way that is essentially permanent.

There is also an honest uncertainty worth stating: for most abstract games, including chess, go, shogi and xiangqi, the value is unknown and will very likely remain unknown. Strong engines are not proofs. An engine that plays superhumanly is still searching heuristically, and its evaluation is a well-calibrated guess.

sections.heading: The Deep History: Boards Before Records
sections.body:
Board games are older than writing, and the earliest evidence for them is frustratingly mute: we have the boards and almost never the rules.

The oldest generally accepted gaming artefacts come from the ancient Near East. Senet appears in Egyptian tomb paintings and burials from around 3100 BCE, played on a grid of three rows of ten squares; its full rules are lost, though reconstructions exist and it plainly involved chance sticks, which places it outside the abstract category proper. The Royal Game of Ur, excavated by Leonard Woolley at the Sumerian royal cemetery in the 1920s and dated to roughly 2600 BCE, is better understood, because a Babylonian cuneiform tablet from around 177 BCE written by the scribe Itti-Marduk-balāṭu preserves rules that could be matched to the surviving boards. It too used tetrahedral dice. The Egyptian game of mehen, played on a coiled snake board, is entirely conjectural.

Games without chance are harder to date because their boards are simpler and therefore less distinctive. Grids for morris-type games — three, six or nine men's morris — are scratched into stone across an enormous range: the roofing slabs of the temple at Kurna in Egypt, Roman fora, medieval cathedral cloisters where bored masons cut them, and Viking-age ship burials. A nine men's morris board has been claimed from Kurna at around 1400 BCE, though the dating of graffiti on a reused surface is inherently unreliable and archaeologists treat such claims cautiously.

Mancala is similarly ancient and similarly hard to pin down. Rows of shallow depressions cut into rock have been found across Africa and the Levant, some claimed as early as the sixth century CE and a few much earlier, but a row of holes in rock can be a game board, a grain measure, a tally or natural weathering, and distinguishing them is genuinely contentious.

The clearer historical picture begins with games that spread through literate empires. Go appears in Chinese texts by the middle of the first millennium BCE, mentioned in the Analects of Confucius and in the Zuo Zhuan, with a legendary origin attributing its invention to the Emperor Yao. Chaturanga is described in Indian sources by around the sixth century CE and is the ancestor of chess. Latrunculi, a Roman capture game, is documented well enough that its board and pieces survive though its rules do not. The Norse game of tafl is described in sagas and had a board recovered from the Gokstad ship burial.

What emerges from this record is that the abstract game is a cultural universal in the same way that music and cooking are. Independent invention is the norm, convergent structure is common — alignment games, capture games, sowing games and race games appear in unrelated cultures — and the transmission that did occur followed trade routes with remarkable fidelity, which is why the ancestry of chess can be traced across three continents with some confidence.

sections.heading: The Chess Family: One Root, Many Branches
sections.body:
The chess family is the best-documented lineage in the history of games and one of the few where a genuine family tree can be drawn with confidence.

The root is chaturanga, played in northern India by the sixth century CE. The Sanskrit name means "four limbs" and refers to the four divisions of the classical Indian army — infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots — which map onto the pawn, knight, bishop and rook. The game passed into Persia as chatrang, where the counsellor piece was the farzin, and Persian vocabulary entered the game permanently: shah for king, and shah mat, "the king is helpless", giving checkmate. Arab conquest carried it westward as shatranj, and Arabic scholarship produced the first serious literature of the game, including recorded openings and composed problems called mansubat.

Shatranj reached Europe by the tenth century and remained close to its Persian form for five hundred years, with a weak counsellor that moved one square diagonally and a bishop that jumped exactly two squares. Around 1475, in Spain or Italy, the great rules revolution occurred: the counsellor became the modern queen, moving any distance in any direction, and the bishop gained its long diagonal. Contemporaries called the new game alla rabiosa, "mad queen chess", and it made the game vastly faster and sharper. Castling and the double pawn step followed, and by roughly 1620 the rules were essentially modern.

Meanwhile the eastern branches diverged just as far. Xiangqi, Chinese chess, is played on the intersections of a nine-by-ten grid divided by a river, with a general confined to a three-by-three palace and a cannon that captures by jumping over exactly one intervening piece — a mechanic found nowhere in the western game. Janggi in Korea is a close cousin. Shogi in Japan made the most radical innovation of all: captured pieces change ownership and can be dropped back onto the board as reinforcements. This single rule almost eliminates draws, keeps material constant, and makes shogi enormously more complex than chess despite a similar board size; its state-space complexity is estimated around 10 to the 71 against chess's 10 to the 47. Makruk in Thailand and sittuyin in Myanmar preserve features closer to the older shatranj.

The unifying structure is easy to state: differentiated pieces with distinct movement rules, replacement capture, and a royal piece whose loss or entrapment ends the game. Around that skeleton, cultures made very different choices about mobility, about what happens to captured material, and about whether the board's geography constrains movement. Chess variants designed in the modern era — Fischer Random, three-check, atomic, and the many fairy-piece constructions of the problemist tradition — continue the same experiment deliberately rather than by cultural drift.

sections.heading: Go and the Territory Family
sections.body:
Go, called weiqi in China, igo in Japan and baduk in Korea, is the deepest game humans play by most reasonable measures, and it works on principles almost opposite to those of chess.

The rules are extraordinarily short. Players alternately place a stone of their colour on any empty intersection of a 19 by 19 grid. Stones do not move once placed. A connected group of stones with no adjacent empty intersections — no liberties — is captured and removed. A player may pass. When both pass, the game ends and territory is counted. Two additional rules handle pathologies: the ko rule forbids immediately recreating the previous board position, which prevents infinite capture loops, and suicide is generally forbidden. That is essentially the whole game.

From this minimal ruleset an immense strategic structure emerges. Because stones are immobile, everything depends on shape — the relationship between stones and the empty space around them. The concept of life and death is fundamental: a group that can form two separate enclosed empty points, two eyes, can never be captured, and enormous quantities of go theory concern making, denying and reading eye shapes. The tension between influence and territory, between playing high for outward power and low for secure points, is the central strategic dialectic. Sente and gote, the initiative and its absence, govern the order in which moves are made and are worth more than any single point count.

The game's balancing devices are unusually elegant. Komi is a fixed point compensation given to White for playing second, typically 6.5 or 7.5 points depending on ruleset, with the half point ensuring no draws. Handicap stones let players of very different strength play a genuinely competitive game: the weaker player places two to nine stones before play begins, and the ranking system is calibrated so that one stone of handicap corresponds to one rank. This is arguably the best handicap mechanism in any game, and it is a major reason go supported a mass amateur culture.

Ranks run in kyu, descending from about 30 kyu for a beginner to 1 kyu, then in dan, ascending from 1 dan to 7 dan amateur, with a separate professional dan scale.

Scoring rules differ between traditions in a way that matters: Japanese rules count territory plus prisoners, Chinese rules count territory plus stones on the board, and the two almost always give the same winner but differ by a point or so and treat some endgame situations differently. A handful of smaller variants exist — 9 by 9 and 13 by 13 boards for quicker games, and derived games such as Gonnect, in which the objective is connection rather than territory, and Atari Go, in which the first capture wins and which is the standard teaching game for children.

sections.heading: Mancala: The Sowing Family
sections.body:
Mancala is not a game but a family of several hundred, played across Africa, the Middle East, South Asia, the Caribbean and the Philippines, unified by a single distinctive mechanic: sowing. A player lifts all the seeds from one hollow and drops them one at a time into successive hollows around the board. What happens at the end of the sowing determines the game.

The physical form is consistent — two, three or four rows of shallow cups, plus in many versions larger stores at each end — and the material is whatever is at hand: cups scooped in earth, carved wooden boards, and seeds, pebbles, cowrie shells or beans as counters. This makes mancala among the most accessible games in existence; a playable board can be made in five minutes with a stick.

The main division is between two-row and four-row games. Two-row games include Kalah, the version sold commercially in Europe and North America, and Oware, the West African game of the Akan people, which is the most studied. In Oware each player owns six houses and the aim is to capture more than half of the 48 seeds. Sowing is anticlockwise; if the last seed lands in an opponent's house bringing it to exactly two or three seeds, those seeds are captured, and captures propagate backwards through consecutive qualifying houses. A player must not starve the opponent — if the opponent has no seeds, you must make a move that gives them some if one exists. This "feeding" obligation is a rule of real subtlety and appears in many African variants.

Four-row games such as Bao, played in Swahili-speaking East Africa and regarded by many as the most complex of all mancalas, and Omweso in Uganda, add hidden depth: because the back rows are not directly reachable by the opponent, position becomes far more strategic and the games can run very long. Bao's opening phase is so intricate that it has a named repertoire.

Southeast Asian variants such as Congkak in Malaysia and Sungka in the Philippines differ again, often permitting simultaneous starts or multiple laps.

Mathematically the family is interesting because sowing produces highly non-local effects: a single move changes many hollows at once, so the branching factor is small — typically six to twelve legal moves — but the position changes dramatically each turn, which frustrates the pattern-recognition approach that serves well in chess. Awari, a variant of Oware, was strongly solved in 2002 by John Romein and Henri Bal using a 144-processor cluster and a database of 889 billion positions; the result is a draw with perfect play. This makes it one of the largest games ever completely solved, and the solution did essentially nothing to reduce its popularity as a played game, which is a useful data point about what solving means in practice.

sections.heading: Draughts, Checkers and the Jumping-Capture Family
sections.body:
The draughts family is defined by a different capture mechanic from chess: pieces capture by leaping over an adjacent enemy into an empty square beyond, and captures chain, so a single move can remove several pieces in sequence.

The historical origin is usually traced to alquerque, a game documented in the Libro de los Juegos commissioned by Alfonso X of Castile in 1283 and probably of much older Middle Eastern origin, played on a lined board of twenty-five points. Around the twelfth century, in southern France, someone transplanted alquerque's capture rule onto the chessboard, using the dark squares only and the twelve-piece-per-side arrangement now familiar. The move from a game of no forced captures to one where capture is compulsory, and the promotion of pieces reaching the far rank into kings with backward movement, produced the modern game.

The family diverges chiefly over three rules. Board size: English draughts and American checkers use 8 by 8 with twelve pieces each, while international draughts uses 10 by 10 with twenty pieces each. King movement: in international, Russian, Brazilian and most continental versions the king is a "flying king" that moves any distance along a diagonal, whereas in English draughts it moves one square. And backward capture: many versions allow ordinary pieces to capture backwards, English draughts does not. Turkish draughts abandons diagonals entirely, moving and capturing orthogonally. Each of these choices has large consequences for tactics — flying kings make endgames far richer, and the maximum-capture rule of international draughts, which forces the player to take the longest available capture sequence, generates spectacular multi-piece combinations that are the aesthetic heart of the game.

The competitive history of English draughts is instructive about a structural problem. By the twentieth century the game was so thoroughly analysed that top players drew almost every serious game, and the response was to impose randomised openings: the three-move ballot, in which the first three moves are drawn from a list of approved balanced openings. This is a designed patch for a game whose natural opening tree had been exhausted by human study — a fate that has been predicted for chess for a century without arriving.

The computational history is famous. Arthur Samuel's checkers program at IBM, developed from 1952, was among the first machine-learning programs and coined the phrase in 1959. The Chinook program of Jonathan Schaeffer's group drew a match against the long-reigning champion Marion Tinsley in 1992 and won the title in 1994 when Tinsley withdrew for health reasons; Tinsley, who lost only a handful of games in forty years, remains the strongest documented human player of any game relative to his field. In 2007 Chinook's authors announced that English draughts is a draw with perfect play.

sections.heading: Connection Games: Hex, Y and Their Relatives
sections.body:
Connection games are the youngest of the great families and arguably the purest. The objective is topological: build an unbroken chain of your own pieces linking specified regions of the board.

Hex is the founding example, invented independently by the Danish mathematician and poet Piet Hein in 1942 and by John Nash at Princeton around 1948. It is played on a rhombus of hexagonal cells, usually 11 by 11 or larger; each player owns two opposite sides and wins by connecting them with a chain of their stones. Its mathematical properties are exquisite. The Hex theorem states that when the board is completely filled, exactly one player has a winning connection — a draw is impossible, a fact equivalent to the Brouwer fixed-point theorem. Combined with the strategy-stealing argument, this proves that the first player has a winning strategy on any square board. Nobody knows what it is for boards larger than 10 by 10, and the proof reveals nothing about it. Hex therefore sits in a peculiar position: known to be a first-player win, and still played competitively, because the winning strategy is unreachable.

The first-player advantage is real enough at small sizes that a balancing convention is universal: the swap rule, also called the pie rule. The first player makes one move; the second player may either respond normally or take over that move and the colour that made it. This forces the opener to choose a move that is neither too strong nor too weak, and it is one of the most elegant balancing devices ever invented, now borrowed by dozens of other games.

Y, invented by Craige Schensted and Charles Titus, generalises Hex onto a triangular board where the goal is to connect all three sides; Hex can be embedded in Y as a special case. Havannah, designed by Christian Freeling in 1979 on a hexagonal board of hexes, offers three distinct winning shapes — a ring, a bridge connecting two corners, or a fork connecting three edges — which makes it unusually hard to evaluate and which resisted computer play far longer than its simplicity suggests. TwixT, designed by Alex Randolph in the 1960s, uses pegs and links with a knight's-move connection, producing a strikingly different texture. More recent entries include *Star, Gonnect, Slither and Andantino.

The design appeal of the family is that connection is a monotone goal — placed stones never become worse for you — which makes the games clean, draw-free and free of the material-counting heuristics that dominate chess. The corresponding difficulty is evaluation. A connection position resists simple counting, and for decades computers played Hex and Havannah poorly for exactly that reason, until Monte Carlo methods gave them a way to evaluate positions by playing them out rather than judging them.

sections.heading: Alignment Games: Getting Things in a Row
sections.body:
The alignment family is the most widespread and the most immediately graspable: place or move pieces to form a line of a specified length. It is also the family that best illustrates how a tiny change in parameters converts a trivial game into a deep one.

Noughts and crosses, or tic-tac-toe, is the degenerate case. On a 3 by 3 grid with three in a row to win, the game tree is small enough — 255,168 possible games, 26,830 excluding those that end early — that any adult can hold the complete solution and the game is a forced draw. Its value is entirely pedagogical: it is the standard first example in every textbook of game trees and minimax search.

Increase the board and the length and the picture changes utterly. Gomoku, or five in a row, played on a 15 by 15 or 19 by 19 grid, is a serious game — and, notoriously, a broken one in its free form: Victor Allis proved in 1993 that free-style gomoku on 15 by 15 is a first-player win. The Japanese and Chinese response was Renju, which handicaps Black with a set of forbidden moves — Black may not make a double-three, a double-four, or an overline of six or more — plus opening restrictions and a swap mechanism. Renju is thus a designed correction to a solved game, and it is one of the clearest illustrations that a good abstract game is engineered rather than discovered.

Connect Four is the gravity-constrained version: pieces drop to the lowest empty cell in a column, which reduces the branching factor to seven and makes the game tractable. It was solved in 1988 as a first-player win with a centre-column opening.

The morris or mills games form a distinct subfamily, mixing alignment with placement and movement. Nine Men's Morris is played on a board of three concentric squares with connecting midlines, twenty-four points in total. Players first place nine pieces each, then move them along lines; forming a mill of three in a row lets a player remove an enemy piece. When a player is reduced to three pieces they may "fly" to any empty point, a comeback mechanic. Gasser's 1993 analysis found the game is a draw. Six, five and three men's morris variants exist across Europe and Asia, and Twelve Men's Morris with diagonals is played widely in Africa and India.

The unifying design lesson of the family is about the ratio between board size, the number of pieces and the target line length. Too generous and the first player forces a win; too restrictive and everything is a draw. The sweet spot is narrow, which is why so many alignment games required later patching, and why free gomoku, Connect Four and noughts and crosses all fell to computation while renju survives as a competitive game.

sections.heading: Hunt Games and Asymmetric Boards
sections.body:
Most abstracts are symmetric: both players have the same pieces and the same goal. Hunt games break that symmetry deliberately, giving the two sides different armies and different victory conditions, and the result is a design space that is unusually rich and unusually hard to balance.

The tafl games of northern Europe are the best known. Hnefatafl and its relatives — tablut in Sápmi, brandubh in Ireland, ard rí in Scotland, tawlbwrdd in Wales — were the principal board games of Scandinavia before chess displaced them, and they are documented in sagas, in law codes and in archaeological finds including a partial board from the Gokstad ship burial. The structure is consistent: a king and a small defending force occupy the centre of a board of odd dimension, surrounded by an attacking force roughly twice as numerous placed at the edges. The king wins by escaping to a corner or an edge, depending on the version; the attackers win by capturing the king, usually by surrounding him on all four sides. Pieces move orthogonally like a rook and capture by custodian capture — sandwiching an enemy between two friendly pieces.

The rules were partially recorded by Carl Linnaeus, who observed tablut being played in Lapland in 1732 and wrote down what he saw in his diary, in Latin, with some evident confusion. Every modern tafl ruleset descends from that fragmentary record, which is why versions differ so widely, and why balancing tafl remains an active argument among players: many rulesets are strongly biased toward one side and require corner restrictions, king-armed or king-unarmed variations, or shieldwall rules to even out.

Elsewhere the family is well represented. Bagha-Chall from Nepal pits four tigers against twenty goats; the tigers capture by jumping, the goats win by immobilising the tigers. Fox and Geese, played on a cross-shaped board across Europe, gives one fox against thirteen to seventeen geese, and the geese win by penning the fox. Rimau in Malaysia, Komikan in Chile and Adugo among the Bororo of Brazil are all variations on the same tiger-and-goats theme, which suggests either extraordinarily wide diffusion or genuine independent invention of a natural idea.

The design problem in all of these is inherent: an asymmetric game with a large numerical imbalance is exceptionally sensitive to small rule changes, and it is very easy to produce a version in which one side simply wins. The traditional solution is that players alternate sides across a series of games, so that a bias affects both equally and skill decides the match. That convention is a genuine piece of design wisdom and is worth borrowing whenever a game cannot be balanced directly.

sections.heading: The Modern Designed Abstract
sections.body:
For most of history abstract games evolved. Since roughly the mid-twentieth century they have also been designed, by named individuals, with stated goals, published rulesets and copyright — and this has produced a body of work that deserves treating as a field in its own right.

Sid Sackson's 1969 book A Gamut of Games is a reasonable starting point for the modern era: it collected and published original abstracts alongside old ones, treating design as a creative act. Alex Randolph, working largely in Germany, produced TwixT and a stream of other abstracts. But the figure most associated with the movement is the Dutch designer Christian Freeling, who created Havannah, Grand Chess, Dameo, Emergo and a long list of others, and who articulated a design philosophy centred on emergent complexity from minimal rules.

The commercial landmark is the GIPF Project of the Belgian designer Kris Burm, begun in 1997: six interlocking games — GIPF, TAMSK, ZÈRTZ, DVONN, YINSH and PÜNCT — each excellent independently and each contributing optional pieces to the others. DVONN in particular is often cited as one of the finest abstracts ever designed, with a shrinking board and a stacking mechanic that produces an unusually sharp endgame.

Other significant modern games include Amazons, invented by Walter Zamkauskas in 1988, in which pieces move like chess queens and then fire an arrow that permanently blocks a square, so that the board relentlessly shrinks and the game becomes a pure territory contest with an elegant connection to combinatorial game theory. Lines of Action by Claude Soucie is a connection game with movement determined by the number of pieces on a line. Hive by John Yianni escapes the board entirely, with tiles forming their own playing surface. Santorini, Onitama, Yinsh and Blokus have all found substantial audiences.

Several stated design principles recur among these designers and are worth knowing because they generalise. Rules should be short enough to teach in two minutes but generate positions that cannot be evaluated at a glance. Draws should be structurally impossible or rare, because a draw is an unsatisfying resolution to a contest of skill. The first-player advantage must be addressed explicitly, usually by the pie rule or by a compensating rule. And the board should preferably change in a way that forces the game to end — shrinking boards, filling boards or diminishing material all guarantee termination without an arbitrary move limit.

There is also a distinct amateur design community, historically centred on the Abstract Games magazine and now on online forums and servers where new games can be implemented and tested rapidly. Playtesting against strong Monte Carlo engines has become a normal part of the process, and it kills weak designs quickly by finding degenerate strategies that human testers miss.

sections.heading: How Machines Learned to Play
sections.body:
The history of computer game-playing is largely the history of abstract strategy games, because they offered a clearly defined, self-contained problem that was nonetheless hard.

The foundational idea is minimax, formalised by John von Neumann in 1928 and applied to chess by Claude Shannon in his 1950 paper "Programming a Computer for Playing Chess". The program builds a tree of possible continuations, applies an evaluation function to the leaves, and propagates values upward assuming each player picks the move best for themselves. Alan Turing wrote a paper-and-pencil chess algorithm called Turochamp around 1948 that he executed by hand, taking about half an hour per move.

The critical optimisation is alpha-beta pruning, developed independently by several people in the late 1950s and early 1960s, including John McCarthy's group at MIT. It exploits the observation that once you know one branch is already worse than a branch you have fully examined, you need not examine it further. With perfect move ordering, alpha-beta reduces the effective branching factor to its square root, which roughly doubles the search depth achievable in a given time. Everything else in classical engine design — iterative deepening, transposition tables using Zobrist hashing, quiescence search to avoid stopping in the middle of a capture sequence, null-move pruning, opening books and endgame tablebases — is refinement around this core.

The high-water mark of the classical approach was IBM's Deep Blue defeating Garry Kasparov in a six-game match in May 1997, searching on the order of 200 million positions per second with special-purpose hardware and a hand-tuned evaluation function containing thousands of terms.

Go resisted this approach completely. The branching factor of about 250 versus chess's 35 made deep search impossible, and, more fundamentally, nobody could write a good positional evaluation function for go; the value of a position depends on subtle whole-board relationships that resisted hand-coding. The breakthrough came in 2006 with Monte Carlo Tree Search, which evaluates a position not by judging it but by playing thousands of fast random games from it and counting wins, guided by the UCT formula that balances exploring new moves against exploiting promising ones. MCTS lifted computer go from roughly amateur 8 kyu to strong amateur dan level.

The final step was combining MCTS with deep neural networks. DeepMind's AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol 4–1 in March 2016; AlphaGo Zero in 2017 learned entirely from self-play with no human games, and AlphaZero generalised the method to chess and shogi, learning each from the rules alone in hours. The consequences for human play have been substantial and somewhat unexpected: engine analysis has overturned long-standing positional dogma in both games, and go professionals now routinely study machine-derived openings that contradict several centuries of accumulated theory.

sections.heading: Playing Well: Study, Rating and Handicap
sections.body:
The practical question for a player is how to improve, and the abstract-game tradition has developed a set of answers that transfer remarkably well between games.

The most important is the study of patterns rather than lines. Strong players in every abstract game are distinguished less by calculating further than by recognising more. The classic psychological work is by Adriaan de Groot in the 1940s and by William Chase and Herbert Simon in 1973, who showed that chess masters recall realistic positions far better than novices but have no advantage at all with randomly scattered pieces. Their explanation, chunking, holds that expertise consists of a large vocabulary of meaningful configurations, estimated at perhaps 50,000 to 100,000 chunks for a master. The implication for study is direct: solve large numbers of tactical problems, learn named shapes and standard sequences — joseki in go, tesuji for local tactics, standard endgames in chess — and review your own games to find where your pattern vocabulary failed.

The second is the discipline of losing. Playing opponents slightly stronger than you produces improvement; playing weaker ones produces comfort. Reviewing losses without an engine first, forming your own judgement about where the game turned, and only then checking against analysis, avoids the well-documented failure mode of passive engine consumption where players absorb evaluations without understanding them.

Rating systems came out of this tradition and have since spread everywhere. The Elo system, devised by the Hungarian-American physicist Arpad Elo and adopted by FIDE in 1970, models each player's performance as a random variable and updates ratings after each game according to the difference between actual and expected score. A 200-point gap corresponds to roughly a 76 per cent expected score for the stronger player, and a 400-point gap to about 91 per cent. Glicko, developed by Mark Glickman, adds a ratings-deviation term that widens with inactivity; TrueSkill extends the idea to multiplayer teams.

Go's kyu-dan system predates Elo by centuries and has a property Elo lacks: it is directly convertible into a handicap. A player five ranks weaker takes five handicap stones and the game becomes roughly even. This is enormously valuable socially, because it lets players of wildly different strength compete meaningfully, and it is one reason go clubs sustain mixed-ability play better than chess clubs, where the equivalent — removing material — distorts the game badly.

For most abstracts without an established handicap convention, the practical substitutes are time odds, which preserve the position entirely, and playing a match of even length with sides alternating, which cancels any structural imbalance.

A last point about time. Slow play and fast play train different things, and most improving players get the ratio wrong. Long games build the habit of calculating before moving and of checking your opponent's threats, which is where the majority of amateur errors originate; fast games build pattern recall and stamina but reinforce whatever habits you already have, good or bad. The usual recommendation is a majority of long games during a period of active study and a shift toward faster play only once the patterns are secure.

sections.heading: Design Pathologies and Failure Modes
sections.body:
Abstract games fail in a small number of characteristic ways, and because there is no theme or randomness to disguise the failure, they fail visibly. Recognising these patterns is useful both for designers and for players deciding whether a game is worth their time.

The first pathology is the forced win, where one side, usually the first player, can win by a known method. Free gomoku, Connect Four and noughts and crosses all suffer from it. The standard remedies are the pie rule, a compensating score such as go's komi, forbidden-move handicaps as in renju, or randomised balanced openings as in three-move-ballot draughts.

The second is the draw death, where strong play reliably produces no result. English draughts approached this before the ballot was introduced, and the possibility hovers over top-level chess, where the draw rate in elite classical events regularly exceeds 60 per cent and occasionally passes 80. Structural fixes include making draws impossible — Hex cannot be drawn, shogi's piece drops make them very rare — or scoring systems that reward decisive results.

The third is the degenerate strategy: a single line of play that dominates and reduces the game to one idea. This is what playtesting against a fast engine catches most reliably, and it is why many modern designers publish only after machine testing.

The fourth is the failure to terminate. Chess needed the threefold repetition and fifty-move rules bolted on; go needed the ko rule and, for pathological cases, superko rules that forbid recreating any previous whole-board position. Games with shrinking boards or permanently placed stones avoid the problem structurally.

The fifth affects multiplayer abstracts specifically: kingmaking, where an eliminated or losing player determines who wins by choosing whom to hinder. This is why nearly all serious abstracts are two-player, and why three-player chess variants have never gained traction.

A sixth, subtler failure is the analysis-paralysis game — one with a large branching factor and no strong heuristics for pruning, so that players are faced with a genuinely open choice at every turn and take an unreasonable time over it. Amazons flirts with this in the opening; it is managed with clocks. A related complaint is the runaway leader, where an early advantage compounds so steeply that the remainder of the game is a formality; games with shrinking boards are especially prone to it, and the usual mitigation is a resignation convention rather than a rule change, since forcing a player to grind out a won position wastes everyone's evening.

There is also a failure mode of the player rather than the game. Studying openings without studying endgames, memorising sequences without understanding their purpose, and playing only fast games are the three habits that most reliably stall improvement. If a game has stopped being interesting, the honest diagnostic questions are whether the position types have become repetitive, whether you have stopped losing, and whether you have stopped reviewing — the last being by far the commonest cause.

sections.heading: Getting Started, and What to Do When You Are Stuck
sections.body:
The practical barrier to abstract games is rarely the rules; it is finding an opponent and finding the right game. Both problems are more tractable than they look.

On game choice, a rough guide by temperament works better than a guide by prestige. If you like sharp tactics and material calculation, chess, shogi or international draughts will reward you. If you prefer slow, whole-board judgement and are comfortable with ambiguity, go is unmatched, and playing on a 9 by 9 board first — a full game takes fifteen minutes — is the standard on-ramp rather than a lesser version. If you dislike memorised opening theory, connection games such as Hex and Havannah, or modern designs such as DVONN and Amazons, have almost no book to learn. If you want something playable with objects already in the house, mancala needs only an egg box and dried beans, and morris or hex can be drawn on paper.

Almost every game in this survey can be improvised. A go board is a grid drawn on card with black and white counters; hex is a hexagonal grid on paper played with two colours of pencil; tafl is a paper grid with coins and buttons; mancala is holes in the ground. The absence of a manufactured set is never a real obstacle and never has been, which is why these games survived the collapse of the civilisations that invented them.

For the common experience of hitting a plateau, the reliable interventions in order of usefulness are: play longer games with a clock rather than more short ones; review your own losses in writing before consulting any engine; deliberately study the phase you avoid, which for most people is the endgame; and play a stronger opponent regularly even though it is unpleasant. Improvement in these games is famously non-linear — long flat periods punctuated by sudden jumps when a set of patterns finally consolidates — and the flat periods are not evidence that you have reached your ceiling.

If the game itself has gone stale rather than your progress, the honest answer may be to change games. Skills transfer more than players expect. Reading sequences ahead, recognising shape, evaluating initiative and managing a clock are general competences, and a strong chess player picking up Amazons or a go player picking up Havannah typically reaches a respectable level fast.

Finally, it is worth holding onto the fact that none of these games is solved in any sense that touches human play, with the narrow exceptions noted for checkers, Connect Four, morris and awari. Chess and go have been played seriously for well over a thousand years each, by tens of millions of people, with machines now assisting, and there is no sign of either being exhausted. Whatever else these objects are, they are very deep.

guides.title: Chaturanga: The Indian Origin of Chess
guides.summary: How chess began as chaturanga in northern India around the sixth century CE, what its board, pieces and rules actually were, and how it travelled through Persia and the Islamic world into Europe and East Asia to become the family of games played today.

sections.heading: What Chaturanga Was and Why Its Origin Matters
sections.body: Chaturanga is the ancestor of chess. It was a board game played in northern India by roughly the sixth century of the common era, on a square grid of sixty-four cells, between two players commanding miniature armies of foot soldiers, horses, elephants and chariots led by a king and his counsellor. Nearly every board game in the world that involves capturing enemy pieces on a grid while protecting a single irreplaceable royal piece descends from it: European chess, Chinese xiangqi, Japanese shogi, Thai makruk, Burmese sittuyin, Mongolian shatar and a dozen regional cousins. To understand chaturanga is to understand the common grammar underneath all of them, and to see clearly which features of the modern game are ancient and which are recent inventions that a player raised on the modern rules is likely to mistake for eternal truths. The queen that dominates a modern board, for example, is about five hundred and fifty years old. The board underneath her is at least fifteen hundred. The question of chess's origin matters beyond antiquarian curiosity for three reasons. First, chess is one of the very few cultural artefacts that has been transmitted across essentially every literate civilisation of Eurasia and North Africa while remaining recognisably itself, which makes its diffusion an unusually clean tracer of trade, conquest and scholarly contact along the Silk Road and the Indian Ocean routes. Where the game went, people and books went. Second, the origin question has been the subject of nationalist claims from India, Persia, China and elsewhere for well over a century, and separating the documented record from the patriotic reconstruction is a useful exercise in how historical evidence is actually weighed. Third, the rule changes the game underwent are a natural experiment in game design: chaturanga and its immediate descendants were slow, and the fifteenth-century European revisions that made two pieces vastly more powerful transformed a leisurely positional pastime into the sharp tactical game recognised today. The evidence base is thinner than most people assume. There is no surviving rulebook from India of the period, no illustrated manuscript, and no archaeological find from the Indian subcontinent that is unambiguously a sixth-century chess set. What exists is a scatter of literary allusions in Sanskrit, a Middle Persian narrative written down a century or two after the events it describes, a rich Arabic technical literature from the ninth century onward that describes a game already fully formed, and a small number of excavated pieces. From these, historians reconstruct backwards. The reconstruction is solid in outline and genuinely uncertain in several important details, and any account that does not admit this is overselling. A reader who wants a single benchmark for how much is inference should note that no text written in India before the eleventh century sets out the rules of the game in full; the earliest complete rulebooks that survive anywhere are Arabic, and they describe the game two or three centuries and two cultural translations downstream of its invention.

sections.heading: The Word Chaturanga and the Fourfold Army
sections.body: The name is Sanskrit: chatur, four, plus anga, limb or member, giving chaturanga, 'having four limbs' or 'four-membered'. It is a military term long predating the game. In the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, and in Kautilya's Arthashastra, a chaturanga-bala is the complete army in its four classical divisions: patti or padati, the infantry; ashva, the cavalry; gaja or hastin, the elephant corps; and ratha, the chariotry. A king who fields all four commands a full army; one who fields fewer is deficient. The word appears in epics that in some form long predate the sixth century, and this creates the single most common error in popular accounts of chess history. Finding chaturanga in an old Indian text proves nothing about chess, because in almost every such case the word simply means an army. Only where the context is unmistakably a board, pieces or play does a reference count. That the game took its name from the army tells us something real about its design intent. Chaturanga is not an abstract game onto which a military skin was later painted; it was conceived from the start as a representation of a battle between two royal hosts, and the pieces were chosen because they were the four arms of a real Indian army plus its two commanders. The infantry are numerous, weak and expendable, and they advance and never retreat, exactly as a line of foot soldiers does. The cavalry moves in an odd oblique bound that lets it pass through gaps, which is a fair abstraction of light horse skirmishing through a line. The elephants are ponderous and short-ranged but were feared out of proportion to their actual battlefield record. The chariots sweep in straight lines down open ground and are useless in a press, which is exactly the tactical truth about chariots. Alongside the four arms stand two pieces that are not army divisions at all: the raja, the king, and the mantri or senapati, variously the minister, counsellor or army commander. The king is the object of the game rather than a fighting unit, which reflects a real convention of Indian and Persian warfare in which the capture or death of the king ended the battle regardless of the state of the field. The counsellor was originally feeble, moving a single step diagonally, which is worth holding in mind: for roughly nine hundred years the piece that stood beside the king was the second weakest on the board rather than the strongest. Its later transformation into the queen is the largest single rule change in the game's history, and it happened in Europe, not in India. The Sanskrit terminology also leaves a small puzzle: the counsellor is called mantri, minister, in some contexts and senapati, army commander, in others, and it is not clear whether these were competing regional names for one piece or evidence that the piece's identity was still unsettled when the game began to travel.

sections.heading: Dating the Game: The Evidence for Sixth-Century India
sections.body: The consensus date for the appearance of chaturanga is the sixth century CE, in northern India, most probably in the Gangetic plain under the late Gupta or immediately post-Gupta states. That date rests on a small number of literary passages, none individually decisive, which together bracket the game's emergence. The earliest commonly cited is a simile in Subandhu's Sanskrit romance Vasavadatta, usually placed in the sixth or early seventh century. Describing the monsoon, Subandhu writes of the rainy season playing its game with frogs for pieces, yellow and green in colour, upon the dark field of the earth chequered with moss like an ashtapada. The passage names the board and speaks of coloured pieces in play. It does not describe the rules, and some scholars have argued the reference could be to the older race game played on the same board rather than to chess. The stronger passage is in the Harshacharita of Banabhatta, court poet to King Harsha of Kannauj, written around 625 CE. Praising the peace of Harsha's reign, Bana produces a chain of puns: under this king, only bees quarrel for honey, the only feet cut off are those of verse, and the only ones learning the ordering of the chaturanga are the ashtapadas. The line only works as a joke if chaturanga can mean both an army and a game arrayed on a board, which is exactly the double meaning required, and most historians take it as a firm reference to chess before 625. Working from the other direction, the Middle Persian text known as the Chatrang-namag, or Explanation of Chess, tells how an Indian embassy brought the game to the Sasanian court of Khosrow I Anushirvan, who reigned from 531 to 579, as a diplomatic riddle, and how the vizier Wuzurgmihr solved it and sent back backgammon in reply. The text as we have it was composed later, and the story is plainly a courtly legend rather than a minute of a meeting, but legends of this kind normally attach to real events, and its insistence that the game arrived from India, complete, in the sixth century agrees with the Indian evidence. Another Persian work, the Karnamag of Ardashir, of the early seventh century, lists chatrang among the accomplishments expected of a prince. The physical evidence is later and sparser. Seven small ivory pieces excavated at Afrasiab, the old city of Samarkand, are dated to roughly the mid eighth century and are unambiguously a chess set: a king, an elephant, a horse, a chariot and foot soldiers, still carved as recognisable figures rather than the abstract cylinders that Islamic aniconism would later encourage. They are the earliest chess pieces anyone has convincingly identified, and they are already two centuries downstream of the invention.

sections.heading: The Board: Ashtapada and the Older Race Games
sections.body: The board on which chaturanga was played was not invented for it. It was the ashtapada, literally 'eight-footed', an eight-by-eight grid already in use in India for at least several centuries as the field for a race game in which pieces travelled a fixed circuit under the direction of dice or throwing-sticks. Ashtapada is named in Buddhist texts, including a list of games the Buddha is said to have abstained from, in versions that may go back to the early centuries BCE, though the games in such lists are named and not described. That an existing, widely available board was adopted is one reason chess spread so easily: the equipment was already in every household that played anything. The ashtapada was not chequered. Alternating light and dark squares are a European addition, appearing in the eleventh or twelfth century and standard by the thirteenth; every Indian, Persian and Arabic board before that was a uniform grid of sixty-four cells marked only by their dividing lines. This is not a trivial cosmetic point. On an unchequered board it is genuinely hard to see diagonals at a glance, which suited a game whose diagonal-moving pieces were short-ranged and largely irrelevant, and which became untenable the moment Europe invented long-range bishops and queens. The chequering and the explosion in diagonal power arrived within a few centuries of each other, and the first probably enabled the second. The ashtapada carried a distinctive feature that chess inherited and then abandoned: certain squares, usually the corners and several marked cells along the edges and centre, bore a cross or X mark. In the race game these were almost certainly safe squares or castles where a piece could not be captured, a device familiar from pachisi and from race games worldwide. Chaturanga made no use of them, and Arabic boards drop them entirely, but they survive as an inert decoration on some early boards and in the diagrams of some manuscripts. Their presence is one of the clearest signs that chess borrowed its furniture rather than designing it. Traces persist elsewhere in the family: Thai makruk and Burmese sittuyin still mark particular squares, and Chinese xiangqi retains marked points where pieces are initially placed. A second and more consequential inheritance concerns coordinates. Because the board was square and unmarked, description of positions in early Arabic literature used a system of naming files after the pieces that began on them and ranks by number, an awkward scheme that produced ambiguity and that modern algebraic notation only replaced in the nineteenth century. Anyone attempting to read a medieval chess problem in the original will meet this immediately. It also means that where a manuscript diagram and its accompanying text disagree, as they often do, reconstructing the intended position takes real editorial judgement, and different scholars have reached different answers about the same problem.

sections.heading: The Pieces and Their Original Powers
sections.body: Six kinds of piece stood on a chaturanga board, and each side had sixteen men: eight foot soldiers and one each of the other five types except that chariots, horses and elephants came in pairs. The powers of four of them are certain, because they are unchanged from India to Persia to Arabia to Europe and are still the moves used today. The ratha, chariot, moved any number of empty cells in a straight line along a rank or file and captured the first enemy piece it met. This is the modern rook, and it has never changed in the entire recorded history of the game, in any branch of the family, which makes it the single most stable element in chess. The ashva, horse, moved two cells in one direction and one at right angles, leaping over anything in between. This is the modern knight, equally unchanged, and its leap is chaturanga's most original contribution to the vocabulary of board games. The raja, king, moved one cell in any of the eight directions and could not move into capture; the game ended when he could not escape attack. The padati or bhata, foot soldier, moved one cell straight forward, could not retreat, and captured one cell diagonally forward. There was no initial double step and consequently no en passant capture, both of which are late European conveniences introduced to speed the opening. The mantri or counsellor moved exactly one cell diagonally, in any of the four diagonal directions. It was worth roughly a foot soldier and a half. Because it could only ever stand on cells of one colour, and because it moved so slowly, a counsellor took a long time to bring into contact with the enemy, and endgames in which each side had king and counsellor were routinely drawn. The gaja, elephant, is the genuinely contested piece and the one place where honest reconstruction has to hedge. Three distinct elephant moves are attested in the descendants, and there is no decisive evidence which was original. The Persian and Arabic fil leapt exactly two cells diagonally, passing over any occupied cell in between; this confines it to eight of the sixty-four cells for the whole game and makes it very weak. A second attested move is a two-cell leap orthogonally, forward, back or sideways, which survives in some Indian and Russian traditions. A third, preserved in Thai makruk and Burmese sittuyin, allows one step diagonally in any direction or one step straight forward, giving a piece of five destinations that is markedly stronger and not colour-bound. Historians including H. J. R. Murray generally favour the diagonal leap as the original because it is what the earliest documented branch carries, but the argument is one of transmission rather than proof.

sections.heading: How a Game of Chaturanga Was Played
sections.body: The two armies faced each other across the board, each occupying two ranks. The eight foot soldiers stood in a line on the second rank. Behind them, on the first rank, stood a chariot in each corner, then a horse beside each chariot, then an elephant beside each horse, leaving the two central cells for the king and his counsellor. Which of the two central cells held the king is a real problem in the sources: Persian and Arabic practice put the two kings on the same file facing each other, which forces the two counsellors to face each other too, while some Indian descriptions place the king on the other side, producing a diagonal asymmetry between the armies. Reconstructions usually adopt the facing-kings arrangement because it is what the earliest detailed sources describe. White and black in the modern sense did not exist; the two sides were distinguished by colour, commonly red and green or red and black in Indian tradition. Who moved first was not fixed by a universal rule and appears to have been settled by agreement or lot. Play proceeded by alternate single moves. The object was to trap the enemy king, and the Persian phrase for the terminal position, shah mat, gave every European language its word for checkmate. The phrase is widely mistranslated as 'the king is dead'; in Persian mat means helpless, defeated or at a loss, and the sense is that the king is cornered with no recourse, which is precisely the rule. The Arabic verb mata, to die, is a coincidence that produced the folk etymology. Two further ways of winning existed that modern players find surprising, and both follow from the weakness of the pieces. Baring the enemy king, that is, capturing every one of his other pieces, was a win in its own right, because with such feeble men a lone king could often not be mated at all and the game would otherwise never end. In most codes, if the bared player could immediately bare his opponent in reply, the game was drawn. Stalemate, where a player to move has no legal move but is not in check, was treated inconsistently: in most of the shatranj tradition it was a win for the stalemated player's opponent, in some medieval European codes a win for the stalemated player himself, and only in the nineteenth century did the modern draw become universal. A promoted foot soldier reaching the far rank became a counsellor and nothing else. Since the counsellor was worth less than two foot soldiers, promotion was a modest gain rather than the decisive event it is today, and this single fact explains most of the difference in character between chaturanga and modern chess.

sections.heading: The Four-Handed Variant and the Dice Question
sections.body: A four-player relative of chaturanga, usually called chaturaji, 'four kings', is well documented in Indian sources and was described in detail by the Persian polymath al-Biruni in his account of India written around 1030 after long residence in the subcontinent. Four small armies of four pieces and four foot soldiers occupy the four corners of the same sixty-four-cell board. Each army has a king, an elephant, a horse and a boat, the boat replacing the chariot and leaping two cells diagonally. Play runs around the circle, and in the version al-Biruni records an oblong four-sided die is thrown to determine which class of piece must move: a throw of two moves the boat, three the horse, four the elephant, and five or one the king or a foot soldier. Captured pieces score points on a fixed tariff, and the players may be allied in pairs or each for himself. The four-handed game matters because of an old and now largely settled argument about which came first. In the mid nineteenth century Duncan Forbes, working chiefly from a passage in the Bhavishya Purana, argued that chaturaji was the original and that two-handed chess was a later simplification, and he pushed the invention back some five thousand years. The claim was influential and is still repeated. It does not survive scrutiny. The Purana passage is a late interpolation of uncertain date; the four-handed game is attested only from the tenth and eleventh centuries, well after two-handed chess is firmly documented in Persia and Arabia; and the boat, which replaces the chariot, is plainly a substitution made in a region where riverine transport mattered more than chariotry. H. J. R. Murray dismantled Forbes's chronology in his monumental History of Chess of 1913, and the modern consensus is that chaturaji is a derivative, probably an adaptation of chess to the format of the older dice-driven race games played on the same board. The dice question is separate and more interesting. Because the ashtapada was a dice board, and because some Indian sources refer to chess with dice, a persistent theory holds that the original chaturanga used dice to select which piece a player might move, and that the game we know is the result of stripping the randomiser out, perhaps under religious pressure, since gambling was condemned in Brahmanical and Buddhist teaching alike. The theory is plausible and cannot be proved. What can be said is that every branch that leaves India, from the Persian chatrang onward, is dice-free, that dice chess in India is attested alongside rather than before dice-free chess, and that the deterministic version is the one that took root everywhere. Whether the dice were removed or never present in the two-handed game is one of the genuine open questions of the field, and confident assertions in either direction outrun the evidence.

sections.heading: Rival Origin Theories and the China Problem
sections.body: The Indian origin is the mainstream position, but it is a position rather than a certainty, and the alternatives deserve a fair hearing because the strongest of them exposes a real gap. The Chinese case rests on xiangqi, the Chinese game, which differs from chess in ways that are hard to explain as mere drift. Its pieces stand on the intersections rather than in the cells; a river divides the board; the king is confined to a nine-point palace and may never leave it; and it has a cannon that moves like a chariot but must leap over exactly one intervening piece to capture, a move found nowhere in the Indian family. Some scholars, notably the amateur historian David Li, have argued for a Chinese invention centuries before the Indian evidence, attaching the game to the Han general Han Xin around 200 BCE. That specific claim has no support in contemporary sources and is not accepted. But a weaker and more serious version of the Chinese argument points out that a term xiangqi appears in a Northern Zhou text of 569 CE, roughly contemporary with the earliest Indian evidence, and that the earliest xiangqi may have been an independent development from Chinese divination or race games. The counterargument is that the 569 reference almost certainly describes an astronomical or cosmological game, that xiangqi in its recognisable form is attested only from the Tang and Song periods, and that the cannon cannot predate the military use of gunpowder artillery in China, which puts it no earlier than about the tenth century. The most economical reading is that chess reached China from India or Central Asia and was extensively remodelled onto a native board idiom. A Persian origin has occasionally been proposed, but the Persian sources themselves insist the game came from India, and a culture does not usually credit a foreign country with its own invention. Attempts to find chess in ancient Egypt, Greece or Mesopotamia founder on the fact that the games actually excavated from those cultures, senet, the Royal Game of Ur, petteia and latrunculi, are race games or capture games with uniform pieces and none has the defining features of chess: differentiated piece powers and a royal piece whose capture ends the game. The honest summary is that chess appears in the sixth century in India, that no earlier attestation anywhere has withstood examination, that the transmission chain from India through Persia to the Arabs to Europe is documented at every link, and that the East Asian branch is probably but not certainly a further branch of the same tree. It is worth adding that nothing about the Indian attribution is nationally flattering to the scholars who established it, most of whom were nineteenth and early twentieth century Europeans working from Arabic and Persian manuscripts; they followed their sources to India because the sources pointed there, which is a mild but real argument that the conclusion is not an artefact of anyone's patriotism.

sections.heading: Transmission to Persia: Chatrang and the Shahnameh
sections.body: The first branch out of India ran west to the Sasanian empire of Persia, where the game was called chatrang, a straightforward Middle Persian borrowing of the Sanskrit name. The transfer is usually placed in the sixth century, and the Persian court took to it thoroughly enough that chess appears in royal instruction manuals as a princely accomplishment alongside riding, archery, hunting and polo. The Persians preserved chaturanga's structure exactly. The board, the sixteen pieces a side, the powers of chariot, horse, king and foot soldier, and the object of the game all crossed unchanged. What changed were the names, and those names are the ones that ultimately reached Europe: raja became shah, king; mantri became farzin, the wise man or counsellor; gaja became pil, elephant; ashva became asp, horse; ratha became rukh, a word whose exact original sense is disputed but which most probably meant chariot; and padati became piyadeh, foot soldier. Practically every European chess word is a corruption of one of these six. The Persian literary tradition preserved an origin story that is worth knowing precisely because it is not history. In the Chatrang-namag, and later in far more elaborate verse in Firdawsi's Shahnameh, completed around 1010, an Indian raja sends the game to Khosrow Anushirvan as a challenge: work out how these pieces move within a set time, or acknowledge our superiority and pay tribute. The court is baffled until the vizier Wuzurgmihr, called Bozorgmehr in the later Persian, deduces the rules in three days by reasoning from the pieces' military identities. He then invents a second game, nard, essentially backgammon, carries it to India, and the Indian sages fail to solve it, so tribute flows the other way. The tale is a piece of courtly propaganda about Persian intellectual superiority, and its details are not reliable. Its historical value lies in its unhesitating assumption that chess is Indian and backgammon Persian, which is exactly what an origin legend written near the events would be expected to get right even while inventing everything else. The Shahnameh also carries a separate and much longer Indian origin story, in which two half-brothers, Gav and Talhand, contest a throne; Talhand dies on the battlefield without a wound, and their grieving mother is shown the events on a board so she can understand how her son fell. It is a beautiful story and pure fiction, but it captures something true about the game's early reception: chess was understood from the beginning as a model of a real battle, a device for reasoning about war rather than merely a diversion. The Persian phase of the game's life lasted barely a century before the Arab conquest swallowed the Sasanian state, but it was decisive out of all proportion to its length, because it was in Persian hands that the Sanskrit vocabulary was translated into the words that every later culture would inherit, and because Persian courtly prestige is what made chess a game a conquering elite wanted to learn rather than one it wanted to suppress.

sections.heading: Shatranj: The Arabic Game and Its Golden Age
sections.body: The Arab conquest of the Sasanian empire in the 630s and 640s brought chess into the Islamic world, where it acquired the name shatranj, an Arabic reshaping of chatrang forced by the absence of a hard g in Arabic. Within two centuries it had become the object of the most sophisticated body of technical game literature produced anywhere before the modern era, and almost everything specific that is known about how the ancestral game was actually played comes from these Arabic books rather than from Indian or Persian sources. The rules the Arabs received were chaturanga's, with the pieces renamed once more: shah, firzan or firz for the counsellor, fil for the elephant, faras for the horse, rukhkh for the chariot and baidaq for the foot soldier. The firzan stepped one cell diagonally; the fil leapt two diagonally over any obstruction, reaching only eight cells of the sixty-four; the baidaq promoted only to firzan. Practical evaluations survive: a rukhkh was reckoned worth roughly a firzan and two baidaqs, a faras somewhat more than a fil, and a fil barely more than a baidaq. Because the strongest piece was a rook and the second strongest a knight, and because no piece could cross the board quickly on a diagonal, the game was slow. Contact between the armies took many moves to establish, and material advantages were converted by patient manoeuvre rather than by combination. Two consequences shaped the literature. First, opening play was formalised into ta'biyat, standard arrays that each side built up independently over the first dozen or so moves without interference, because there was no way to strike quickly enough to prevent them. Named formations such as the Mujannah, the Sayyal and the Mashaikhi were memorised as complete pictures rather than as move sequences, which is the exact opposite of modern opening theory. Second, since real games were long and hard to teach from, masters composed mansubat, artificial positions with a forced win to be found, usually a mate in a specified small number of moves. Hundreds survive, and many are elegant by any standard. The names of the great players are known. Al-Adli ar-Rumi, active around 840, wrote the first known Arabic chess book, classified players into five grades of strength, and was famously defeated before the caliph al-Mutawakkil by ar-Razi, an event treated as a title match. Abu Bakr as-Suli, who died in 946, was so dominant that 'to play like as-Suli' remained an idiom for supreme skill in Persian for centuries; his own book and that of his pupil al-Lajlaj, 'the stammerer', survive only in later copies and quotations. Legal and religious opinion on the game was divided, with jurists variously permitting it if no wagering, no neglect of prayer and no bad language attended it, or forbidding it outright, and this ambivalence recurs everywhere chess travels.

sections.heading: The Routes into Europe and the Renaming of the Pieces
sections.body: Chess entered Europe by at least three doors more or less simultaneously in the tenth and eleventh centuries. The broadest was Islamic Spain, al-Andalus, from which the game passed into Christian Iberia and thence to France; the second was Muslim Sicily and the trading cities of Italy; the third was Byzantium, where the game was called zatrikion, and the Rus trade routes north through the Caspian and Volga into Scandinavia. There may have been a fourth, more diffuse route through pilgrim and crusader contact in the Levant. The multiplicity of doors explains why European chess terminology is a mongrel and why early European rules varied so much from region to region. The earliest firm European evidence is a Latin poem, the Versus de scachis, in a manuscript from the monastery of Einsiedeln in Switzerland, dated to the late tenth century, which describes the pieces and already calls the counsellor regina, queen. A will of 1008 by Count Ermengol I of Urgell in Catalonia bequeaths his chess pieces to a convent, which tells us both that sets were valuable and that ecclesiastical objections were not universal. The famous Lewis chessmen, carved from walrus ivory in Norway or Iceland around 1150 to 1200 and found in the Outer Hebrides, show the game fully naturalised at the far northern edge of Europe, with the pieces reimagined as a Norse court complete with berserkers biting their shields. The renaming is a study in creative misunderstanding. Islamic sets were usually abstract, because figurative representation was discouraged, so a European receiving one had shapes without meanings and supplied his own. Fil, the elephant, entered Spanish as alfil and Old French as aufin, neither of which meant anything; French speakers heard fou, fool or jester, and English speakers looked at a cleft-topped abstract piece and saw a bishop's mitre. Rukhkh became roc and rook, and the abstract wedge shape was read as a fortress tower, giving the castle of every modern set, though the piece had been a chariot for five hundred years. Firzan became alferza and fers, then was reinterpreted as the lady standing beside the king, becoming regina, dame and queen. Baidaq became pedes, peon and pawn, correctly preserving the sense of foot soldier. Europe also chequered the board, introduced light and dark armies in place of red and green, and produced a vast moralising literature, above all the Liber de moribus of Jacobus de Cessolis around 1300, in which each piece stands for a social estate with its duties, a sermon that became one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages.
