One further European borrowing deserves notice because it is invisible to modern players: naming the two sides white and black, rather than red and green as in India and much of the Islamic world, arrives with the chequered board, and it is the reason every subsequent European diagram, problem and opening book takes colour as a fundamental category of the game when the ancestral rules never referred to it at all.

sections.heading: The Mad Queen Revolution of the 1470s
sections.body: For roughly nine hundred years chess changed only at the margins. Then, in the last quarter of the fifteenth century, in a span of perhaps two decades, two pieces were given enormously greater powers and the game was transformed into the one played today. The counsellor, by then the queen, gained the combined movement of rook and bishop, going from the weakest piece but one to by far the strongest. The elephant, by then the bishop, exchanged its two-cell leap for unlimited diagonal movement. Foot soldiers gained an optional double step from their starting rank, with en passant capture introduced to stop that double step evading an enemy pawn's guard, and promotion to any piece, which meant in practice promotion to a queen. The king's various leaps and privileges were consolidated into castling over the following century. The change appears first in Valencia, in the kingdom of Aragon. The earliest document showing the new moves is a Catalan poem, Scachs d'amor, written by Francesc de Castellvi, Bernat Fenollar and Narcis de Vinyoles, generally dated to about 1475, in which a complete game is played out as an allegory of courtship with the modern queen already in force. The new game spread through Italy and France within a generation, and the Spanish books of Lucena in 1497 and Damiano in 1512 and Ruy Lopez in 1561 codified it. Contemporaries called it scacchi alla rabiosa, chess of the mad queen, or the game of the lady, and the old game persisted alongside it for decades before dying out. Why it happened is not settled. The most substantial argument, advanced by the Spanish historian Ricardo Calvo and developed by Marilyn Yalom, connects the empowered queen to the reign of Isabella I of Castile, crowned in 1474, a monarch who ruled in her own right and led armies, at the precise place and moment the change is first attested. It is a striking coincidence and may be more than one, but it cannot be demonstrated. A simpler and complementary explanation is purely ludic: shatranj was slow, players had experimented for centuries with house rules speeding it up, including a queen allowed one long leap, and the chequered European board made long diagonals legible for the first time. The effect on the game was total. Mating attacks became possible within a dozen moves, opening theory became about contesting the centre rather than building formations in peace, promotion became decisive, and the endgame acquired a completely different theory. Everything a modern player recognises as chess strategy dates from after this change; the fifteen preceding centuries produced a different game with the same pieces. It is also the last change of comparable scale. Everything since, the standardisation of castling, the abolition of the bare-king win, the settling of stalemate as a draw in the nineteenth century, and the Staunton pattern of pieces adopted in 1849, has been housekeeping by comparison.

sections.heading: The Eastern Children: Xiangqi, Shogi, Makruk and Sittuyin
sections.body: Chess travelling east produced games that diverged far more than the western branch, because they met board conventions and military realities quite unlike India's. Chinese xiangqi, the elephant game, is played on the intersections of a nine-by-ten grid rather than in the cells, an idiom borrowed from weiqi, the game known in the West as go. A blank horizontal band, the river, crosses the middle. The general, the king's equivalent, is confined to a three-by-three palace and may never leave it, though the two generals may never face each other along an open file, a rule that produces beautiful tactics. Advisers move one point diagonally within the palace, elephants move two points diagonally without leaping and cannot cross the river, and soldiers gain the ability to move sideways once across it. The chariot is the familiar rook and the horse the familiar knight, except that the horse can be blocked by a piece adjacent to it, a restriction absent everywhere west of China. The distinctive piece is the cannon, which moves as a chariot but can capture only by leaping exactly one intervening piece of either colour, and it cannot predate gunpowder artillery. Xiangqi is today probably the most played member of the family by absolute numbers. Japanese shogi arrived, most likely through Korea, by the eleventh century, and made one alteration so radical that it changes the entire character of play: captured pieces change sides and may be dropped back onto the board as reinforcements on a later turn. That single rule, standard by the sixteenth century, removes the exchange-and-simplify logic that dominates chess, makes draws vanishingly rare, and keeps material on the board from beginning to end. Shogi is played on nine by nine with flat wedge-shaped pieces bearing written names, promotion is achieved by entering the last three ranks and flipping the piece to reveal a second inscription, and the historical Japanese tradition also produced enormous variants, including a twenty-five by twenty-five board with hundreds of pieces. Thai makruk and Cambodian ouk chatrang preserve the medieval game more faithfully than European chess does. The counsellor still steps one cell diagonally, the elephant moves one cell diagonally or one straight forward, and foot soldiers start on the third rank and promote on the sixth, all of which produce games that a tenth-century Baghdad master would recognise immediately. Burmese sittuyin adds a unique opening phase in which the pawns are placed on fixed squares and then each player arranges his remaining pieces anywhere behind his own pawn line, alternately, so that no two games begin identically and opening theory in the European sense cannot exist. Mongolian shatar, Tibetan chandaraki and the chess of Ethiopia, senterej, each keep their own local rules about promotion, opening and the conditions for victory. Taken together the family shows what the ancestral game must have been like: everywhere the chariot and the horse are unchanged, and everywhere else the local culture rewrote what it wished.

sections.heading: Strategy in the Ancestral Game
sections.body: A modern club player dropped into a game of chaturanga or shatranj usually loses, and loses to principles rather than to blunders, because most modern strategic instinct is calibrated to piece powers that do not exist here. Understanding the ancestral game on its own terms takes deliberate unlearning. The first adjustment is tempo. Nothing crosses the board quickly except the chariots, and there are only two of them a side. Bringing an elephant from its home cell into contact with the enemy takes several moves and, because it is locked to eight cells, it may never be relevant at all. The consequence is that the opening cannot be fought over; both sides get to build whatever formation they choose. Development in the modern sense, racing to activate pieces before the opponent does, buys almost nothing, and time spent on it is time not spent on the structure that will actually decide the game. The second adjustment is that the foot soldiers matter more than anything else. Since promotion yields only a counsellor, worth about a soldier and a half, a passed soldier is not the winning weapon it is today, but soldiers are a large fraction of the total force, and the shape of the soldier chain determines which cells the short-range pieces can ever reach. Soldier structure in the ancestral game is closer in importance to what modern players call pawn structure in a closed position, permanently, in every game. Exchanging soldiers carelessly opens files for the chariots, which is often the only way either side can generate real threats. The third is that the counsellor is a defensive piece, not an attacking one. The standard practice in shatranj was to keep the firzan adjacent to the shah as a shield, because a king with a counsellor beside him on the correct colour is far harder to mate than a bare one. Trading counsellors was generally good for the side with the initiative and bad for the defender. The fourth is that the two supplementary victory conditions govern the endgame. Because a lone king against a king and knight, or against a king and elephant, cannot be mated, the bare-king rule is what converts a material advantage into a result, and this means that in the late stages both sides count remaining men rather than evaluating attacking chances. Endgame technique in the mansubat literature consists largely of forced mating nets constructed with chariot and horse, since nothing else has the power to deliver mate against a defended king. A player used to promoting a pawn and winning has to learn instead to hunt the last enemy piece. The overall texture that results is closer to a siege than to a duel. Advantages accumulate slowly, are rarely reversed by a single tactical shot, and are cashed in over dozens of moves, which is why the medieval literature is so much richer in composed problems than in annotated games: the interesting moment in a real shatranj game is often only two or three moves long, and the rest is preparation.

sections.heading: Playing Chaturanga Today: A Practical Reconstruction
sections.body: Chaturanga can be played tonight with an ordinary chess set, and doing so teaches more about the ancestral game in one evening than any amount of reading. What follows is the standard scholarly reconstruction, which is really the documented shatranj of the tenth century used as a proxy for the undocumented Indian original. Where the sources disagree, the alternatives are flagged so that a group can settle them before starting. Expect games to run long: sixty to a hundred moves is normal, and the first contact between the armies may not happen until move fifteen. The two changes that feel strangest are that a promoted soldier becomes a nearly worthless piece and that capturing the opponent's last man wins outright, which together make the endgame about extermination rather than promotion.
ingredients: A standard chess set and board. The board's chequering is anachronistic but harmless; ignore the colours entirely, since no rule in the ancestral game refers to them.
Two markers, coins or reversed pawns, to identify the queens as counsellors and remind both players that they step one cell diagonally only.

Optionally, paper labels reading chariot, horse, elephant, counsellor, king and foot soldier, taped to the pieces for the first few games. The renaming genuinely helps, because a bishop's shape pulls a modern player toward the modern move.
Pencil and paper for a running count of each side's remaining men, which matters for the bare-king win.
A written copy of the rule changes, kept between the players, since every one of them will be forgotten at least once.
steps: Set up as for modern chess: rooks in the corners as chariots, knights beside them as horses, bishops beside those as elephants, and the king and queen on the two central cells, with the kings facing each other on the same file and therefore the counsellors also facing each other.

Agree the elephant's move before the first move is played. The default is a leap of exactly two cells diagonally, jumping over any occupying piece, so an elephant can reach only eight cells all game. The main alternative, from the Thai tradition, is one cell diagonally in any direction or one cell straight forward.
Play the chariot, horse and king exactly as the modern rook, knight and king. Remove castling entirely; there is none.
Play the counsellor as one cell diagonally in any of the four diagonal directions, and nothing more.
Play foot soldiers one cell straight forward, capturing one cell diagonally forward. Allow no initial double step and therefore no en passant capture.
Promote a foot soldier reaching the far rank to a counsellor, and to nothing else, even if a counsellor is already on the board.

Win by checkmate; by capturing every enemy piece other than the king, which is called baring the king; or, by agreement before play, by stalemating the opponent. If a bared player can bare the opponent on the immediate reply, declare the game drawn.

Record the game, and afterwards count how many moves passed before the first capture. Comparing that number with a modern game is the quickest demonstration of what the fifteenth-century rule changes did.

sections.heading: What We Still Do Not Know
sections.body: A responsible account of chaturanga ends by marking the edges of what is actually known, because the popular literature on chess origins is unusually full of confident claims that dissolve on inspection. The date and place of invention are inferred, not recorded. Nobody knows who invented chaturanga, in what decade, or in which kingdom. The sixth-century northern Indian attribution rests on two literary allusions and a Persian legend, and a single new find, an inscription, a dated set, an unambiguous manuscript, could move it a century in either direction. The elephant's original move is genuinely unknown, with three candidates each surviving in a living tradition. Whether dice were originally used is unknown. Whether the game was invented at a stroke by an individual, as the legends insist, or assembled gradually from features of existing race and battle games, as most historians suspect, is unknown and probably unknowable. Several specific claims should be treated with suspicion whenever encountered. Any dating of chess before roughly 500 CE has no evidentiary support. The story of the inventor who asked for one grain of wheat on the first square and doubling thereafter is a mathematical parable of Arabic and Persian literary origin, not a record; the total, two to the sixty-fourth power minus one grains, about eighteen and a half quintillion, is a fine illustration of exponential growth and no evidence about anything. Claims that a particular ancient artefact is a chess piece should be checked against the criterion that distinguishes chess from every other early board game, namely differentiated piece powers, which a lump of carved stone cannot demonstrate on its own. Several supposedly ancient sets in museum and private collections are of uncertain or contested date. There is also a scholarly hazard in the other direction. H. J. R. Murray's History of Chess of 1913 is so comprehensive and so well argued that it has functioned for over a century as the final word, and later work by Ricardo Calvo, Yuri Averbakh and others has revised parts of it, particularly on the European transmission and on the queen's transformation. Citing Murray is sound; treating him as unrevisable is not. None of this uncertainty undermines the central claim. The chain from an Indian sixth-century game, through Sasanian Persia, through the Arabic world, into Europe and separately into East Asia, is documented at every link by contemporaries who name their sources, and no rival account explains the vocabulary, the shared piece powers and the geographic distribution nearly as well. Chess came from India. Almost everything more specific than that is a reconstruction, and should be held accordingly. For a reader who wants to test any new claim about chess origins, three questions do most of the work: does the evidence describe pieces with different powers, or merely differently shaped counters; is the dating of the source itself secure, or does it rest on the traditional date of a text that survives only in much later copies; and does the claim explain the vocabulary, which is the hardest thing for a false origin story to fake.

guides.title: Shatranj and the Medieval Chess Ancestors
guides.summary: The chess played across the Islamic world and medieval Europe for nearly a thousand years before the queen and bishop were given their modern powers: its pieces and rules, its openings, endgames and masters, how it travelled, and how to play it today with an ordinary chess set.

sections.heading: The Thousand-Year Game Nobody Plays Any More
sections.body:
Modern chess is roughly five hundred and fifty years old. The game it replaced is older, was played over a far wider geographical area, and lasted considerably longer. Shatranj, the form of chess played across Persia, the Arab world, Central Asia, North Africa, Muslim Spain and eventually much of Christian Europe, dominated from roughly the seventh century until the last decades of the fifteenth. It produced the first chess literature, the first named masters, the first tournaments and rankings, the first recorded games and the first composed problems. Almost everything people think of as the deep history of chess is in fact the history of shatranj.

The differences from the modern game are not cosmetic. Two of the pieces moved so weakly that whole categories of modern strategy simply did not exist. The queen, or rather the counsellor who occupied that square, moved one step diagonally and nothing more. The piece on the bishop's square jumped exactly two squares diagonally, could never be blocked, and could reach only eight of the sixty-four squares on the board for the entire game. Pawns had no initial double step, so there was no en passant capture and no pawn storm as understood today. There was no castling. A promoted pawn became another one-step counsellor, which is to say it became almost worthless.

The consequence was a game of a completely different tempo and texture. With no long-range pieces except the rook, and with the two diagonal pieces reduced to near-impotence, positions developed slowly and could not be blown open. Attacks had to be constructed piece by piece over many moves. Material was hard to convert into a win, and an enormous proportion of games ended in draws or in the peculiar shatranj win by stripping the opponent of every piece. The masters accordingly wrote about endgames and about carefully memorised opening formations, because those were the phases in which the game could actually be decided.

It would be a mistake to treat this as a primitive version of something better. Shatranj was a serious, deeply studied intellectual pursuit with a professional class, a body of theory, a critical literature and a vocabulary of praise and insult that survives in Arabic and Persian sources. Its practitioners were capable of analysis that is still respected: the composed endgame studies of the tenth century remain sound today, and players of that era demonstrably calculated deep forced sequences. Understanding it also explains a great deal about the modern game, from the shape of the board and the names of the pieces to why a European bishop is called an elephant in Russian and a fool in French, and why the modern queen is the most powerful piece on a board where its ancestor was nearly the weakest.

sections.heading: Chaturanga: The Four-Limbed Army of Northern India
sections.body:
The ancestor of every game in the chess family is generally accepted to be chaturanga, which arose in northern India, most probably in the Gupta period around the sixth century of the common era. The name is Sanskrit and means having four limbs or four parts, a term already used for an army composed of infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. Those four arms map directly onto the four non-royal piece types, and it is that mapping, rather than any surviving rulebook, that gives the strongest evidence for the origin. A game whose pieces are named after the divisions of an Indian army, played on a board already used in India for other games, is most economically explained as Indian.

The board was the ashtapada, an eight by eight grid known in India well before chess and used for race games played with dice. Early ashtapada boards carry decorative crossed markings on certain squares, which appear to have had a function in those earlier games and no function in chess; their survival on chess boards is a fossil, and the modern chequered light and dark pattern is a much later European innovation, first clearly attested around the eleventh century. Before that, boards were plain.

Direct evidence for the earliest rules is thin, and honest treatments say so. There is no surviving Indian rule text from the sixth or seventh century. What exists are literary allusions, later texts, and the strong inference backward from the Persian and Arabic forms, which are well documented and which the Indian game clearly resembles. The most cited early reference is in the Harshacharita, a Sanskrit biography written by Bana around the middle of the seventh century, which contains a pun on ashtapada and on the word for elephants in a passage praising a peaceful reign. Slightly earlier or contemporary references appear in Persian and Middle Persian sources.

A persistent and unresolved question is whether chaturanga was originally a game for four players using dice, sometimes called chaturaji, with two allied pairs. Some later Indian texts describe such a game, and the nineteenth-century orientalist Duncan Forbes argued strongly that the four-handed dice game came first and the two-player game was a later refinement. Most modern historians, following Harold Murray's monumental History of Chess of 1913 and the later work of Ricardo Calvo and others, reject that sequence and treat the four-handed version as a later Indian derivative of the two-player game. The evidence genuinely does not settle it, and anyone who states the answer confidently is overstating the case. What is not in doubt is that a two-player, diceless, eight by eight game with a king, a counsellor, elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers existed in India and reached Persia by the sixth century.

sections.heading: Chatrang and Shatranj: The Persian Bridge
sections.body:
The game entered the Persian-speaking world under the Sasanian empire, where it was called chatrang, a direct borrowing of the Sanskrit chaturanga. When Arabic speakers adopted it after the Islamic conquests of the seventh century they adapted the word to their own phonology: Arabic has neither the ch sound nor the word-final g, so chatrang became shatranj. That single sound change is a fingerprint of the transmission route, and it is repeated across the vocabulary of the game.

The most colourful Persian source is the Chatrang-namak, the Explanation of Chess, a short Middle Persian text probably composed between the seventh and ninth centuries but describing events at the court of Khosrow the First, who reigned from 531 to 579. In it an Indian king sends the game to the Persian court as a challenge, with the demand that the Persians work out its rules or pay tribute. The vizier Wuzurgmihr solves it, then invents the game of nard, a backgammon ancestor, and sends it back to India, where nobody can solve his puzzle in turn. The story is legend rather than history, but it is early, it is Persian, and it consistently points to India as the source, which is meaningful testimony from a culture that had no reason to give credit away.

Persian also supplied the vocabulary that the whole world eventually inherited. Shah means king. The declaration shah, meaning the king is attacked, became check in English, echec in French, scacco in Italian, Schach in German. Shah mat, usually rendered the king is helpless or the king is ambushed, became checkmate. The precise sense of mat is debated: the common gloss the king is dead is probably wrong, since the Persian and Arabic root carries a sense of being defeated, stupefied or without resource, and the point of chess is precisely that the king is never actually captured. The word rukh, the chariot, survives directly as rook.

Under the Abbasid caliphate, and especially in Baghdad in the ninth and tenth centuries, shatranj became an object of systematic study. This was the same intellectual environment that produced major work in mathematics, astronomy and medicine, and chess was treated with comparable seriousness: written treatises, formal analysis, a notation for recording positions, classification of openings, composition of problems, and a graded ranking of players. There was some religious controversy about whether the game was permissible, turning on whether it involved gambling, whether it distracted from prayer and whether the pieces constituted images; the general resolution among jurists was that chess played without stakes and without neglecting religious duty was acceptable, though opinions differed and still do. The game travelled with the caliphate: by the tenth century it was played from Transoxiana and the Iranian plateau to Egypt, Ifriqiya and al-Andalus, and a player from Baghdad could sit down opposite one from Cordoba and need to agree almost nothing before starting.

sections.heading: The Board, the Array and the Look of the Pieces
sections.body:
Shatranj is played on an eight by eight board of sixty-four squares, and the initial array is almost identical to the modern one. Along each player's back rank stand, from the corner inward, the rukh or chariot, the faras or horse, the fil or elephant, and then the two royal pieces, with the mirror image completing the rank. In front of them stands a full rank of eight baidaq, foot soldiers. Anyone who can set up a modern chess board can set up a shatranj board without learning anything new, which is one reason the game is easy to revive.

There is one detail that differs and it catches people out. In shatranj there is no requirement that the counsellor stand on its own colour, and no convention that the two kings face each other on the same file. Sources indicate the two players simply placed the king and counsellor as they wished within the two central squares, provided both did the same, or in some traditions placed them oppositely. Because the counsellor is a one-step diagonal mover it is permanently confined to squares of one colour, so whether the two counsellors share a colour or not materially changes the game: on the same colour they can meet and oppose each other, on opposite colours they can never interact at all for the whole game.

The board itself was normally unchequered. The alternating light and dark pattern that now seems inseparable from chess is a European contribution appearing around the eleventh century, and it makes the diagonal moves far easier to read, which may be one small reason European play developed as it did. Islamic boards were plain, sometimes with the ashtapada markings inherited from India.

The pieces themselves were usually abstract. Islamic tradition generally discouraged representational sculpture, so the shatranj sets that survive are small turned or carved forms in ivory, wood, rock crystal or ceramic, identified by shape and by convention rather than by depiction: a knob for the king, a smaller knob for the counsellor, a cylinder with a cleft or two projections for the elephant, a form with a distinct nub for the horse, and a plain block or split cylinder for the chariot. The two projections on the elephant piece represented tusks, and the cleft or notch on the chariot piece is the ancestor of the crenellations on the modern rook, which is why the modern rook looks like a tower despite being named after a chariot. Simple abstract sets of this kind spread with the game and were still in use in Europe alongside the more famous figurative sets. The Lewis chessmen, a hoard of walrus ivory pieces found on the Isle of Lewis in Scotland and usually dated to the second half of the twelfth century and attributed to Norwegian workshops, are the most celebrated figurative survival, and they show a European game already thoroughly at home: seated kings and queens, bishops with crosiers, and berserker warders biting their shields.

sections.heading: The Pieces and Exactly How They Moved
sections.body:
Three of the six shatranj pieces move exactly as their modern counterparts do, and three do not. Learning the three differences is the whole of learning the game.

The shah, the king, moves one square in any of the eight directions, exactly as the modern king. It may not move into check. There is no castling of any kind; the king walks to safety if it goes anywhere at all, which takes several tempi and is a major strategic burden.

The rukh, the chariot, moves any number of unobstructed squares along a rank or file, exactly as the modern rook. It is by a wide margin the most powerful piece on the board, and in a game where nothing else has long-range mobility it dominates in a way the modern rook does not. Reasonable modern estimates of relative value put the rook at around five points and everything else far below.

The faras or asb, the horse, moves in the familiar extended L, two squares along one axis then one square perpendicular, jumping over anything in between. It is identical to the modern knight and is, in shatranj, the second most valuable piece and often the most dangerous attacker, worth something in the region of three points. Because the two diagonal pieces are so weak, knight play carries a much larger share of the game's tactical content than it does today.

The firzan, also written firz or fers and meaning counsellor or wise man, moves exactly one square diagonally in any direction. That is its entire repertoire. It cannot move straight, cannot move two squares, and is permanently bound to squares of a single colour. It is worth roughly one and a half to two points, comparable to a pawn or slightly better, and it functions as a short-range defender of the king and as a blockading piece rather than as an attacker. This is the piece that stood where the modern queen stands.

The fil or alfil, the elephant, moves exactly two squares diagonally, always two, never one, and it jumps: an intervening piece on the square between does not block it. It cannot capture the piece it jumps over. This is the weakest and strangest piece in the game.

The baidaq, the foot soldier, moves one square straight forward and captures one square diagonally forward, exactly as a modern pawn does. It has no initial double-step option, so there is no en passant capture. On reaching the eighth rank it promotes, and it can promote only to a firzan. Since a firzan is worth barely more than the pawn that became it, promotion is a modest gain rather than the game-deciding transformation it is today, and this single rule is responsible for much of the character of shatranj endgames.

sections.heading: The Elephant Problem: A Piece Trapped on Eight Squares
sections.body:
The alfil deserves separate treatment because it is the most alien feature of the game and because working out its consequences teaches more about shatranj than any amount of description. Because it always moves exactly two squares diagonally, an alfil starting on a given square can only ever reach squares of the same colour that are an even number of steps away along both diagonals. Work through the reachable set and it comes to precisely eight squares out of sixty-four, including its starting square. Each alfil is locked in its own little lattice for the entire game.

Several consequences follow immediately. The four alfils on the board, two per side, occupy four distinct lattices, and no alfil can ever attack, defend, capture or be captured by any of the other three. They pass through the game as though the other three did not exist. Two alfils belonging to the same player likewise cover disjoint sets of squares, so they cannot support one another. Because it jumps, an alfil can never be blocked, which is its one virtue: it can slip out of a crowded position and it can defend a square through a wall of pawns.

The valuation follows. Modern reconstructions typically put the alfil at around one and a half points, similar to the firzan and roughly on a par with a pawn, and some analysts rate it below a pawn in many positions. It cannot deliver mate. It cannot control a diagonal. It cannot participate in most of the board. As-Suli and other classical authors treated the loss of an alfil as a minor matter and were willing to give one away as odds to a weaker player.

The strategic effect on the whole game is profound. With both diagonal pieces reduced to short, colour-bound movers, the diagonals are effectively unpoliced by anything long-range. Pawn chains cannot be attacked at their base by a bishop. Positions cannot be prised open, because there is nothing waiting to exploit the opening. Fianchetto ideas, long diagonal batteries, the entire modern concept of bishop pair advantage and the good-bishop-versus-bad-bishop distinction are all meaningless. What remains is rook play along files, knight manoeuvring, and slow pawn advances supported by the king and counsellor.

It is worth pausing on how thoroughly this shaped play. The reason shatranj games are slow is not that medieval players were unsophisticated but that the pieces genuinely could not generate fast attacks. When the alfil became the modern bishop and the firzan became the modern queen in the late fifteenth century, the same board and the same array suddenly permitted a mate in four moves from the opening position, and the entire accumulated theory of eight centuries became obsolete almost at once.

sections.heading: Winning, Losing and the Peculiar Bare King
sections.body:
Shatranj recognised more ways to win than modern chess does, and the extra ones exist because checkmate was genuinely hard to achieve with such weak pieces.

Checkmate, shah mat, worked exactly as it does now: the king is attacked and there is no legal move that ends the attack, and the game is over at once. The king is never actually captured. This has been constant throughout the game's history and across every branch of the family.

The distinctive shatranj addition is the bare king, in Arabic often rendered as stripping. If a player captures every one of the opponent's pieces and pawns, leaving only the lone king on the board, that player wins. This is not a technicality; it is a routine and frequently pursued objective, and it exists for the obvious practical reason that a lone king cannot be mated by many of the material combinations that shatranj commonly produced. There is an important qualification recorded in the sources: if the opponent can immediately bare the other king in reply, on the very next move, the game is a draw rather than a win. Some traditions treat that reciprocal case slightly differently, which is a reminder that shatranj rules were never universally codified and varied by region and century.

Stalemate is where the sources become genuinely awkward, and it is worth being candid rather than tidy. In the Arabic shatranj tradition, a player who has no legal move is generally reckoned to have lost, which is the reverse of the modern rule that stalemate is a draw. Medieval Europe was wildly inconsistent on this point. Different regions at different times treated stalemate as a win for the stalemating player, as a draw, as a half-win, or as a loss for the player who delivered it; that last, counterintuitive convention persisted in England into the eighteenth century, and was only settled toward the modern draw in the nineteenth. Anyone organising a game today simply has to pick a convention and state it before starting.

There was also a form of resignation by perpetual check, and the general recognition of a drawn game when neither side could make progress, though without anything like the modern fifty-move rule or threefold repetition, which are much later administrative inventions.

The combined effect of these rules is a game whose endgames are dominated by a question that barely arises today: can you actually force mate with what you have left? A king and rook mates comfortably. A king and knight cannot mate at all. A king and firzan cannot mate. A king and two alfils cannot mate. Whole classes of material advantage that would be trivially winning in modern chess are, in shatranj, insufficient, and the bare-king rule exists precisely to give those advantages some way of paying off.

sections.heading: Ta'biyat: Opening Formations Reached Without Contact
sections.body:
The most alien feature of shatranj practice to a modern player is its treatment of the opening. Because every piece except the rook moved slowly and short, and because pawns had no double step, the two armies could not come into contact for a considerable number of moves. Estimates vary with the formation but something in the region of ten to fifteen moves each could be played before any capture was possible. That meant a player could choose an arrangement of pieces and simply build it, without interference, regardless of what the opponent did.

These prepared arrangements were called ta'biyat, a word meaning battle arrays or dispositions, and they were the subject of serious study. Rather than analysing move orders, as modern opening theory does, the literature catalogued target positions and argued about which was strongest and which was strong against which. Named formations recorded in the Arabic sources include the Sayyal, the torrent, the Mujannah, the flanked or winged array, and the Mashaikhi, the sheikh's array, among others whose identifications and exact configurations are debated among historians because the surviving diagrams and descriptions are sometimes ambiguous.

The strategic logic behind them is coherent and recognisable. A good ta'biya typically placed pawns on mutually defending squares to make a chain that the slow pieces could not easily break, kept the alfils on squares from which their eight-square lattices covered useful entry points, developed the knights toward the centre where their mobility was greatest, arranged the rooks on open or half-open files, and tucked the king behind a solid pawn shelter with the firzan alongside as a bodyguard. Since there was no castling, that last job took several moves and was one of the main things the opening was for.

What did not exist was any concept of fighting for the initiative in the opening, or of gambits, or of development tempo in the modern sense, because there was no way to punish a slow set-up. If your opponent spent twelve moves building a formation, you spent twelve moves building yours. The competitive question was not who got there first but whose completed structure was better suited to the middlegame that followed, and whether you had correctly anticipated which structure your opponent would build.

This has an interesting historical consequence. Because ta'biyat were fixed positions rather than move sequences, shatranj opening theory was essentially a catalogue of good shapes, transmitted by diagram. When the pieces were strengthened in the fifteenth century the entire catalogue became worthless overnight, since any of those leisurely twelve-move set-ups would now be demolished long before completion. The modern discipline of opening theory, concerned with concrete move orders and tempo, had to be invented from nothing, and largely was, by Spanish and Italian writers in the sixteenth century.

sections.heading: The Middlegame and Endgame: A Game of Slow Manoeuvre
sections.body:
Once the formations were complete and contact was made, shatranj became a game of patient manoeuvring in which small advantages accumulated slowly and were rarely decisive on their own. The dominant strategic assets are easy to list. Rooks on open files are enormously valuable, since the rook is the only piece with reach. Knights posted on strong central squares, where they cannot be driven away by pawns, are the principal attacking force. Advanced and connected pawns matter, both because they cramp the opponent and because they threaten promotion. The king is much more active than in modern chess, because there is comparatively little long-range firepower to punish it, and an aggressive king in the middlegame is normal rather than reckless.

Because material advantages converted so poorly, the game placed great weight on transitions. Exchanging into an endgame you knew was winning was the standard method of turning an advantage into a result, and this is exactly why the surviving literature is so heavily weighted toward endgame technique. A shatranj master needed to know with certainty which material combinations mated, which could only bare the king, and which were dead drawn, because the choice of which pieces to trade off depended entirely on those facts.

The essential endgame knowledge is compact enough to state. King and rook against king mates, by the same driving technique used today. King, rook and anything against a lone king mates. King and knight against king cannot mate. King and firzan against king cannot mate. King and two alfils against king cannot mate, and neither can king, alfil and firzan in general. King and two knights cannot force mate, exactly as in modern chess. King and pawn against king turns on whether the pawn can be escorted to promotion, but promotion yields only a firzan, so king and firzan against king is a draw and the whole pawn endgame is far less rewarding than its modern equivalent. Combinations of firzan and alfil with a rook or knight give a rich and genuinely subtle body of theory.

A further consequence is that the drawn game was very common and was not regarded as a failure. Contemporary accounts of matches describe long series of games in which most were drawn and the match turned on one or two decisive results. This, together with the difficulty of forcing mate, is the practical reason for the bare-king rule and for the prevalence of odds-giving, since a strong player needed some way of creating imbalance against a weaker one when the game itself resisted decisive outcomes so stubbornly. Modern players who take up shatranj usually report the same discovery within a few games: it rewards patience, and it punishes the ingrained modern assumption that a material advantage will somehow convert itself.

sections.heading: Mansubat: The First Chess Problems
sections.body:
The richest surviving body of shatranj material is not games but composed positions, called mansubat, singular mansuba, meaning something set up or arranged. These are the direct ancestors of the modern chess problem and endgame study, and several hundred survive in Arabic manuscripts, some copied and recopied for centuries.

A mansuba presents a position, usually with a stipulation such as White to play and mate in five, and usually with a solution that is forcing, elegant and surprising. The compositional aesthetic is recognisable to any modern problemist: the solution should be unique, it should begin with a move that looks absurd, it often involves sacrificing the most valuable material available, and the point should be concealed until the last moment. Sacrificing both rooks to force a mate with a knight and an alfil is exactly the sort of thing a good mansuba does, and it works precisely because the pieces are weak enough that only a forced sequence can achieve anything.

The most celebrated is the Dilaram position, attached to a romantic legend that a player named Dilaram was the wife or slave of a nobleman who, having gambled away everything else, staked her on the game; facing mate, he was prompted by her cry to sacrifice both rooks and deliver a forced mate instead. The story is almost certainly a later attachment to an existing composition, as such stories usually are, but the position itself is genuine, old and sound, and it remains a standard demonstration piece.

Mansubat mattered for reasons beyond entertainment. They were the teaching material of the game, the medium in which technique was transmitted, and the basis of a professional practice: strong players carried a repertoire of them, wagered on solving them, and used them to demonstrate skill. Because a mansuba is a position rather than a game score, it also survives transmission far better, which is why we have hundreds of problems and very few complete games from the period.

A caution about the surviving material is warranted. Manuscripts were copied by scribes who were not necessarily players, and pieces were occasionally misplaced, stipulations garbled and solutions corrupted. Modern analysis with computers has confirmed that a substantial majority of the classical mansubat are sound, which is a striking testament to the analytical depth of tenth-century players, but it has also found a minority that are cooked, meaning they have unintended alternative solutions, or that are simply unsound as transmitted. Distinguishing a composer's error from a copyist's is often impossible. The honest position is that classical Arabic chess composition was of a very high standard and that some of what survives has been damaged in transmission.

sections.heading: The Masters: al-Adli, ar-Razi, as-Suli and al-Lajlaj
sections.body:
Shatranj had a professional elite whose names, reputations and rivalries are recorded, making them the first identifiable chess masters in history. They clustered around the Abbasid court in Baghdad in the ninth and tenth centuries, where patronage was available and where a strong player could make a living.

Al-Adli ar-Rumi, active in the middle of the ninth century, is the earliest whose work is substantially known. His Kitab ash-shatranj, the Book of Chess, is the first known systematic chess treatise. It does not survive complete, but large parts are preserved through quotation in later manuscripts, and it appears to have covered opening arrays, endgame classifications, a ranking of players and a body of problems. Al-Adli was reckoned the strongest player of his generation until, in a match before the caliph al-Mutawakkil, who reigned from 847 to 861, he was defeated by ar-Razi, an event recorded as a notable upset and one of the first documented competitive results in the history of the game.

The towering figure is Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Yahya as-Suli, who died around 946. A courtier, historian, poet and scholar as well as a player, as-Suli served several caliphs and was so completely dominant that his name entered the language: to say that someone played like as-Suli was, in Arabic, the highest available compliment for a chess player, and the phrase was still current centuries after his death. He wrote extensively on the game, systematised the study of ta'biyat and endgames, and composed problems, at least one of which was reputedly unsolved for something like a thousand years until analysed in the twentieth century. He also had a reputation for a particular kind of showmanship, playing blindfold and giving heavy odds.

His pupil Abu al-Faraj al-Muzaffar ibn Sa'id, known as al-Lajlaj, the stammerer, working in the second half of the tenth century, wrote a detailed treatise on openings that develops as-Suli's material and is one of the more substantial surviving analytical works. Later figures include Abu al-Fath Ahmad as-Sinjari and the thirteenth-century compiler generally known as the author of the Alfonso manuscripts' Arabic sources.

It is worth noting how little we can say about their actual playing strength. Modern comparisons are speculative, since we have almost no complete games and since strength in shatranj is not commensurable with strength in modern chess. What we can say is that they analysed forced sequences many moves deep, that their compositions withstand computer scrutiny, and that they built a body of theory that remained authoritative for five hundred years, which are all the marks of genuine mastery. Their names also survive largely because chess was written about by literate courtiers, so the record we have is the record of one particular social class; whatever strong players existed in the markets and caravanserais never came near a court, and are simply invisible to us.

sections.heading: Grades, Odds and the Culture of Play
sections.body:
Shatranj had a formal ranking system, which makes it one of the earliest games anywhere to have one. Players were graded into classes, with the highest, the aliyat or grandees, reserved for a very small number of acknowledged masters at any given time; below them ran a series of ordinary classes, with sources describing roughly five grades in all. The system was not merely honorific. It was tied directly to the odds a stronger player was expected to concede, which is how competitive equality was engineered in a game whose rules otherwise made decisive results scarce.

The odds ladder is a small piece of applied game design. Between adjacent classes the convention was to give a pawn; between more distant classes, a pawn and the move, or an alfil, or a knight, or in extreme cases a rook. Because piece values in shatranj were compressed and the alfil was so weak, the ladder is not the same as its modern equivalent: giving up an alfil is closer to giving up a pawn than to giving up a bishop. Odds play remained the normal way of arranging a fair contest between unequal players in Europe well into the nineteenth century, and its disappearance is a consequence of rating systems rather than of any change in the underlying logic.

Blindfold play was practised and admired. As-Suli and others are recorded as playing without sight of the board, and given the slow, structured nature of shatranj positions and the small mobility of the pieces, the feat is perhaps somewhat easier than its modern equivalent, though still remarkable. Simultaneous exhibitions and problem-solving contests are also attested.

Chess was played across social classes but was strongly associated with courts, with scholarly circles and with the educated urban professions. It appears constantly in poetry as a metaphor for fate, statecraft and the vanity of ambition, and the image of the king who is checkmated regardless of his rank is one of the standard moral figures of medieval Persian and Arabic literature, later borrowed wholesale into European writing. Women played, and are depicted playing in Persian and later Indian miniatures and in the Spanish manuscripts.

The religious debate over the game was real and was never conclusively settled. The objections turned on three points: whether it constituted maysir, gambling, which is forbidden; whether it distracted from the obligation of prayer; and whether figurative pieces were forbidden images. The mainstream resolution among many jurists was that chess played for no stake, at a time that does not displace prayer, with abstract pieces, is permissible, and that is largely why the surviving Islamic sets are abstract. Other authorities disapproved regardless, and the disagreement continues in some quarters to this day. The argument was conducted in the hadith literature and in the legal manuals at considerable length, and it is one reason so much of what survives about the early game comes to us through religious scholars rather than through players.

sections.heading: Into Europe: Routes, Names and Creative Misunderstanding
sections.body:
Shatranj reached Christian Europe by several routes at roughly the same period. The best documented is through al-Andalus, Muslim Spain, where the game was long established and from which it passed into the Christian kingdoms of the north. A second route ran through Sicily, under Muslim rule from the ninth century and then Norman from the eleventh, a famously permeable cultural frontier. A third ran through Byzantium, where the game was known as zatrikion. A fourth, less often discussed but supported by archaeological finds of early pieces, ran north from the Islamic world along the Volga trade routes into the lands of the Rus and thence to Scandinavia, which may explain why Russian retains elephant, slon, for the bishop rather than adopting a western reinterpretation.

The earliest secure European evidence clusters around the year 1000. The Versus de scachis, a Latin poem describing the game and preserved in a manuscript at the abbey of Einsiedeln in Switzerland, is usually dated to the late tenth century. The will of Count Ermengol the First of Urgell, in Catalonia, dated 1008, bequeaths his chess pieces to a monastery, which incidentally establishes both that the game was present and that a set was a valuable object. From there references multiply rapidly across the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The great compendium is the Libro de los juegos, the Book of Games, commissioned by Alfonso the Tenth of Castile and completed around 1283, which contains rules, over a hundred problems drawn substantially from Arabic sources, and superb illustrations of players of both sexes and several faiths.

What happened to the names is a study in creative misunderstanding. The Arabic al-fil, the elephant, was heard in Spain as a single word and became alfil, which it remains in Spanish. Elsewhere the unfamiliar word was reinterpreted according to local sense. Italian took it as alfiere, standard-bearer. French heard fol or fou, the fool or court jester. English and the Nordic languages made it a bishop, apparently because the abstract two-pronged piece resembled a mitre. German made it Laufer, the runner. Russian kept the elephant. The firzan or fers was similarly reshaped: the counsellor beside the king was naturally read in a European court context as the king's wife, and by the twelfth century the piece is regularly regina or queen.

Alongside the reinterpretation came a genuine Europeanisation of the game's meaning. The Liber de moribus hominum et officiis nobilium of Jacobus de Cessolis, a Dominican friar writing around 1300, turned chess into an allegory of the estates of society and became one of the most widely copied works of the later Middle Ages. Chess ceased to be an exotic import and became a European possession, which is precisely the condition under which Europeans felt free to start changing its rules.

sections.heading: The Reform of 1475 and the Sudden Death of Shatranj
sections.body:
European players had been tinkering for centuries. The pawn's initial double step appears in medieval sources well before the major reform, together with the en passant capture that exists to answer it. Various forms of the king's leap, an early move in which the king jumped two squares to get to safety, are attested from the thirteenth century onward and are the ancestor of castling. Some regions allowed the fers a single initial leap. These were incremental adjustments to a game everyone recognised as slow.

The decisive change came in Valencia, in the kingdom of Aragon, in the last quarter of the fifteenth century. The fers was given the combined powers of rook and old-style diagonal movement, becoming the modern queen, the most powerful piece on the board. The alfil was released from its two-square jump and given the full diagonal, becoming the modern bishop. The earliest firm documentary evidence is the Catalan poem Scachs d'amor, Chess of Love, dating from about 1475, which describes a game between Francesch de Castellvi and Narcis Vinyoles with Bernat Fenollar as commentator, and which is played under the new rules. The poem is both a literary conceit and a rulebook, and it is the earliest recorded game of recognisably modern chess.

The new game spread with astonishing speed and acquired names that reflect what people thought of it: in Italy scacchi de la donna and in Spain and France variations on the mad queen or the enraged queen, alla rabiosa. The speed of adoption is itself evidence of how much more exciting the reformed game was. Within a generation the first modern chess books appear, Luis Ramirez de Lucena's Repeticion de amores e arte de axedres of about 1497 and Pedro Damiano's work of 1512, followed by Ruy Lopez de Segura in 1561. Shatranj theory, accumulated over eight centuries, was obsolete.

Why Valencia, and why then, is not settled. One much discussed suggestion, argued notably by Govert Westerveld, connects the elevation of the queen to the contemporary prominence of Isabella the First of Castile, a reigning queen of exceptional political power, which is a satisfying story but circumstantial. Others emphasise a straightforwardly ludic explanation: players wanted a faster game, and a series of local experiments happened to converge on a combination that worked outstandingly well. Both may be partly right.

Shatranj did not vanish immediately everywhere. It persisted in parts of the Islamic world into the nineteenth century, and in some regions much longer, but the reformed game eventually displaced it almost universally. Its last widespread stronghold was the very tradition that had studied it most carefully. Isolated players kept the older rules alive as a curiosity, but the continuous line was broken, and the modern revival of shatranj is a scholarly and hobbyist reconstruction rather than an unbroken tradition.

sections.heading: Living Relatives: The Branches That Never Reformed
sections.body:
Chess is best understood as a family of games descended from a common ancestor, and several branches never underwent the European reform. Studying them is the closest thing available to seeing shatranj alive.

Makruk, Thai chess, is the most conservative of the widely played survivors and is in several respects closer to shatranj than anything else still in daily use. Its met, the counsellor, moves one square diagonally, exactly like a firzan. Its khon moves one square diagonally or one square straight forward, which is a slightly strengthened elephant. The pawns start on the third rank rather than the second, which removes much of the slow approach, and promote on the sixth rank to a met. The rook and knight are as in modern chess. Cambodian ouk chatrang is a close relative, with an initial leap for the king and counsellor.

Sittuyin, Burmese chess, preserves the old piece powers and adds a striking feature: the pawns are placed on fixed squares but the pieces behind them are deployed freely by each player at the start, in alternating turns, so that every game begins with an opening set-up phase. This is arguably a formalisation of exactly what the ta'biyat tradition was doing informally.

Xiangqi, Chinese chess, and its Korean cousin janggi are the great eastern branch, and the relationship to the Indian game, while generally accepted, is genuinely disputed in its details, including which direction the influence flowed. Xiangqi is played on the intersections of the lines rather than on the squares, has a river across the middle that some pieces cannot cross and a palace of nine points to which the general is confined, and includes a piece with no western counterpart at all: the cannon, which moves like a rook but must jump exactly one intervening piece in order to capture. Its elephants move two points diagonally without jumping and cannot cross the river, which makes them defensive in a way that rhymes with the alfil.

Shogi, Japanese chess, is the most divergent and the most vigorous. Its defining innovation is the drop: captured pieces change ownership and may be re-entered onto the board as a move, which means material is never permanently lost and draws are extremely rare. Almost every piece can promote on reaching the far ranks.

Finally there were medieval enlargements, of which the best documented is Tamerlane chess, shatranj al-kabir, the great chess, a ten by eleven board with an enlarged and highly differentiated set of pieces plus citadels, associated with the court of Timur around 1400. It is a reminder that the alternative to strengthening the pieces was to add more of them, and that the reformers chose the better answer.

sections.heading: Playing Shatranj Today: Setup, House Rules and Common Errors
sections.body:
Shatranj needs no special equipment. An ordinary chess set and board serve perfectly: the queen is used as the firzan and the bishops as the alfils, with the players simply agreeing to move them differently. The only real work is disciplining the reflexes, and the errors that spoil a first game are predictable enough to warn about.

The commonest by far is forgetting that the alfil jumps and moves exactly two squares, never one: players try to move it one square, and assume a piece in between blocks it. The second commonest is playing the pawn's double step out of habit, which quietly wrecks the whole opening tempo, since without it the armies genuinely cannot meet for a dozen moves. The third is attempting to castle. The fourth is promoting a pawn to a queen, which in shatranj is a rules violation rather than a strong move.

Two conventions must be agreed before starting, because the record is not consistent and a mid-game argument is worse than an arbitrary rule. The first is stalemate: decide whether it is a win for the stalemating player, following the Arabic tradition, or a draw, following the modern one. The second is the bare king: decide whether it wins outright, and whether the reciprocal exception applies. Beginners generally find the game more satisfying with the bare-king win in force, because without it a great many positions are simply drawn.

A final caution. A first game will feel slow, and that is not a fault in the players. Give it three or four games, because the interest of shatranj lies in the qualities a modern player first experiences as absence: the difficulty of forcing anything, the value of a single pawn, and the way a knight on a strong square becomes decisive when nothing can drive it off.
steps: Set up a standard chess board with the usual array. Agree that both players place king and counsellor the same way round, and note the counsellors' square colours: if they differ, they can never interact.

Agree that the queen is now the firzan, moving exactly one square diagonally, and that the bishops are now alfils, moving exactly two squares diagonally, jumping anything in between and never stopping short.
Agree that pawns move one square only, with no double step and therefore no en passant, and that a pawn reaching the far rank promotes to a firzan and to nothing else.
Agree that there is no castling in any form.
Agree the two variable rules before the first move: whether stalemate wins for the player delivering it or is a draw, and whether baring the enemy king wins outright.
Play the opening as a build rather than a fight: connected pawns, knights toward the centre, rooks on open files, king tucked behind pawns with the firzan beside it.
Treat the rook as dominant and the knight as the main attacker, and activate the king far earlier than modern instinct allows.
Before every late exchange, check what you would be left holding: king and knight, king and firzan, and king with two alfils cannot force mate at all.

guides.title: Shogi: Japanese Chess and the Drop Rule
guides.summary: A complete introduction to shogi, the Japanese member of the chess family: the board and pieces, how promotion works, and above all the drop rule that returns captured pieces to play and makes the game unlike any other chess variant. Covers openings, castles, endgame technique, notation, handicaps, history and the errors beginners reliably make.

sections.heading: What Shogi Is, and the One Rule That Makes It Different
sections.body:
Shogi is the Japanese branch of the chess family, played on a nine-by-nine board with twenty pieces a side, and it shares an ancestor with Western chess, Chinese xiangqi, Thai makruk and Indian chaturanga. A newcomer looking at a shogi board recognises a great deal immediately. There is a king that must be protected. There is a piece that slides along ranks and files exactly as a rook does, and another that slides on diagonals exactly as a bishop does. There are pawns that trudge forward one square at a time, a jumping knight, and a general shape of play in which one side develops, attacks a weakness, and tries to trap the enemy king. If you can play chess you can be pushed through a first game of shogi inside twenty minutes. 

What you cannot do is transfer your chess judgement. The reason is a single rule, and everything strategically distinctive about shogi flows from it. When you capture an enemy piece, that piece is not removed from the game. It goes into your hand, it changes colour, and on any later turn you may place it back on the board as your own piece, on almost any empty square you like, as your entire move for that turn. This is the drop rule, and in Japanese the pieces held off-board are the komadai or, more usually in game talk, the mochigoma, the pieces in hand. 

Consider what this destroys. In chess, material trades simplify the position: every exchange takes two pieces off the board permanently, the board empties, and drawn endgames become more likely as the fighting force shrinks. In shogi nothing ever leaves. The total force on and off the board is constant at forty pieces from the first move to the last. An exchange does not simplify; it converts a piece on the board, which has a location and a limited set of squares it can reach, into a piece in hand, which has no location and can appear anywhere. Trading is therefore not a way of defusing an attack. It is often the way an attack is armed. 

Two consequences follow that shape every game. First, draws are rare. Professional shogi draws at something on the order of one or two per cent of games, against roughly half of top-level classical chess games in the modern era, because the material to force a decision never disappears. Second, no fortification is permanent. In chess a king behind three unmoved pawns is objectively safe against many attacking schemes. In shogi an attacker with a gold and a silver in hand can manufacture threats against that structure from thin air, planting pieces directly against the king's shelter. Defence in shogi is therefore not about building walls; it is about counting how many moves the walls will survive and whether your own attack lands first.

sections.heading: The Board, the Set, and the Opening Array
sections.body:
The shogi board, the shogiban, is a nine-by-nine grid of eighty-one squares. Unlike a chessboard the squares are not coloured; they are plain, usually pale wood ruled with fine black lines, and pieces stand on the squares rather than in chequered alternation. Four small dots are printed at the corners of the central block of nine squares, marking the boundaries of the promotion zones, so a player can see at a glance where the last three ranks begin. 

The pieces are the second thing a newcomer notices. They are not figurines. Each is a flat, five-sided wedge of wood, wider at the base and pointed at the top, with the piece's name written on it in kanji. Every piece in the set is the same colour. This is not decoration; it is the physical expression of the drop rule. Because a captured piece changes ownership, it cannot be marked as belonging to one side, so ownership is shown purely by orientation. Your pieces point away from you toward the opponent; the opponent's point back at you. Pick a piece up off the board, turn it around, and it is now yours. Beginners who learn on a set with red and black lettering, or on a computer screen with arrowheads, should understand that the pointing wedge is the real notation. 

Each side has twenty pieces: one king, one rook, one bishop, two gold generals, two silver generals, two knights, two lances, and nine pawns. The array is symmetric and fills three ranks. On the back rank, reading from the player's left edge to the right edge, the order is lance, knight, silver, gold, king, gold, silver, knight, lance. The second rank holds only two pieces, and they are placed asymmetrically, which is one of the small surprises of the game: the bishop stands on the second rank on the same side as the player's left hand as seen from behind the board, and the rook stands on the second rank two files in from the right edge. In standard coordinates, where files are numbered one to nine from the right and ranks lettered a to i from the far side, Black's bishop begins on 8h and Black's rook on 2h. The third rank is a solid wall of nine pawns. 

The convention for who moves first is worth learning early. The first player is called Sente, written with the character for 'first hand', and is conventionally shown with a filled black pentagon in printed notation. The second player is Gote, 'after hand', shown with an outline. In casual play the two are often called Black and White respectively, but no piece is actually black or white. Who moves first is decided by furigoma: one player scatters five pawns; if more land face up than tokin-side up, the scatterer takes Sente.

sections.heading: How the Pieces Move: The Sliders and the King
sections.body:
Three shogi pieces move exactly as a chess player expects and can be learned in seconds. The king, ousho or gyokusho, moves one square in any of the eight directions. There is no castling in shogi; the king walks to safety a step at a time, which is why king safety is built by moving several pieces over several turns rather than in a single manoeuvre. Formally the two kings have different names, the senior player using the character for jewelled general and the junior the character for king general, but they move identically and nothing hinges on which you hold. 

The rook, hisha, slides any number of empty squares along a rank or a file and captures the first enemy piece in its path. It cannot jump. The bishop, kakugyo, slides any number of empty squares diagonally, with the same capture rule. Together these two are called the ogoma, the big pieces, and they carry most of a shogi player's attacking power. But note something structural about the opening array: the rook and bishop both start hemmed in behind the pawn wall, and the bishops face each other along the long diagonal from 8h to 2b, blocked only by the pawns on 7g and 3c. Almost every opening in shogi is, at some level, an argument about that diagonal and about which file the rook will eventually operate on. 

The lance, kyosha, is the piece that has no chess equivalent and that teaches the beginner the game's most important asymmetry. It slides any number of squares straight forward and only straight forward. It cannot move sideways, it cannot move backward, it cannot turn. Once a lance has advanced up a file it is committed, and the square it vacated behind it is permanently unguarded by it. Lances are consequently a defensive liability in front of the king and a powerful battering tool when dropped behind an enemy piece on an open file, where they attack the piece and everything behind it at once. 

The general principle that unites this group is directional bias. Western chess is very nearly symmetric front-to-back: a rook, bishop, queen and knight all move backward exactly as well as they move forward, and only the pawn is one-way. In shogi, only the king, rook and bishop are fully reversible. Every other piece is at least partly forward-biased, and two of them, the pawn and lance, cannot retreat at all. This means that advancing a shogi piece is a genuine commitment, that a piece which overextends cannot simply come home, and that the whole board has a grain to it. Attacks flow forward and are hard to recall, which is a large part of why the game rewards accurate calculation of a single attacking sequence over flexible manoeuvring.

sections.heading: How the Pieces Move: Generals, Knight and Pawn
sections.body:
The gold general, kinsho, is the workhorse of shogi and its move should be memorised as a shape rather than a list. It moves one square to any of six destinations: straight forward, diagonally forward-left, diagonally forward-right, left, right, and straight backward. What it cannot do is move diagonally backward. Drawn on paper, its reachable squares make a blunt arrowhead pointing forward. The gold is the best defensive piece in the game precisely because it covers the two forward diagonals and the square in front, which are the approaches an attacker uses, while retaining the straight retreat that lets it stay connected to the king. Uniquely among the promotable pieces, the gold does not promote; it is already at its ceiling. 

The silver general, ginsho, moves one square to five destinations: straight forward and all four diagonals. It cannot move straight sideways or straight backward. Its shape is an X with a spike on top. Comparing the two generals is the first real piece of shogi judgement a student acquires. The silver is worth slightly less than the gold in the abstract because it defends worse: an enemy piece placed directly beside or directly behind a silver is not attacked by it, so silvers are easier to walk around. But the silver attacks better, because its two backward diagonals let it advance into enemy territory and still retreat, whereas an advanced gold that is chased has only one square to run to. The working rule taught to beginners is: golds toward the king, silvers toward the enemy. 

The knight, keima, is the only piece in shogi that jumps over intervening pieces, and it is far weaker than its chess cousin. It has exactly two possible destinations, both forward: two squares forward and one to the left, or two squares forward and one to the right. It cannot move sideways, cannot move backward, and cannot reach the other six squares a chess knight can. A shogi knight is therefore a one-way missile. Dropped two ranks below an enemy king with support, it is lethal, because it attacks two squares that no other piece attacks from that angle and cannot be blocked. Left sitting on its home square it is nearly useless, and a knight that advances into a dead end can never come back. 

The pawn, fuhyo, moves one square straight forward and captures on that same square. This is the single most important difference from chess and the one that most often trips converts. There is no diagonal pawn capture, no two-square first move, no en passant. Two enemy pawns facing each other on the same file are simply stuck, and neither can take the other. Because pawns capture straight ahead, pawn structures in shogi are not chains; they are a rank of independent blockers, and files open and close in a completely different rhythm from chess.

sections.heading: Promotion: The Zone, the Choice, and the Forced Cases
sections.body:
The last three ranks on the opponent's side of the board form the promotion zone. For the first player these are ranks a, b and c, the three ranks the opponent's pieces started on; for the second player they are ranks g, h and i. The four dots printed on the board mark the corners of this territory. Any piece that moves into, out of, or entirely within the promotion zone may promote at the end of that move, and promotion is executed physically by flipping the wedge over to reveal a second set of characters on the reverse, conventionally written in red or in a cursive script. 

Promotion is normally optional. This is a real decision, not a formality, and it is one of the places where shogi differs sharply from chess, where a pawn reaching the last rank simply becomes a queen. Six of the eight piece types can promote; the king and the gold general cannot. Four of them promote to the same thing: a promoted pawn, called tokin, a promoted lance, a promoted knight and a promoted silver all move exactly as a gold general. The remaining two gain rather than change: a promoted bishop, the dragon horse or ryuma, keeps all its diagonal sliding and adds the king's four orthogonal single steps; a promoted rook, the dragon king or ryuo, keeps all its orthogonal sliding and adds the four diagonal single steps. 

Promotion is compulsory in exactly the situations where declining it would leave a piece with no legal move ever again. A pawn or a lance that reaches the furthest rank must promote, because an unpromoted pawn or lance there could never move. A knight that reaches either of the two furthest ranks must promote for the same reason. There is no other compulsion. 

Knowing when to decline is genuine skill. The clearest case is the silver. A promoted silver moves as a gold, gaining the sideways and straight-backward steps but losing both backward diagonals. An attacking silver that has driven deep into enemy territory frequently wants those retreat diagonals more than it wants sideways coverage, so strong players routinely leave silvers unpromoted when they intend to keep manoeuvring. A second case is deliberate self-limitation to avoid a fork or to keep a piece capturable only on squares you control. A third and subtler case involves the value of the piece if captured: a promoted piece reverts to its base form when taken, so promoting a lance deep in enemy territory hands your opponent nothing extra, but it does convert a long-range piece into a short-range one that may be less useful to you. The default, however, is to promote a rook or bishop essentially always. A dragon or a horse is so much stronger than its base form that declining requires a concrete reason.

sections.heading: The Drop Rule in Detail
sections.body:
When you capture an enemy piece, you take it off the board, turn it to face the opponent, and set it on your komadai, the small stand to your right. If the captured piece was promoted, it reverts: a captured dragon king becomes an ordinary rook in your hand, a captured tokin becomes an ordinary pawn. The reversion is total and permanent for that instance; nothing remembers that it was once promoted. 

On any subsequent turn, instead of moving a piece on the board, you may take one piece from your hand and place it on any empty square. That placement is your whole move for the turn. The dropped piece arrives unpromoted, even if it is dropped inside the promotion zone, and it may not promote on the turn it lands; it must survive to make an ordinary move later before it can be flipped. A drop may give check. A drop may deliver checkmate. A drop may not capture, because it must go to an empty square, and it may not block by removing an enemy piece. 

The strategic consequences are large. A piece in hand is worth more than the same piece badly placed on the board, because a piece in hand attacks every square on the board conditionally and commits to none. Strong players speak of the flexibility premium of the hand and will accept an inferior-looking exchange to convert a passive board piece into an active reserve. Equally, a piece in hand does nothing until spent, so a player sitting on three golds while the opponent's attack lands is simply losing. The rhythm of a shogi game is often the rhythm of accumulating exactly the right pieces in hand and then spending them in a single burst. 

Two specific patterns illustrate the rule's power. First, the pawn drop as a battering ram: because pawns capture straight ahead and cannot be captured by an enemy pawn on the same file, dropping a pawn directly in front of an advanced enemy piece attacks it with your cheapest unit and forces a response. The tare-fu, a dangling pawn dropped one rank away from a gold or silver so that it threatens to promote to tokin next move, is a fundamental attacking device: your opponent must spend a move dealing with a pawn, and if he does not, a one-point piece becomes a six-point one adjacent to his camp. Second, the gold or silver dropped in contact with a castled king. In chess, an attacker must physically march a piece across the board to reach the enemy king, which takes moves the defender can use. In shogi the attacker teleports it.
