This is why counting attacking and defending pieces around the king, rather than eyeballing the pawn shelter, is the correct way to assess safety.

sections.heading: The Three Drop Restrictions
sections.body:
Drops are almost unrestricted, and the exceptions are few enough to memorise quickly, but they decide real games and one of them is the most famous rule in shogi. 

The first restriction is the dead-piece rule. You may not drop a piece onto a square from which it would have no legal move for the rest of the game. In practice this means exactly three things: you may not drop a pawn or a lance on the furthest rank, and you may not drop a knight on either of the two furthest ranks. The logic is that a dropped piece arrives unpromoted and cannot promote on arrival, so a pawn dropped on the last rank would be frozen forever. Note that this restriction applies only to drops. A pawn that walks to the last rank is fine, because it promotes on arrival. 

The second restriction is nifu, literally 'two pawns'. You may not drop a pawn onto a file that already contains one of your own unpromoted pawns. You may have as many pawns as you like on a file if you get them there another way, and crucially a tokin, a promoted pawn, does not count: if your pawn on the fifth file has promoted, that file is legally empty of pawns and you may drop a fresh one. Nifu is an instant loss in tournament play, not merely an illegal move to be taken back, and it is the most common way a strong amateur loses a game to a rule rather than to an opponent. The defence against your own carelessness is a habit: before dropping a pawn, run your eye up and down the whole file, not just the squares near the target. 

The third restriction is uchifuzume, the rule against dropping a pawn to deliver immediate checkmate. If a pawn drop would give check and the opponent has no legal reply at all, the drop is illegal. Everything about that sentence matters. Dropping a pawn to give ordinary check is legal. Moving a pawn forward to deliver checkmate is legal. Dropping any other piece, a lance or a silver or a gold, to deliver checkmate is legal. Only the pawn drop that mates on the spot is banned. The rule has no obvious logical justification; it is a historical convention, usually explained as a mark of respect that the game's cheapest piece should not be permitted to finish a king outright, and it survives because it makes for better endgames. 

Uchifuzume is not a curiosity. It is a defensive resource that mating attacks must be checked against, and a whole class of composed mate problems turns on it. The characteristic trick is a sacrifice that changes the position just enough to make the pawn drop legal: you give away a piece so the defending king gains a flight square, so that the pawn drop is now merely check rather than mate, and then a follow-up seals the escape. Conversely, a defender in a lost-looking position should always ask whether the only mate is a pawn drop, because if it is, there is no mate.

sections.heading: How Games End: Mate, Resignation, Repetition and Impasse
sections.body:
Shogi is won by checkmating the enemy king, exactly as in chess: the king is attacked, and no legal move removes the attack. In practice, professional games almost never reach a mate on the board. Resignation, in Japanese makemashita, is the norm and comes early by chess standards, often the moment a forced mate becomes visible several moves out. The culture treats playing on in a dead position as poor form rather than as fighting spirit. 

Stalemate essentially does not exist as a practical outcome. A shogi king that has no legal move but is not in check is, by the standard modern rule, simply lost, but the situation is so vanishingly rare given the drop rule and the number of pieces in play that most players go a lifetime without seeing one. There is no draw by insufficient material either, because material never becomes insufficient. 

Repetition is handled by sennichite, the thousand-day rule. If the same position occurs four times with the same player to move and the same pieces in each player's hand, the game is drawn and, in professional play, replayed with colours reversed. The critical exception is perpetual check: if the repetition was produced by one side checking continuously, that side must vary, and if he does not he loses. This is the reverse of chess, where perpetual check is the classic saving resource for the weaker side. In shogi, a losing player cannot rescue himself by giving endless check; he must find a repetition that includes non-checking moves. 

The remaining ending is jishogi, the impasse or mutual entering-king. Both kings march into their opponents' promotion zones, where they become extremely hard to mate, because most attacking pieces are forward-biased and cannot easily strike backward at a king behind them. Once neither side can realistically mate, the game is decided on a point count. Rooks and bishops, promoted or not, are worth five points each; every other piece except the king is worth one; the total on the board is fifty-four. Under the traditional rule a player with twenty-four points or more is not lost, so if both clear twenty-four the game is a draw and if one falls short that player loses. 

The traditional rule is loose about who declares and when, and computer shogi forced the issue, since engines are happy to shuffle indefinitely. The modern declaration rule used in computer events and increasingly in serious amateur play is stricter: to declare, your king must be in the promotion zone, you must not be in check, you must have at least ten other pieces inside the zone, and you must hold at least twenty-eight points as the first player or twenty-seven as the second. Meet all conditions and you win outright; declare falsely and you lose. Which rule set applies is a matter of local regulation, and it is worth agreeing before a serious game.

sections.heading: Reading and Recording Games: Notation
sections.body:
Shogi coordinates label files with Arabic numerals one to nine and ranks with something that distinguishes them. Files are counted from the first player's right to his left, so the rightmost file is file 1 and the leftmost is file 9, which is the mirror image of the chess habit. Ranks are counted from the far side toward the first player: the opponent's back rank is rank one, the first player's own back rank is rank nine. Japanese notation writes both as kanji numerals and puts the file first, so the square at file two, rank six is written with the characters for two and six. Western-language sources normally keep the numeral for the file and substitute a letter a through i for the rank, so that same square becomes 2f. Black's rook starts at 2h and Black's bishop at 8h under this scheme. 

A move is written as piece letter, then destination. The standard English abbreviations are K for king, R for rook, B for bishop, G for gold, S for silver, N for knight, L for lance and P for pawn. So P-7f means a pawn moves to square 7f, and the classic first move of the game, advancing the pawn in front of the bishop, is P-7f for Black and P-3d for White. Promotion is marked with a plus sign appended to the move: B-2b+ means the bishop moves to 2b and promotes. Declining promotion when it was available is marked with an equals sign, B-2b=, because the fact that a player chose not to promote is information. Promoted pieces are named with a leading plus thereafter, so +P is a tokin, +B is a horse and +R is a dragon. 

Drops have their own symbol and it is worth internalising, because a drop and a move are strategically different acts. A drop is written with an asterisk in place of the dash: P*5e means a pawn is dropped from hand onto 5e. Some older Western sources use an apostrophe instead, so P'5e means the same thing. When two identical pieces could both reach the same square, the origin square is added in parentheses to disambiguate, as in S(3i)-4h. 

Japanese game records add two useful conventions. The side to move is shown by a small pentagon before the move, filled for Sente and hollow for Gote, which lets a reader open a record in the middle and instantly know whose move it is. And when a piece moves to the square the previous move ended on, the character for 'same' replaces the coordinates entirely, so a long recapture sequence on one square reads as a column of identical-looking entries. This is compact and, once learned, faster to read than the Western equivalent. Modern electronic records use two machine formats, KIF, which is close to the Japanese written record, and CSA, which is a terser fixed-width form designed for programs; both are widely supported by free viewers.

sections.heading: Material Values and the Economics of Exchange
sections.body:
Every chess player carries a table of piece values, and shogi has one too, but it must be handled with more care because the drop rule changes what a value means. The traditional teaching scale, used in Japanese instructional books for decades, runs: pawn one, lance three, knight four, silver five, gold six, bishop eight, rook ten. Promoted forms are valued higher, with the dragon king around twelve or thirteen and the dragon horse around ten. A tokin is usually taught as worth about six, the same as a gold, with the important qualification that when captured it reverts to a one-point pawn, so it is worth six to you and one to your opponent, which makes it the most efficient attacker in the game. 

Modern engine evaluations, derived by machine learning from millions of positions, differ in the details. Typical learned tables put the silver and gold much closer to each other than three-to-two, place the bishop and rook nearer to each other, and value the knight lower relative to the lance than the traditional table does. Nobody should treat either scale as exact. What matters is a small number of relationships that hold in nearly all positions. 

The first relationship is that the two big pieces are worth roughly two generals each, which sets the price of the most common trade in the game. Giving up a rook to win a gold and a silver is approximately even in material but usually good in practice if it opens a file toward the enemy king. The second is that a pawn in hand is far more valuable than a pawn on the board, perhaps two or three times as much in an attacking position, because a pawn in hand can be dropped as a tare-fu, as a blocker, as a decoy, or as a wedge to disrupt a defender. Professionals routinely say that having no pawn in hand at the moment an attack starts is worse than being a piece down. 

The third relationship is that value is contextual to an extraordinary degree. A lance is a three-point piece sitting in the corner and a decisive one dropped behind an enemy gold on an open file. A knight is a four-point piece on its home square and a mating piece when dropped at the right angle to a castled king. Because pieces can be summoned anywhere, the question 'what is this worth' is nearly always 'what is this worth in hand, given the enemy king's shape'. 

The practical rule this yields is that shogi rewards trading down for the right pieces rather than avoiding trades. If your attack needs a gold and you have a rook, trading rook for gold plus silver may be the correct decision even at a nominal loss, because two dropping generals near a king outweigh one sliding rook that the defender can block.

sections.heading: Castles: How a Shogi King Is Made Safe
sections.body:
Because there is no castling move, a shogi player builds king safety by hand, walking the king two or three squares sideways and then arranging generals around it over five to ten moves. The resulting formations are called castles, kakoi, and there are perhaps a dozen in common use with dozens of variants. Learning three of them well is worth more than recognising all of them. 

The design logic is constant. A castle wants the king off the central files, where both rooks and both bishops operate, and tucked onto the second or bottom rank behind a cluster of golds and silvers. Two or three generals is the standard prescription, captured in the old maxim that you attack with rook, bishop, silver and knight and defend with three golds and silvers. Crucially, a castle is not judged by how many pieces surround the king but by which directions those pieces cover, because the drop rule means an attacker can appear from any direction he can generate pressure on. 

The Mino castle is the standard shelter for a player who has swung his rook to the left, and it puts the king on the second rank near the right edge, on 2h in standard coordinates, with a silver in front of it and two golds forming a diagonal staircase back toward the centre. Mino is fast, taking about six moves, and it is exceptionally solid against pressure arriving horizontally from the centre, because the golds cover the approach squares from the side. Its known weakness is from above and from the edge: a lance and pawn assault down the first file, or a knight dropped at the right angle, gets at the king much faster than a frontal attack does. 

The Yagura is the classic formation when both players keep their rooks at home, and it sits on the opposite wing, with the king around 8h, golds on 7h and 6g and a silver on 7g, so the king is roofed by a slanting wall of generals. Yagura is slow, often fifteen moves or more, and superb against attacks that come straight down the file, but the diagonal from the enemy bishop is its permanent anxiety and a bishop that gets onto the right diagonal can undo the whole structure. 

The Anaguma, the bear in the hole, is the extreme case. The king goes right into the corner square, the lance in front of it is nudged up one, and a silver and two golds seal the box. Nothing in shogi is harder to mate; the king is often untouchable for twenty moves. The price is that it takes ten to fifteen tempi to build, the king has no escape squares at all if the box is ever cracked, and the pieces committed to the corner are useless for anything else. Anaguma games are therefore races in which one side is betting that his fortress outlasts the other's, and they end abruptly when it does not.

sections.heading: Openings: The Static Rook and Ranging Rook Divide
sections.body:
Shogi opening theory organises itself around a single early decision: does the rook stay on the file where it started, or does it swing across the board? A player who leaves the rook at home is playing Ibisha, static rook. A player who moves it to the left is playing Furibisha, ranging rook. Every named opening in the game sits in one of the four resulting pairings, and knowing which of the four you are in tells you where the fighting will happen before a single piece is exchanged. 

Ranging rook is named by the file the rook lands on. Fourth File Rook, shiken-bisha, is the traditional workhorse and remains the most common amateur choice. Third File Rook and its aggressive Ishida-style development aim at a quick attack on the third file. Central Rook, naka-bisha, puts the rook on the fifth file and in its modern Gokigen form has been a professional main line since the 1990s. Opposing Rook, mukai-bisha, drops the rook on the eighth file, directly opposite the enemy rook. The unifying idea is that the rook goes where the enemy king is not, so that the attacking rook and the defending king end up on opposite wings and each side attacks the side the other has left thin. 

Static rook against ranging rook is the classic asymmetric fight, and it has a specific shape. The ranging rook player builds a Mino on the right and prepares a counter-strike on the file he has occupied; the static rook player builds a Boat castle or, more ambitiously, a Static Rook Anaguma on the left and tries to break through on the second file with a climbing silver or a rook-and-silver battery. It is essentially a race between an early attack and a slow but crushing fortress, and the arrival of the Anaguma in the 1980s changed the balance so much that ranging rook fell out of professional favour for a generation. 

When both players keep their rooks at home, the game is symmetric and divides into four historic families. The Yagura is a slow, closed, positional fight in which both sides build the heavy castle described above and then manoeuvre for twenty moves. Bishop Exchange, kakugawari, begins by trading the bishops off early, which means both players hold a bishop in hand and every weak diagonal square becomes a permanent worry. Side Pawn Capture, yokofudori, is the sharpest opening in the game, with the rooks raking each other's third ranks by move ten and both kings still on their original squares. Double Wing Attack, aigakari, opens both rook files early and leads to fast, forcing play. 

The practical advice for a new player is to pick one ranging rook system and one castle and play them for a hundred games. Shogi opening theory is deep enough that breadth is worthless before pattern recognition.

sections.heading: The Middlegame: How a Castle Is Broken
sections.body:
The middlegame in shogi is a counting exercise. Once castles are built, the question is not who stands better in some vague positional sense but who can generate a decisive attack first, and that reduces to arithmetic about attackers, defenders and tempi. The single most useful maxim is that an attack needs at least three pieces. Against a two-general castle, a rook alone will not break through, a rook and a silver will usually not break through, and a rook, a silver and a knight, with a pawn in hand, usually will. Counting the attacking pieces you can actually bring to bear on one sector, and the defending pieces that cover that sector, is the fundamental middlegame skill. 

The standard breakthrough technique is a sacrifice to open a line. Because pieces return to your hand rather than leaving the game, giving one away is far less costly than in chess, and the classic pattern is to shove a piece into a defended square specifically so that the recapture pulls a defender out of position or opens a file for the rook behind it. A silver thrown at a gold that must take it, followed by a rook that now sees through to the king, is the shape of a thousand shogi games. The Japanese term for such an offering is sutegoma, a thrown-away piece, and learning to see them is the main thing that separates a strong amateur from a weak one. 

Pawn techniques deserve their own study because they are the cheapest lever available. The tare-fu is a pawn dropped one square short of the enemy camp, threatening to step forward and become a tokin: the opponent must react, and every move he spends is a move you gain. The tsugi-fu, the joining pawn, is a second pawn dropped behind the first so that when the first is captured the second immediately replaces it. The soko-fu is a pawn dropped on the bottom rank behind an enemy piece to undermine it. Against a Mino castle the standard demolition is an edge attack: push the edge pawn, sacrifice it, drop a lance behind, and follow with a knight. Four cheap pieces, correctly sequenced, dismantle a castle that three generals were defending. 

The counting that matters most is tempo counting in the mutual attack, the ai-gakari situation in which both sides are attacking each other's king simultaneously. Here you calculate not who is winning but who mates first, and a single wasted move loses the game outright. Two rules govern this phase. Never make a checking move that does not shorten the mate, because check often pushes the king toward open ground where it is harder to trap. And prefer to remove a defender's escape squares before you begin checking, since a mating net built first and executed second is far more reliable than a series of checks hunting for one.

sections.heading: The Endgame: Tsume Shogi and the Mating Race
sections.body:
Shogi has no endgame in the chess sense. There is no phase where the board empties and technique replaces calculation, because the board never empties. What shogi has instead is yose, the closing, a phase that begins the moment one side's attack makes contact with the enemy castle and ends in mate, usually within twenty moves and often within ten. Yose is the most calculation-intensive part of the game and the part where strength differences show most brutally. 

The central concept is the distinction between tsume, a forced mate, and hisshi, usually translated as brinkmate: a position where there is no immediate forced mate but the opponent cannot prevent one next move either. Hisshi is often the correct practical goal, because it does not require you to find the whole forcing sequence and it cannot be escaped by a defensive drop. A player who can reliably build a hisshi is stronger than one who hunts only for tsume. 

Tsume shogi, the composed mating problem, is the standard training tool and is treated in Japan as a discipline in its own right, with its own composers, magazines and aesthetic standards. The rules of a tsume problem are strict and differ from ordinary play. The attacker must give check on every single move without exception. The defender must play the move that resists longest, and must interpose or capture rather than simply allowing mate. All pieces not shown on the board and not in the attacker's hand are assumed to be in the defender's hand, so the defender always has maximum drop resources. And the solution must be unique. Working ten three-move problems a day is the single most recommended improvement exercise in shogi, and its effect is not memorisation of patterns so much as the training of accurate forward calculation under the constraint that every move must be check. 

The commonest mating patterns are worth knowing by name. The head gold, atama-kin, is a gold dropped directly in front of the enemy king with support behind it, and it is the most frequent mate in the game because a gold covers the three squares in front of the king as well as its own retreat. The knight mate exploits the knight's unblockable jump to cover two squares no other piece attacks from that angle. The lance dropped down a file behind a defender is the standard way to mate a king with escape squares to the side. 

The governing practical maxim is that check is not progress. The Japanese phrase, oute wa ou te, puns on the words for check and for chasing: a check that merely drives the king somewhere is a check that helped it escape. Correct yose technique is to spend your early moves eliminating flight squares and pulling defenders away, and only then to begin the forcing sequence. Counting the mutual race honestly, including the possibility that a defensive drop buys the opponent exactly one tempo, is the difference between a win and a resignation.

sections.heading: Origins, Handicaps, and the Modern Professional Game
sections.body:
Shogi descends, like all the chess games, from the Indian chaturanga, arriving in Japan by a southern route through China or Southeast Asia. The earliest physical evidence is a cache of wooden pieces excavated at the Kofuku-ji temple in Nara, found alongside a wooden document dated to 1058, which gives a firm floor for the game's presence in Japan by the middle of the eleventh century. Several larger variants coexisted for centuries, including chu shogi on a twelve-by-twelve board and dai shogi and its relatives on boards up to fifteen squares a side, some of which are still played by enthusiasts. The drop rule is not original; it appears to have entered the small nine-by-nine game around the sixteenth century, and it is what allowed the small board to outcompete the large ones, since it made a compact game endlessly complex. 

Professionalisation began under the Tokugawa shogunate. Ohashi Sokei received a stipend from the government in the early 1600s and is counted the first Meijin, a title that then passed by hereditary appointment within a few families for three centuries. In 1935 the hereditary system was abolished in favour of competition, and the modern era began; the Japan Shogi Association, founded in 1924, has organised professional play ever since. There are today eight major titles, including the Ryuo, the Meijin, the Kisei and the Oi, and holding them all at once is the game's supreme achievement. Habu Yoshiharu held all seven of the titles that then existed simultaneously in 1996. Fujii Sota, who qualified as a professional at fourteen in 2016, held all eight in 2023. 

The route into the profession is famously narrow. Aspirants enter the Shoreikai apprentice school as children and must reach fourth dan by the age of twenty-six or be expelled permanently; only a handful qualify each year. Amateur grading runs from about fifteenth kyu for a raw beginner up through first kyu and then amateur first to sixth dan, and the amateur and professional dan scales are not equivalent, an amateur fifth dan being roughly comparable to a strong club player rather than to a professional. 

Handicap play, komaochi, is the institution that makes this ladder teachable, and it is far more central to shogi than odds games are to chess. The stronger player removes pieces from his own side and the weaker player always moves first. The ladder runs from lance odds, through bishop odds, rook odds, rook and lance, two-piece odds, which removes rook and bishop, and on through four, six, eight and ten-piece handicaps, the last leaving the teacher with a king and nine pawns. Each rung corresponds to roughly one grade of difference, and each has its own established theory, so a beginner learns real technique rather than merely being allowed to win. Machines have since surpassed all of this: engines beat professionals decisively from about 2013, and the NNUE evaluation method invented for shogi in 2018 was later adopted by the strongest chess programs.

sections.heading: Common Errors, Limits, and What To Do When It Goes Wrong
sections.body:
The failure modes of a new shogi player are predictable enough to list, and most of them come from importing chess habits. The first is trading pieces to relieve pressure. In chess this defuses an attack; in shogi it arms one, because every exchange hands the attacker a piece that can be dropped next to your king. If you are under attack and considering a trade, count what the opponent will hold in hand afterwards before you take. 

The second is treating the pawn wall as protection. Shogi pawns capture straight ahead, so they do not defend each other and they do not defend the squares diagonally in front of them. A castle's safety comes entirely from its generals. A beginner who counts three pawns in front of the king and feels safe is misreading the position. 

The third is attacking with too few pieces. A rook and a bishop look overwhelming and will bounce off two golds every time. If you cannot bring a third and preferably a fourth attacker to the sector, and hold at least one pawn in hand, the attack is premature and will simply donate material. The fourth is the mirror image: hoarding pieces in hand. Pieces in hand are potential, and potential that is never spent loses to force that is. 

The fifth is the illegal move, and it is worth taking seriously because in tournament play an illegal move loses the game instantly rather than being taken back. The two that catch people are nifu, dropping a second unpromoted pawn onto a file you already have a pawn on, and uchifuzume, dropping a pawn for immediate checkmate. Both are avoidable with a deliberate habit: scan the whole file before any pawn drop, and before dropping a pawn that gives check, verify the king has at least one legal reply. A third illegal move, dropping a knight on the last two ranks, catches almost nobody once they have seen it named. 

The sixth is checking without a plan during the mating race, which reliably drives the enemy king into open space and loses the tempo that decides the game. If you cannot see the mate, do not start checking; build a brinkmate instead. 

When a game has gone wrong, the honest options are narrow. There is no fortress draw to aim for and no perpetual check to rescue you, because perpetual check loses. What does exist is the entering king: if your king can march into the opponent's promotion zone, most of his attacking pieces cannot strike backward, and a lost middlegame can become a point count you survive. This is a real and underused resource and it is why the impasse rules exist. Failing that, the culturally expected move is to resign cleanly, and then to replay the game and find the move where the piece count in hand turned against you.

sections.heading: What Tsume Shogi Is and Why It Matters
sections.body: Tsume shogi, literally "mating shogi," is the problem art of Japanese chess: a composed position in which the attacking side must checkmate the defending king by force, giving check with every single move, against the most stubborn defense the rules allow. It occupies roughly the niche that the mate-in-two problem occupies in Western chess, but the comparison understates both its difficulty and its centrality to the parent game. Shogi is played on a nine-by-nine board with twenty pieces per side, and its defining rule is the drop: a captured piece changes allegiance and may later be parachuted back onto almost any empty square by its captor. Material therefore never leaves the game, attacks never run out of ammunition, and the endgame of shogi is not a slow grind of technique but a race between two mating attacks. Because of this, the ability to calculate forced mates quickly and accurately is the single most valuable technical skill a shogi player owns, and tsume shogi is the purpose-built instrument for training it. Every professional in the Japan Shogi Association solves mating problems; strong players describe working through hundreds of short problems a day during their formative years, and Fujii Sota, the dominant player of the current generation, first became nationally famous not for tournament results but for winning the national tsume-solving championship at the age of twelve. At the same time, tsume shogi is a genuine art form with four centuries of continuous history. Edo-period masters presented hundred-problem collections to the shogun as proof of their school's supremacy; the greatest of those books, composed in the 1730s and 1750s, remain in print, remain studied, and are still regarded as being near the summit of the art. Modern composers publish in dedicated magazines, compete for annual prizes, and push technical records: the longest problem generally accepted as sound, Microcosmos, runs to 1,525 moves. A tsume problem differs from a game position in precise, formalized ways. The solver is told exactly which pieces the attacker holds in hand; the defender is assumed to hold every piece not otherwise shown; the attacker must check on every move; the defender must resist as long as possible; and a correct problem has exactly one solution. These conventions convert a messy practical question, "can I mate this king," into a closed logical puzzle with a provable answer, which is why the genre is sometimes described as the mathematics of shogi. Even a reader who never plays a game of shogi has reasons to understand tsume: it is among the oldest continuously practiced puzzle traditions on earth, it shaped how the Japanese game is taught, graded, and ranked, and it demonstrates what happens to the logic of checkmate when captured pieces come back. This guide explains the rules of the game the problems assume, the special conventions of the genre, the standard mating patterns and sacrifice themes, the defensive resources that make problems deep, the history from castle libraries to computer-verified record problems, and the practical craft of actually solving.

sections.heading: The Shogi Essentials a Solver Must Know
sections.body: Shogi is played on an uncheckered nine-by-nine grid of eighty-one squares. Each side begins with twenty pieces: one king, one rook, one bishop, two golds, two silvers, two knights, two lances, and nine pawns. Pieces are flat, wedge-shaped tiles pointed toward the opponent; ownership is shown by orientation, not color, which is what makes the drop rule physically natural. The king steps one square in any direction, exactly as in Western chess. The rook slides any distance along ranks and files; the bishop slides any distance along diagonals. The gold general moves one square in any of six directions: straight forward, both forward diagonals, sideways left and right, and straight back; it cannot step to the two rear diagonals. The silver general moves one square in any of five directions: straight forward and all four diagonals; it cannot move sideways or straight back. The knight jumps to one of only two squares, two ranks forward and one file to either side, leaping over anything in the way; it is the only shogi piece that jumps, and it can never move backward or sideways. The lance slides any distance straight forward and only forward. The pawn moves one square straight forward and, unlike the Western pawn, captures the same way, straight ahead rather than diagonally. Promotion works by zone: the three ranks farthest from a player form that player's promotion zone, and any move that starts in, ends in, or passes through the zone entitles the moving piece to promote, flipping the tile to reveal its promoted face. Promotion is optional except when the piece would otherwise be left with no legal move, so a pawn or lance reaching the last rank, or a knight reaching either of the last two ranks, must promote. A promoted pawn, called a tokin, moves exactly like a gold, as do promoted lance, promoted knight, and promoted silver. The rook promotes to the dragon king, usually just called the dragon, which keeps the rook's sliding power and adds a one-square step to each diagonal. The bishop promotes to the dragon horse, called the horse, which keeps the bishop's diagonals and adds a one-square step orthogonally. Golds and kings do not promote. Two consequences matter enormously for mating problems. First, four different pieces in hand can become gold-movers on the board, so the gold's six-direction pattern is the fundamental unit of attack, and the tokin is celebrated as the most cost-efficient attacker in the game: it fights like a gold, but if the defender captures it, the defender gains only a pawn. Second, the asymmetry of the generals, the gold blind to its rear diagonals and the silver blind to its sides and back, dictates the geometry of mating nets: golds are strongest attacking from the front of a king, silvers from behind or diagonally, and much of tsume technique is choreography that brings each general to the side of the king where its blind spots do not matter.

sections.heading: Drops and the Hand: The Mechanism That Defines the Genre
sections.body: When a shogi piece is captured, it is not removed from play. It goes to the capturer's hand, always in its unpromoted state, and on any later turn its new owner may, instead of moving a piece on the board, drop it onto almost any empty square, where it immediately functions as that owner's piece. A dropped piece arrives unpromoted even if it lands inside the promotion zone, though it may promote on a later move made within the zone. Three restrictions apply. A piece may not be dropped onto a square from which it could never legally move again: a pawn or lance may not be dropped on the farthest rank, and a knight may not be dropped on either of the two farthest ranks. A pawn may not be dropped onto a file that already contains another of the owner's unpromoted pawns; this is the famous two-pawn rule, called nifu. And a pawn may not be dropped to deliver immediate checkmate, a prohibition called uchifuzume. Everything distinctive about tsume shogi flows from the drop. In Western chess, a mating attack is limited by the pieces that survive to reach the enemy king; in shogi, every capture the attacker makes replenishes the attack, and every capture the defender makes replenishes the defense. Checks can rain in from an empty sky: a gold dropped directly against the king's face, a knight dropped on a square no piece could have reached by movement, a pawn dropped to seal an escape route. Conversely, any check delivered from a distance along a rank, file, or diagonal can be answered by dropping an interposing piece, so long-range checks alone almost never mate a king whose side holds pieces in hand. Tsume problems formalize the hand explicitly. The diagram shows the pieces on the board and states which pieces the attacker holds; by convention, the defender is assumed to hold every piece in the full forty-piece set that is neither on the board nor in the attacker's hand. This "defender holds the rest" rule matters constantly, because it means the defender can nearly always interpose against sliding checks, and the solver must mentally test every one of those interpositions. It also creates the attacker's central economic problem. Each checking sacrifice the defender captures transfers a piece into the defender's hand, potentially arming the defense; each defending piece the attacker captures arms the attack. A well-composed problem is a tight budget in which the attacker's hand is exactly sufficient, spent in exactly the right order. Experienced solvers read the hand the way a detective reads a suspect list: two golds in hand suggest a smothering frontal net, a lone knight hints at a jump no drop can block, a stack of pawns promises walls and sealing moves. The hand is not a supplement to the position; in tsume shogi it usually is the position, and the board is merely the stage on which it will be spent.

sections.heading: The Rules and Conventions of a Tsume Problem
sections.body: A tsume problem is governed by a small constitution of rules, some inherited from the game and some special to the genre. The attacker, conventionally Black and conventionally moving up the board, moves first, and every attacking move without exception must give check. The defender may reply with any legal move: capturing the checking piece, moving the king, or interposing a piece, including any piece dropped from the defender's hand. The attacker must force checkmate; if any defensive line survives with no checking continuation, the attempted solution is simply wrong. The defender is obliged to put up the longest and best resistance, which gives the problem its length: a problem's advertised size is the number of moves, counted in individual half-moves, of the main line against optimal defense, and it is always an odd number, because the attacker both opens and closes the sequence. A three-move problem, or three-te, is attacker, defender, attacker; famous classical problems run to hundreds of moves. Composition adds further conventions that a solver must know because they prune the search. A sound problem has exactly one solution: at every attacking turn there is exactly one correct check, though the defender may have several equally stubborn replies leading to variations of equal length. An alternative winning attack is called a cook, and its discovery demotes a published problem to flawed. At the final checkmate the attacker's hand should be empty; a problem whose solution leaves surplus pieces in the attacker's hand is considered blemished, and solvers exploit this convention in reverse, reasoning that every piece given must be spent. The defender, for all the stubbornness required, is barred from resistance that is merely tempo-wasting gift-giving: a defensive interposition that does not change the outcome or the character of the solution but only feeds the attacker material to lengthen the count is called a useless interposition, muda-ai, and by convention it does not count toward the problem's length. Distinguishing a useless interposition from a meaningful one, a chuai, whose capture genuinely alters the attacker's resources, is one of the subtler skills in the art, and composers build entire problems around interpositions that look useless and are not. Finally, the position itself must be legal in a loose sense: it must be reachable in principle under shogi rules, with no side having more pieces of a type than the set contains and no pawns doubled illegally, though no one requires a plausible game history. These conventions have a purpose beyond neatness. They make the problem a closed system with a unique, provable answer, so that a printed solution can be checked, disputed, and, in the modern era, verified exhaustively by computer. They also define the contract between composer and solver: everything on the diagram matters, everything in hand will be used, and the shortest forced mate against the toughest defense is the one and only truth of the position.

sections.heading: The Two Pawn Laws: Nifu and Uchifuzume
sections.body: Two special prohibitions govern the humble pawn, and both are load-bearing walls of tsume composition. The first is nifu: a player may never have two of their own unpromoted pawns on the same file. The rule bites at the moment of dropping, since a pawn already on a file makes any further pawn drop there illegal, and in professional play violating it means instant loss. Crucially, a tokin, the promoted pawn, does not count; a file with your tokin on it will happily accept a fresh pawn drop. In problems, nifu is a hidden hand on the scales. A defender who would like to interpose a pawn, normally the cheapest and best interposition because its capture yields the attacker almost nothing, may find the drop illegal because of a distant pawn the composer placed on that file for exactly this reason. Symmetrically, an attacker's obvious pawn-drop check can be forbidden, forcing a more expensive piece onto the square, and whole solutions turn on promoting a pawn to a tokin precisely to vacate the file for a second pawn. The second law is uchifuzume, the prohibition on delivering checkmate by dropping a pawn. Only the drop is forbidden: mating with a pawn that pushes forward from a square it already occupies is perfectly legal, as is a pawn drop that gives check without mate, or a pawn drop that leads to mate next move. The rule's historical origin is genuinely uncertain; explanations range from etiquette about the meanest soldier felling a king to game-balance judgments made centuries ago, and honest sources present it as simply inherited. Its consequences, though, are precise and delicious. A composer can arrange a position where the natural pawn-drop mate is illegal, and the solution must therefore perform surgery: sacrifice a piece to drag a defending unit onto a square so that the pawn drop becomes check but not mate, or deliberately open an escape square so the drop is legal, then close the escape one move later, or decline a promotion so that a later pawn mate is delivered by push rather than drop. There is even a celebrated family of problems in which the attacker must shed strength, unpromoting nothing but choosing weaker options at every fork, purely to stay on the right side of uchifuzume. Related but distinct are the dead-piece drop rules: pawns and lances may not be dropped on the final rank, knights may not be dropped on the final two ranks, because they would have no legal move afterward. These also shape mating geometry near the edge, where a knight cannot be dropped close enough or a lance cannot seal from ahead. Solvers burn themselves on all of these rules constantly, announcing a mate that a two-pawn file quietly forbids or a pawn-drop finish the law disallows, which is why checking every candidate line against the pawn laws is part of the basic hygiene of solving.

sections.heading: Core Mating Patterns Around the King
sections.body: Checkmate in shogi has an exact anatomy: the king must be in check, the checking piece must be uncapturable or its capture must leave the king still lost, every square the king could step to must be occupied by a defender or covered by an attacker, and, if the check comes from a distance along a line, every interposition from the board and from the defender's ample hand must fail. Solvers therefore think in terms of liberties, the count of squares the king can currently use, and in terms of standard final pictures toward which a solution steers. The most fundamental picture is the head gold, atama-kin: a gold planted directly on the square in front of the enemy king, supported by another attacker so it cannot be taken. Consider a bare defending king on the center square of its back rank, and an attacking rook far down the same file with a gold in hand. Dropping the gold directly in front of the king is immediate mate: the gold, protected by the rook behind it, attacks the king's square and the two diagonal squares beside itself, its body occupies the square ahead of the king, and its sideways reach covers the two squares flanking its own position, so all five of the king's potential flight squares on and beside the front rank are attacked or blocked, and the gold cannot be captured because the rook recaptures. That single geometric fact, a supported gold-mover on the king's head, ends more shogi games and more tsume problems than any other pattern, and it explains the value of the tokin, which produces the same mate at the price of a pawn. The second family is the silver from behind: because the silver attacks all four diagonals, a supported silver dropped diagonally behind a king pressed against an edge covers the retreat squares a frontal gold cannot see. The third family belongs to the knight. A knight checks from two ranks away, its jump cannot be interposed, and its checking square is not adjacent to the king, so the king cannot capture it; against a knight check the defender can only flee or capture with another piece, which makes knight drops the classic finishing blow on a king whose side squares are already sealed. Edge and corner mates form a fourth family: a king driven to the corner can be mated by a lance sliding up its file, by the knight-and-lance duet that exploits the corner's poverty of flight squares, or by the dragon parked adjacent, whose combined rook lines and diagonal steps blanket the corner. Finally there are smothered patterns, in which the king's own defenders occupy its liberties and a single unassailable check, often a knight or a supported pawn push, ends everything. Strong solvers do not calculate toward a vague goal; they recognize which of these final pictures the attacker's hand can afford, then search for the forcing sequence that assembles it.

sections.heading: How Each Piece Delivers Mate
sections.body: Each shogi piece has a characteristic role in the mating attack, dictated by its blind spots. The gold is the executioner. Six-directional coverage with no forward weakness makes it the ideal piece to stand against the king's face, and because four other piece types promote into gold-movers, gold-style mates are always in the air. Its one blindness, the rear diagonals, means a gold rarely mates from in front of a king that can slip diagonally past it toward the attacker; golds want the king pinned against an edge or a wall of its own pieces. The silver is the infiltrator. Its diagonal reach and its ability to retreat diagonally let it dive into the king's position, give check, and threaten to promote or fall back; a silver dropped diagonally behind the king covers the escape squares golds cannot, and silver checks often serve as decoys, since whether the defender captures with the king or with a guard determines which mating picture follows. The knight is the sniper. Checking from a distance of two ranks, immune to interposition, uncapturable by the checked king, it is the piece that punishes a king whose adjacent squares are all guarded but whose two forward-knight squares are not. Because it may not be dropped on the last two ranks and never moves backward, its mates cluster in the middle of the enemy camp, and a promoted knight, moving as gold, is often deliberately declined so the jump remains available. The lance is the spear. It mates along the file from below, typically against a corner or edge king, and a lance drop far from the king can be the quiet engine of a long solution, its threat rolling forward square by square. The pawn is the wall and the pittance. Barred by uchifuzume from drop-mating, it seals flight squares, feeds itself to defenders to open lines, and push-mates legally; the tokin it becomes is a full gold that costs the defense a piece to remove and yields the attack almost nothing to lose. The rook and bishop are the artillery, and their promoted forms are the heart of most long problems. The dragon, rook plus one-step diagonals, is the strongest piece in the game: it pins, it cuts off whole ranks as escape barriers, and adjacent to the king it covers eight squares almost by itself. The horse, bishop plus one-step orthogonals, is famous both as an attacker and as the best defensive piece in shogi, and problems often hinge on luring the defending horse away or capturing it to disarm the defense. The major pieces also serve as fuel: a rook or bishop sacrificed on the king's head to drag it one square forward, into range of golds and silvers waiting in hand, is perhaps the single most common opening gesture in the whole literature, and beginning solvers are taught the proverb that in tsume the most violent-looking sacrifice of the biggest piece is the first candidate to read.

sections.heading: Solving Method: Reading Checks in Order
sections.body: Tsume solving is exhaustive search made humane by heuristics. The mechanical fact underneath everything is that legal checks in any position are finite and enumerable: checks by moving a board piece, checks by dropping each type of piece in hand onto each relevant square, and discovered checks, which exist in shogi as they do in chess. A disciplined solver can always fall back on full enumeration, and on hard problems eventually must. But order matters enormously, and the craft lies in reading the right candidates first. The classical advice is to begin with the most forcing and least plausible moves: sacrifices of the largest pieces, drops directly adjacent to the king, checks that seem to lose material for nothing. Composers know solvers resist giving away a rook, so the rook sacrifice is disproportionately often the key. The second discipline is backward reasoning. Before calculating forward, ask what the final mate could possibly look like given the attacker's hand: with gold and pawn in hand and a rook on the board, the plausible endings are a head gold supported by the rook or a sealed edge with a pawn push, and the middle of the solution is whatever forcibly assembles one of those pictures. Third, count liberties and guards. Note which squares around the king are already covered, which defending piece guards what, and which single defender is overloaded; the defender's most annoying resources, usually a horse or a gold sitting on exactly the right square, mark themselves as targets for deflection. Fourth, prune honestly. A line ends the moment the defender has a reply after which no check exists; abandon it without sentiment, because in tsume there are no quiet moves, and if you cannot find a check you have either missed one, often a long-range drop far from the king or a discovered check, or the line is dead. Fifth, respect the defender. At every defensive turn, list captures of the checker, king moves, and every interposition the defender's hand allows, and remember the convention that the defender holds everything not accounted for; the most commonly missed defense in all of tsume is an interposing drop on a long diagonal, and the second most common is a capture that arms the defender with exactly the piece that refutes your intended finish. Practical solvers also manage themselves. Short problems should be solved entirely in the head from the diagram, because the whole point is training visualization; setting up a board is reserved for long or artistic problems studied for pleasure. Time-boxing helps: give a three-move problem thirty seconds and a nine-move problem fifteen minutes before consulting the answer, then re-solve from scratch the next day, since a solution recalled is a pattern being installed. And when a problem resists everything, apply the composer's-contract test: find the piece on the diagram whose purpose you cannot explain, because the move you have not considered is almost always the one that piece exists to enable or to stop.

sections.heading: Sacrifice Themes: Pulling, Deflecting, and Sealing
sections.body: Nearly every tsume problem beyond the shortest is organized around sacrifice, because the drop rule makes sacrifice cheap to stage and expensive to decline. The sacrificial themes form a small taxonomy worth learning explicitly. The first and most common is the pull, in which a piece is given check on a square adjacent to the king purely so the king will capture it and thereby step onto a square where the real mate works. A rook dropped onto the king's head, taken by the king, followed by a gold drop that now reaches the advanced king, is the archetype of thousands of problems; the rook's only job was to move the king one square. The second theme is deflection, aimed not at the king but at its guards. If a defending gold protects the critical square, check in a way that only that gold can answer, and its capture or its forced move abandons the post; overloaded defenders, guarding two duties at once, are the composer's favorite victims. The third is sealing, in which a sacrificed piece, or the defender's own interposition, ends up occupying a flight square. Here shogi's economy is beautifully perverse: the attacker sometimes checks from long range precisely to force the defender to interpose, because the interposed piece walls in its own king, a motif called the self-block. The fourth is line-clearing and square-clearing: a piece of the attacker's stands on the square or line the mate needs, so it is flung away with check, spending a tempo the defender must answer while the geometry repairs itself. The fifth is conversion, sacrifice as currency exchange: the attacker's hand holds the wrong pieces, so a check is given specifically to be captured by a particular defender, whose capture is then recaptured, swapping material until the hand contains exactly the mating kit. Long classical problems chain these themes into cascades in which every piece the attacker owns is given away, sometimes a dozen sacrifices in sequence, the king marched step by step across the board by successive pulls, until the final picture snaps shut with the last piece in hand and, by convention, nothing left over. Two practical warnings attend all of this. Sacrifices in tsume must still be checks, so the solver's freedom is narrower than in chess problems, and the real question at each fork is which of several checking sacrifices comes first; order is almost always unique, because a premature pull lets the king slip through a gap that a preliminary deflection was supposed to close. And every sacrifice arms the defense, since the captured piece enters the defender's hand; a line that gives the defender a gold early must be read against gold interpositions ever after. The pleasure of the genre lives exactly here, in sequences where material means nothing, the entire army is spent, and the mate arrives with an empty hand.

sections.heading: Defensive Resources: Interposition and the Fight for Escape
sections.body: A tsume problem is only as deep as its defense, and the defender's arsenal deserves systematic respect. Against any check there are at most three kinds of reply: capture the checking piece, move the king, or interpose. Capture comes first in the solver's checklist because it is so easy to miss that a guard, not the king, can take the checker; a sacrifice intended as a pull fails completely if a silver quietly removes it instead. King moves come second, and the skill is bookkeeping: after every attacking move the map of covered squares changes, and kings in problems routinely escape through squares that were sealed a move ago and silently reopened. Interposition is the third and richest resource, because the tsume convention gives the defender every piece not on the board or in the attacker's stated hand, which in practice means the defender can block almost any distant check with almost anything. The choice of interposer is a genuine decision with consequences. The defender normally interposes the cheapest piece available, classically a pawn, because the attacker will usually capture the interposition and gain it; giving the attacker a pawn is the smallest possible gift. But nifu can forbid the pawn on that file, forcing a costlier block, and composers arrange such positions deliberately. The deepest defensive idea in the genre is the chuai, the intermediate interposition: a piece dropped in the path of a sliding check not adjacent to the king, apparently pointless because the attacker simply takes it, which nonetheless changes the game, by altering what the attacker holds in hand, by costing a tempo that lets the king breathe, or by later blocking a line when recaptured on the wrong square. Distinguishing a chuai, which is legitimate and counts in the solution, from a muda-ai, the useless interposition that merely donates material and by convention does not count, requires judging whether the block changes anything but the move count; problems have been celebrated and prized purely for a single astonishing chuai. The defender also fights with captures that arm the hand: taking a sacrificed rook does not just remove a threat, it loads a rook into the defense, and any later long-range check must now be read against a rook interposition. Finally there is flight preparation, defensive moves that answer the current check while opening a future door, the defending gold that blocks a check by stepping to a square where it shields the king today and clears an escape tomorrow. For the solver the moral is procedural: at every defensive turn, enumerate captures, then king moves, then interpositions including every drop type, and play the defender's side with full hostility. Solvers who merely verify their intended line miss the one defense that refutes it; solvers who genuinely try to save the king find the composer's real problem, which is always a dialogue, not a monologue.

sections.heading: A History from Edo Castle to the Twin Peaks
sections.body: Shogi descends from the same Indian ancestor as chess, arriving in Japan by roughly the Heian period, and the drop rule that defines the modern game is usually dated to the sixteenth century. Composed mating problems appear almost as soon as the modern rules stabilize: the earliest surviving collections come from the beginning of the Edo period, traditionally credited to Ohashi Sokei, the first hereditary master, around the start of the seventeenth century. Under the Tokugawa shogunate, shogi was institutionalized in the iemoto system: three hereditary houses, the main Ohashi line, a branch Ohashi line, and the Ito house, held stipends, competed for the lifetime title of Meijin, and answered to the castle for the art's flourishing. Within this system tsume composition became a formal obligation and a form of scholarly display. A newly appointed Meijin customarily presented the shogunate with a collection, typically of one hundred problems, and these presentation volumes, polished over years, drove the art to extraordinary heights. Two of them tower over everything else and are known in the shogi world as the twin peaks. In 1734, Ito Sokan III, then Meijin, presented Shogi Muso, whose title means peerless; its hundred problems were so difficult that the book acquired the nickname "do they mate or don't they," and it is said, with the usual cautions about legend, that some problems went unsolved for generations. In 1755 came Shogi Zuko, composed by Ito Kanju, Sokan's younger brother, a prodigy who died young, before he could take the Meijin title his talent promised. Zuko is generally judged the greater artistic achievement, and its final two problems are landmarks of the entire puzzle literature. Number ninety-nine is the celebrated first smoke-mate, kemuri-zume: the board begins crowded with pieces and the solution consumes them, the position burning down like a stick of incense until at the final mate only the defending king and two other units remain. Number one hundred, called Kotobuki, meaning longevity or felicitation, runs to 611 moves, a record that stood for roughly two centuries and a length achieved not by padding but by vast, engineered machinery of repeated maneuvers that shuttle the king around the board. Both books remain in print, are studied by professionals as training and by composers as scripture, and set the aesthetic standards the art still honors: unique solutions, no wasted pieces, surprise embedded in economy. With the Meiji Restoration the hereditary houses collapsed along with their samurai stipends, and shogi, tsume included, passed through decades of precarious patronage before newspapers discovered that sponsoring the game sold papers. The modern professional association, formed in the twentieth century, inherited the classics; the problem art, having survived the fall of the world that created it, resumed growing, and the Edo masterpieces became what they remain, the classical canon against which every modern composer implicitly competes.

sections.heading: The Modern Composition World: Magazines, Prizes, and Records
sections.body: Modern tsume shogi is organized much like a small literary world, with journals, juries, prizes, record-keeping, and schools of taste. Its center of gravity since 1950 has been the monthly magazine Tsume Shogi Paradise, universally abbreviated Tsume-Para, which publishes new problems from beginners' three-movers to monstrous long works, runs solving ladders in which readers mail in solutions for points, and hosts the debates through which composition standards evolve. The community's highest honor is the Kanju Prize, named for Ito Kanju of Shogi Zuko, awarded annually since the early 1960s to the year's best problems, customarily in short, middle, and long categories; winning one marks a composer for life, much as a major literary prize would. Around the prize culture has grown a connoisseurship of themes with their own vocabulary: smoke-mates that burn a full board down to a bare few pieces, problems whose diagrams draw pictures or spell characters on the grid, problems built to celebrate a specific rule interaction such as a nifu evasion or an uchifuzume dodge, and miniatures that compress a paradox into under ten pieces. The record chase is its own discipline. The Edo record of 611 moves, Kotobuki, stood until the twentieth century, when composers armed with deeper theory of repetition machinery pushed lengths past a thousand; the current summit, accepted since the 1980s, is Microcosmos by Koji Hashimoto, at 1,525 moves the longest problem generally regarded as sound. Its engine is a set of interlocking gear-like maneuvers in which the attacker repeatedly forces the defender through long cyclic tours, each cycle shifting one small thing, and its verification is itself part of its fame: checking by hand that a 1,525-move tree has a unique solution is beyond human patience, and confidence in Microcosmos ultimately rests on exhaustive computer search. That points to the deepest modern change: the computer. Since the late 1990s, specialized solving programs built on proof-number search techniques have been able to crack essentially any orthodox tsume problem, including the longest classics, in seconds to hours, and every serious composer now machine-verifies soundness and uniqueness before publication. Cooks in the classical canon, alternative solutions and flawed problems that had been suspected or disputed for two centuries, were settled definitively; the machines confirmed that the great Edo works were overwhelmingly sound, which only raised their reputation. Computers have not replaced composers, because soundness is the entry fee, not the art; juries reward surprise, economy, unity of theme, and the specifically human experience of a solution that feels inevitable only in retrospect. Alongside the composing world runs a competitive solving scene, headed by the annual national solving championship established in 2004, in which contestants race a clock through problems of escalating length. Its most famous result came in 2015, when Fujii Sota won the open championship at age twelve, defeating adult professionals, and then defended the title in each of the next four years while ascending to the top of professional shogi itself.

sections.heading: Tsume as Training: How Players Actually Use Problems
sections.body: The practical case for tsume shogi rests on how shogi games end. Because captured pieces return as reinforcements, defenses erode rather than simplify, and most decisive games finish in a mutual mating race in which each side attacks the other's king and victory belongs to whoever mates first, often by exactly one tempo. In that race the fundamental question, asked again and again under a ticking clock, is: is there a forced mate here, and how long is it? A player who reads mates quickly and without error can grab material with one hand while counting the opponent's fastest mate with the other; a player who cannot must defend on superstition. Tsume practice trains precisely this faculty, which Japanese players call yomi, reading. The standard regimen, endorsed across generations of professionals, is volume at short lengths: large numbers of one-, three-, and five-move problems solved in the head from the diagram, fast, daily, and repeatedly. The target for a three-mover is seconds, not minutes; the point is not to eventually find the answer but to make the patterns, head golds, rear silvers, knight snipes, sealing pawns, fire automatically, so that in a real game the endgame is recognition rather than search. Re-solving matters as much as solving: a problem revisited after a day and again after a week installs its pattern permanently, which is why players keep worn copies of the same beginner collections for years. As length grows the training goal shifts from pattern to stamina and accuracy of visualization, holding a nine- or eleven-move tree steady in the mind with all defensive branches; professionals commonly warm up with such problems before official games the way musicians run scales. Two honest caveats bound the method. First, tsume is necessary but not sufficient for endgame strength, because real endgames hinge equally on hisshi, brinkmate, the art of creating an unavoidable mate threat with a quiet, non-checking move, and on speed calculation, judging whose attack is faster; problem books exist for both, and a player who studies only checking sequences develops a characteristic blindness for the strongest move of all, the silent one that threatens everything. Second, the artistic long problems, for all their glory, are inefficient as training; a 1,525-move masterpiece teaches wonder, not technique, and even the classical hundred-problem presentation books are graduate literature, not gym equipment. Amateur ranking practice reflects all this: teachers commonly calibrate that comfortable, quick solving of three-movers corresponds roughly to a solid kyu-level player, fluent five- and seven-movers to the neighborhood of amateur dan rank, with all the imprecision such rules of thumb carry. For a self-learner the concrete prescription is unglamorous: a book of three-movers, ten problems a day in the head, yesterday's ten re-solved first, lengths raised only when the current length is boringly easy, and a hisshi collection added once mates feel automatic.

sections.heading: Reading Solutions: Notation East and West
sections.body: Printed tsume solutions are compact strings of coordinates, and reading them fluently is a small skill worth acquiring deliberately. Japanese shogi notation names each square by file then rank, both counted from the perspective of Black, the attacker, who by convention moves up the board. Files run one through nine from right to left as Black sits, written with Arabic numerals; ranks run one through nine from top to bottom, written with kanji numerals. The square in the top-right corner from Black's seat is thus 1-1, the center is 5-5, and the defending king in most problems lives near rank one or two, deep in what would be White's camp. A move is written as a filled or open triangle marking whose move it is, Black's or White's, followed by the destination square, then the piece's character. The pieces appear as single kanji: king, rook, bishop, gold, silver, knight, lance, and pawn each have their own character, and the promoted rook and bishop have their famous names, dragon and horse, while the promoted pawn is the distinctive tokin character. Several suffixes carry load. One character marks promotion, and its negation marks an explicit refusal to promote, which in problems is never decoration, since declining promotion is a recognized theme. Another character, read "utsu," marks a drop when the same piece could alternatively have moved to that square from the board. The character read "do," meaning "same," replaces the coordinates when a piece captures on the square just used by the opponent, a convention that saves ink and confuses beginners, because a long solution can run through several consecutive "same" captures. When two identical pieces could reach the destination, disambiguating characters specify right or left, advancing, sliding sideways, or pulling back. Western players use a transliterated system: files keep their numerals, ranks become letters a through i from White's back rank downward, so the Japanese 1-1 becomes 1a. Piece initials are Latin, with N for knight and L for lance, promotion is a plus sign before the initial, a move is written with a hyphen, a capture with an x, a drop with an asterisk, and promotion or its refusal with a trailing plus or equals: G*5b is a gold dropped on 5b, +P-5c is a tokin stepping to 5c, N-4c= is a knight landing on 4c and declining promotion. Problem lengths are counted in te, individual half-moves, so a nine-te problem contains five attacking and four defending moves. Solutions are printed as the main line only, with parenthetical branches where the defense forks into equally long resistance, and a solver checking an answer should replay every branch, not just the printed spine. One final convention: diagrams state the attacker's pieces in hand explicitly, often in a margin reading "in hand: gold, pawn," and say nothing about the defender's hand, precisely because the rule that the defender holds everything else is assumed knowledge, the genre's silent handshake.

sections.heading: When You Are Stuck: Failure Modes, Cooks, and Practical Advice
sections.body: Every solver stalls, and the stalls have a taxonomy worth knowing because each has its own cure. The most common failure is the missed defense: your beautiful line works against the king move you expected and dies against an interposition you never tested, usually a drop on a long line, or a capture by a guard you had mentally classified as furniture. The cure is procedural hostility, playing the defender's turn as an advocate: list captures, king moves, and every interposition the hand allows, every time. The second failure is illegality: a mating pawn drop that uchifuzume forbids, a pawn drop on a file your own pawn occupies, a knight dropped too deep, a lance dropped on the last rank. These rules live exactly at the margins where mating geometry is tightest, which is why composers build there; re-check the pawn laws in every candidate finish. The third failure is the promotion blind spot. Promotion is optional, and problems exploit both directions: solvers auto-promote and miss mates that need the unpromoted knight's jump or lance's reach, or auto-decline and miss the tokin whose gold-power seals the net. At every entry into the zone, consciously ask which face of the piece the position wants. The fourth failure is miscounting the objective: the problem asks for the shortest mate against longest resistance, and solvers sometimes announce a longer mate that works while the published answer is shorter, or dismiss the correct first move because one defense seemed to survive when it merely resisted longest. A special species of stall is no fault of yours: the cooked or flawed problem. Older books, especially cheap ones, contain problems with dual solutions or outright refutations, and pre-computer classics carried disputed lines for centuries; if a problem from a venerable or dubious source refuses to behave, entertain the possibility that it is broken, a diagnosis modern solving software settles in seconds. Software should otherwise be the last resort, consulted after a genuine attempt, because the training value lives in the struggle; but as a verifier it is superb, and as a mercy on a problem that has eaten a week it is legitimate. Beyond diagnosis, a few field remedies reliably unstick a position. Recount the king's liberties and name the piece guarding each one; the mate usually removes or overloads exactly one guard. Find the composer's strange piece, the lance on an empty file or a pawn far from everything, and ask what future line it blocks or enables, because nothing on a good diagram is decoration. Try the checks you rejected as absurd, biggest sacrifices first. Reverse-engineer from the hand: list the final pictures those pieces can form and work backward. Put the problem down for a day; visualization fatigue is real and sleep repairs it. And when the answer finally comes, do not just nod, replay the whole tree including branches, then re-solve it cold tomorrow. A problem that defeated you is the most valuable one you own, and the habit of returning to it is what turns puzzles into strength.

guides.title: Shogi Openings: Static and Ranging Rook
guides.summary: How shogi openings are organized around the two great rook strategies, Static Rook and Ranging Rook, covering the major systems, castles, and plans of each family and how to study and play them.

sections.heading: Why Openings in Shogi Are Different
sections.body: Shogi, the Japanese member of the chess family, is played on a nine-by-nine board with twenty pieces per side, and it differs from Western chess in one rule that reshapes everything: captured pieces change sides and may be dropped back onto almost any empty square as a move. Because material never leaves the game, there is no simplification toward a quiet endgame; the fighting intensifies as pieces are exchanged, and the side whose king is caught first loses. This single rule dictates the character of shogi openings. In chess, opening theory is largely about fighting for the center and developing pieces quickly. In shogi, the opening is above all about two slower, more architectural projects: building a fortress of generals around your own king, called a castle, and arranging your rook, bishop, pawns, and attacking generals into a formation that can eventually break through the opponent's camp. A shogi opening commonly lasts twenty to forty moves before the first real clash, and professional players may spend most of that time on maneuvers that would look absurdly leisurely in chess. The entire body of shogi opening theory is organized around one question asked of each player: where do you put your rook? The rook, the most powerful ordinary piece, is the engine of nearly every attack. If a player leaves the rook on or near its starting file on the right side of the board and attacks up that wing, the strategy is called Static Rook, in Japanese ibisha. If instead the player swings the rook sideways in the opening to the center or the left half of the board, the strategy is called Ranging Rook, or furibisha, literally a swung or ranged rook. Every named opening in shogi belongs to one of the four resulting matchups: both sides Static Rook, both sides Ranging Rook, or one of each in either color arrangement. This classification is not a scholar's afterthought; it determines which castle each king should hide in, which files will be torn open, which diagonals matter, and which pawn breaks are thematic. A Static Rook player facing a Ranging Rook opponent castles in a completely different place, and thinks about completely different squares, than the same player facing another Static Rook. Learning openings therefore means learning the logic of the two families before memorizing any concrete sequence. This guide explains the board and notation needed to follow opening lines, the principles that govern the first moves, the main castles, and then the major systems of each family: the Yagura, Bishop Exchange, Double Wing Attack, and Side Pawn Capture for Static Rook; and the Fourth File, Third File, Central, and Opposing Rook systems for Ranging Rook, together with the modern struggle between them. The aim is that a reader with only a board, the rules, and this text could reconstruct the mainstream opening repertoire of club-level shogi and understand why each move is played rather than merely that it is played.

sections.heading: The Board, the Pieces, and the Notation You Need
sections.body: A shogi board is a grid of eighty-one squares, nine files wide and nine ranks deep, uncheckered and traditionally made of pale wood. Files are numbered 1 through 9 from right to left as seen by the first player, called Black or sente, and ranks are lettered a through i (or numbered 1 through 9) from the far side toward Black. A square is named file first: 7f means the seventh file, sixth rank. Black sits at the bottom and moves first; White, or gote, sits opposite. Each player begins with one king, one rook, one bishop, two gold generals, two silver generals, two knights, two lances, and nine pawns arranged in three rows: pawns across the third rank from the player, the bishop and rook on the second, and the back rank running lance, knight, silver, gold, king, gold, silver, knight, lance. The pieces are flat wedges identified by characters, not color, and pointed toward the enemy; when captured they are simply turned around, which is what makes drops possible. Moves are written with the piece initial and destination: P-7f means a pawn moves to 7f, S-4h a silver to 4h; a capture is marked with x, a drop with an apostrophe, as in P'5d, and promotion with a plus sign, as in Rx2c+. The rook moves like its chess counterpart, any distance along ranks and files; the bishop any distance along diagonals. Gold generals step one square in any direction except the two rear diagonals; silvers step one square diagonally or straight ahead, which means a silver can retreat diagonally but not straight back. Knights jump two forward and one sideways, only forward, and lances slide straight ahead any distance. Pawns move and capture one square straight forward. The far three ranks form the promotion zone: a piece ending or starting a move there may promote, and pawns, lances, knights, and silvers promote to gold movement, while the rook and bishop gain a king's step in addition to their sliding power, becoming the dragon and the horse, the two strongest pieces on the board. Two restrictions on drops matter constantly in opening theory: you may never have two unpromoted pawns of your own on the same file, and you may not drop a pawn to give immediate checkmate.
