Because each player's rook begins on the second file from their own right edge, Black's rook sits on 2h and White's on 8b, facing each other across the board on mirrored wings. Black's bishop on 8h and White's on 2b share the long diagonal the moment the bishop pawns advance, which is why the very first moves of a game already signal strategic intent. One more convention is essential for reading shogi literature: diagrams and lines are usually given from Black's point of view, and a formation described for Black, such as a rook on 2h and a castle on the left, is mirrored for White, with the rook on 8b and the castle on the right. All the openings described here work identically for either side.

sections.heading: First Principles: Pawns, King Safety, and the Division of Labor
sections.body: Three principles govern sound opening play in shogi, and each follows from the drop rule. The first is that the king must leave the center and enter a castle before serious fighting begins. In chess a lost attack can be survived; in shogi the attacker's captured pieces come raining back as drops, so an exposed king tends to die quickly once any file near it is opened. A castle is a structure of, typically, three generals arranged around a king that has walked two to four squares away from its starting square. Moving the king itself, not just its guards, matters: a king one file further from the action costs the attacker several extra moves and pieces, and professionals speak of the opening race in terms of castle completeness. The second principle is the division of labor between the generals. Golds are the best defenders because their movement, every orthogonal step plus the two forward diagonals, guards all the squares beside and ahead of a castled king, exactly where enemy drops and general attacks arrive, so golds generally stay near the king with their strong face toward the enemy. Silvers, which can advance diagonally and retreat diagonally, are the natural attackers, marching up the board beside the rook's pawn to force exchanges. A common maxim runs: attack with rook, bishop, silver, and a pawn or two; defend with the golds and the remaining silver. An attack built on fewer than three pieces usually fails, because the defender captures the attackers and uses them as reinforcements. The third principle concerns pawns. Shogi pawns capture straight ahead, cannot defend one another, and are the small change of the game: nearly every attack begins with a pawn sacrifice to open a file or to gain a pawn in hand, and a pawn in hand is worth far more than a pawn on the board because it can be dropped at the critical square at the critical moment. Openings are therefore shaped by which pawn advances are safe. Pushing the pawn in front of your rook creates the threat of exchanging it for the opponent's pawn, gaining tempo and a pawn in hand; pushing the pawn on the bishop's diagonal opens your bishop but also invites an early bishop trade; pushing edge pawns prepares attacks along the lance file or creates escape room for a castled king. The first moves of almost every game are drawn from a tiny set: Black plays P-7f, opening the bishop diagonal, or P-2f, preparing to push the rook's pawn, and White answers with the mirrored P-3d or P-8d. From just these choices the game already begins to sort itself into a family. If both sides push rook pawns and keep rooks at home, a Static Rook battle is coming. If one side answers the bishop-diagonal opening by raising the bishop pawn only one square, defending the diagonal with the silver instead, and then swings the rook leftward, a Ranging Rook game has been announced, and both players will redirect their entire development accordingly. Understanding why those redirections happen is the real content of opening study.

sections.heading: Static Rook: The Idea Behind Ibisha
sections.body: Static Rook, ibisha, is the strategy of leaving the rook on its original file, the second file for Black, or moving it only a short distance nearby, and directing the attack up that right-hand wing. Its logic is direct: the rook pawn advances to 2f and then 2e, threatening to exchange itself on 2d; the opponent must respond, and the resulting open or half-open file becomes a permanent avenue for the rook, which aims eventually to promote to a dragon on the enemy back ranks. Because the rook stays on the right, the king walks left, away from the action, and the castle is built on the left side of the board. Static Rook is the older and, by professional consensus over most of the last century, slightly more ambitious strategy: it fights for the initiative in the center and on the rook file rather than conceding the first attack. Its costs are also real. The Static Rook player's bishop diagonal, opened early with P-7f, is a source of both power and anxiety, because bishop exchanges lead to positions where either side may drop a bishop into the other's camp, and a hasty formation collapses to such a drop on a fork of rook and castle. Development in Static Rook games is therefore a careful choreography: the right silver rises to support the rook pawn's advance, the golds step toward the future castle, the king slides leftward one square at a time, and only when the castle is judged sufficient does the attack begin. Within the family, the character of the game depends mostly on what the opponent does. Against another Static Rook player, both rooks glare at each other on the same wing, mirrored, and the fight revolves around timing: whoever attacks first with insufficient preparation is counterattacked through the very file they opened. These double Static Rook games divide into a handful of great systems, distinguished by whether and when the bishops are exchanged and by how far each rook pawn advances: the Yagura, in which both sides build the heaviest castle in the game and maneuver at length; the Bishop Exchange, in which the bishops leave the board on move ten or so and both players fight with bishops in hand; the Double Wing Attack, a symmetrical sprint in which both rook pawns race down the board; and the Side Pawn Capture, a sharp gambit-like line in which Black's rook grabs a loose pawn sideways and the game explodes into tactics within fifteen moves. Against a Ranging Rook opponent the Static Rook player's task changes entirely: the enemy rook is no longer facing yours, the enemy attack will come through the center or your left, and the main questions become which anti-Ranging-Rook castle to build, the quick Boat castle or the deep Anaguma, and whether to counter with a rapid attack before the opponent finishes castling or to out-fortify them and win a long positional siege. Static Rook rewards patience, file control, and precise counting of attack and defense.

sections.heading: Ranging Rook: The Idea Behind Furibisha
sections.body: Ranging Rook, furibisha, is the strategy of swinging the rook leftward in the opening, before the pawn in front of it has advanced, to the fifth, fourth, third, or second file counted from the player's left, and building the game around a compact, resilient formation rather than an early initiative. The systems are named for the destination file from the mover's perspective: Central Rook on the fifth file, Fourth File Rook, Third File Rook, and Opposing Rook, which places the rook on the file directly facing the opponent's rook. The strategic bargain is explicit. The Ranging Rook player usually keeps the bishop diagonal closed with a short pawn move, defends the head of the bishop with a silver, and voluntarily gives up the race to attack first. In exchange the king walks to the right side of the board, away from every file the opponent can easily open, and settles into the Mino castle, a structure that is faster to build than the Static Rook castles, remarkably sturdy against attacks from the side, and easy to reinforce. The typical Ranging Rook game plan is counterattack: invite the Static Rook opponent to commit to an assault, meet it with exact defense, trade pieces, and then use the pieces gained in hand to strike at the enemy king, which is almost always further from safety than one's own. Because the strategy renounces the first blow, its practitioners have historically been described as counterpunchers, and the style attracts players who prefer structure and judgment to memorized forcing lines. Ranging Rook also has a second, more aggressive face. The rook on a central or leftward file supports pawn breaks the opponent must watch: the Central Rook player threatens to ram the central pawn forward and open the middle; the Third File Rook player aims the rook at the file where the Static Rook side's silver usually stands, and in the Ishida style can launch a genuine attack within a dozen moves. The floating rook on a middle rank can even swing back rightward later, a maneuver called the swinging-back rook, striking where the opponent has thinned their defenses. The perennial matchup, Static against Ranging, has an elegant geometry: the two kings castle on opposite wings less often than in chess; instead both kings usually end up on the same side of the board as each other, each behind its own wall, because each king flees its own rook's file. This produces long games of maneuver punctuated by a single decisive breakthrough. Double Ranging Rook games, where both players swing their rooks, are rarer and looser, often turning into fluid middlegames with early rook exchanges. Historically, Ranging Rook dominated amateur play and enjoyed golden ages professionally, notably in the 1970s under Oyama Yasuharu and again in the 1990s when Fujii Takeshi's system revitalized it; computer engines have since favored Static Rook, but at every human level below the very top, Ranging Rook remains fully competitive and is widely recommended as a first serious repertoire because one setup handles almost anything.

sections.heading: Castles of the Static Rook Side: Yagura, Boat, and Anaguma
sections.body: A castle is judged by three qualities: how many moves it costs, how well it resists attack from the direction the game will actually produce, and how much escape room the king retains. The Static Rook player chooses among three main structures depending on the opponent. The Yagura, or fortress, is the classical castle of double Static Rook games and among the most solid in shogi against attack from the front. In its standard Gold Yagura form, Black's king stands on 8h, golds on 7h and 6g, and a silver on 7g, behind a pawn shell on the seventh rank; the essential picture is a three-general wall on the left wing, each general defending the others, with the king tucked in behind it. Building the full structure takes ten to twelve moves, which is affordable only when the opponent is similarly occupied, and that is why the complete Yagura appears almost exclusively when both sides play Static Rook. Its known weaknesses are the side and the edge: a rook attacking from the flank strikes squares the generals do not cover, and a timed sacrifice of pawn and lance up the ninth file can pry the wall open from the outside. Against a Ranging Rook opponent, whose attack arrives from unpredictable files and often from the side, the Yagura is therefore a poor investment, and the Static Rook player instead uses the Boat castle, funagakoi, a quick structure of about four moves: the king slides left to 6h and then often 7h, sheltering beside the silver on 7i and gold on 6i, while the bishop on 8h forms the boat's prow. The Boat castle is thin, but it faces the correct direction, screening the king against the center-left where the Ranging Rook breakthrough will come, and its cheapness buys tempi for a rapid counterattack launched before the opponent finishes reinforcing the Mino castle. When the Static Rook player wants maximum safety rather than speed against Ranging Rook, the choice is the Anaguma, the bear in the hole. The edge lance steps up one square from its corner, the king walks across the back rank and drops into the vacated corner square 9i, a silver seals the diagonal by sitting on 8h, and the golds stack beside it on 7i and 6i. The finished Static Rook Anaguma is the hardest castle in shogi to kill: the king stands as far from the enemy camp as the geometry of the board allows, it cannot even be checked until the wall is physically breached, and the attacker must feed pieces into the corner faster than the defender can drop reinforcements. Its costs are equally famous: construction consumes a dozen moves during which the opponent attacks elsewhere unopposed, the entombed king has no escape route whatsoever, and an Anaguma that starts leaking collapses all at once. Choosing among these three castles is not a matter of taste but of matchup, and recognizing which castle the position calls for is the first mark of a player who understands the opening rather than memorizing it.

sections.heading: The Mino Castle and Its Family
sections.body: The Mino castle is the home of the Ranging Rook king and one of the most efficient defensive structures in any board game: three moves of the king and one of a gold produce a fortress that repels side attacks better than castles costing twice as much. When Black plays Ranging Rook, the rook leaves the 2h square, and the king simply walks rightward along the back rank into the space the rook vacated, stepping 4h, 3h, and finally 2h, while the left gold slides from 6i to 5h. The finished standard Mino places the king on 2h, the silver on 3h, and golds on 4i and 5h, with the pawn chain untouched in front. Every general defends its neighbors; the structure's signature virtue is lateral resilience, because the enemy dragon that eventually invades the back ranks finds the king screened by two golds in its path. The Mino's soft spots are equally well defined: the head of the king, the pawn on 2g, is defended only by the king itself; the edge file can be forced open by a pawn-and-lance sacrifice; and the squares diagonally in front of the golds are famous lever points for enemy pawns. A knight dropped or advancing to attack the 3g square, forking toward the king's head, is the classic Mino-killer, and every Ranging Rook player learns to watch for it. Because the basic Mino is cheap, it upgrades naturally as the game goes on. Advancing the fourth-file pawn and walking the 4i gold up two squares to 4g produces the High Mino, which adds breathing room, covers the lever point, and shields the knight's head, and pushing further still, with the silver climbing to 2g on the third rank, yields the Silver Crown, ginkanmuri, whose silver sits directly over the king's head and answers the Mino's chief weakness. This upgrade path, Mino to High Mino to Silver Crown, is a strategic resource in itself: the Ranging Rook player improves the castle whenever the opponent has no immediate threat, and the three forms resist different attacks, so the defender morphs to meet the danger. There is also a Ranging Rook Anaguma, built in the same corner the Mino occupies but with the king going all the way into 1i behind a lance on 1h, silver on 2h, and golds stacked alongside; it trades the Mino's flexibility for the Anaguma's absolute depth and became a major professional weapon in double Ranging Rook games and against Static Rook rapid attacks. Finally, the Static Rook side sometimes borrows the structure: a Left Mino, built on the left side with the same shape, is the modern anti-Ranging-Rook choice when the Boat castle feels too thin and the Anaguma too slow, and the engine-era elmo castle is a Left Mino variant with a gold and silver swapped for faster counterplay. The Mino family's lesson generalizes: a good castle is not a static wall but a sequence of improvable shapes.

sections.heading: The Yagura Opening: The Classic Double Static Rook Battlefield
sections.body: When both players choose Static Rook and neither forces an early bishop trade, the game usually flows into the Yagura opening, so central to shogi history that a former Meijin called it the pure literature of the game. Both sides spend the first two dozen moves building matching Yagura castles on their left wings while developing their right-side attackers, and the board takes on a mirrored, monumental character: two fortresses facing each other, two rooks on their home files, and a slow tension about who will commit first. The opening's deep logic is a race with brakes. Attacking too early, before your castle is sealed, invites the classic counterstroke of shogi, where the defender absorbs the assault and drops captured pieces around the attacker's half-built house; attacking too late means the opponent's assault lands first, and in shogi the tempo of the first breakthrough is often decisive. Classical Yagura play therefore revolves around a few thematic attacking formations, all launched from the attacker's right wing toward the enemy castle sitting across from it. The most celebrated modern setup places the right silver on 4f and the knight on 3g, supported by pawns, with the rook waiting behind them; from this shape the standard breaks are the pawn levers on 3e and 2e, which pry open files directly over the defending king. An older and still dangerous plan, Spearing the Sparrow, concentrates rook, lance, and knight against the edge file beside the enemy king, threatening to trade everything down the single outside column where the castle is thinnest. The defender meets these plans with precise gold and silver adjustments, and much of twentieth-century professional theory consisted of cataloguing which attacking formation beats which defensive nuance. Two practical motifs matter even at club level. First, the bishop inside a Yagura usually redeploys: it retreats from the blocked home diagonal and re-emerges on the right side, where it bears down the long diagonal toward the enemy castle, and mistiming this maneuver loses material to a rook-file breakthrough. Second, the edge attack is a constant background threat: pushing the ninth-file pawn forward, sacrificing it, and following with the lance strips the castle's corner, and whole matches have turned on a single tempo in these edge races. The Yagura's modern history is sobering for lovers of tradition. Around 2015, professional preparation armed with early rapid-attack systems, particularly plans where White refuses to castle fully and storms the third file with rook, silver, and pawns before Black's Yagura is sealed, drove the classical double Yagura from fashion, and engines confirmed that many hallowed slow lines concede too much initiative. The opening survives in evolved forms with earlier tension and more flexible king placement, and it remains the best training ground for learning attack-and-defense counting: every Yagura game is a lesson in how many pieces a breakthrough needs and how many moves a castle is worth.

sections.heading: Bishop Exchange: Kakugawari
sections.body: The Bishop Exchange opening, kakugawari, arises when both players open their bishop diagonals and one of them, usually within the first ten moves, captures the opposing bishop and accepts the recapture, leaving each side with a bishop in hand for the rest of the game. This single early transaction transforms the character of the opening. A bishop in hand is a loaded weapon: it can be dropped on any safe square to fork rook and castle, to pin a defender, or to seed a mating net, and so both players must arrange every subsequent move so that no such drop is profitable. Formations in Bishop Exchange games are consequently tight and low, with few loose pieces and no undefended forks, and the opening rewards players with a keen eye for drop tactics. Because the exchange usually costs the initiating side one tempo, theory long held that the player who captures first concedes a small disadvantage, and elaborate move-order finesses exist to induce the opponent to capture instead. The strategic plans of the Bishop Exchange divide by what the attacker does with the right silver. In the Climbing Silver plan, the silver climbs step by step in front of the rook and, together with the rook pawn, forces exchanges on the second file that yield a pawn in hand and an open avenue for the rook behind it; the plan is direct, easy to understand, and the recommended first attacking scheme for improving players. In the Reclining Silver plan, koshikake-gin, the silver instead sits on the central square 5f (5d for White), supported by pawns, from which it eyes both wings; the resulting positions are rich and balanced, and the Reclining Silver main lines have been a laboratory of professional theory for eighty years. A third scheme develops the knight early to prepare central and edge strikes. Defensively, both kings usually settle into compact structures around the 8h and 2b squares behind three generals, since the classic full Yagura is too loose when enemy bishop drops are constantly available; the modern preference is a low, flexible wall with golds connected. Bishop Exchange also contains one of shogi's sharpest theoretical battlegrounds, the One-Turn-Loss Bishop Exchange, in which a player deliberately spends an extra tempo, capturing with the king's gold or taking a route that loses a move, to reach a known favorable structure with colors effectively reversed; that professionals willingly burn a tempo to transpose says much about how concrete and well-mapped these lines have become. For the student, the Bishop Exchange teaches three durable skills: counting the value of tempi, maintaining drop-proof formations, and converting a small structural edge into an attack, because with bishops in hand the first player to create a single exploitable weakness usually wins the game outright.

sections.heading: Aigakari: The Double Wing Attack
sections.body: Aigakari, the Double Wing Attack, is the purest expression of Static Rook logic: both players push their rook pawns down the board at full speed, Black advancing on the second file and White symmetrically on the eighth, each aiming to exchange the pawn in front of the rook and seize the initiative. The opening begins 1.P-2f P-8d 2.P-2e P-8e, with both sides ignoring the bishop diagonals entirely, and the first crisis arrives when the pawns reach the fourth rank from the enemy side: each player must decide when to allow the exchange, how to recapture, and whether to grab a further pawn at the cost of time. After the standard sequence in which both rook pawns are traded, both rooks stand on half-open files with a pawn in hand each, and the game becomes a contest of development and precise timing rather than fixed structure, which is why Aigakari has historically been considered an advanced opening: there are few walls to hide behind, and loose play is punished immediately. The classical attacking scheme is the Climbing Silver, in which the right silver walks up beside the rook pawn's file, step by step, to force a second breakthrough on the wing; against passive defense the silver reaches the third rank from the top, exchanges itself, and the rook crashes through to promote. Because a promoted rook on the enemy back rank is worth roughly two ordinary pieces in attacking power, the whole opening can be understood as a race to dragonhood. The defensive resources are equally thematic: each side posts a gold beside its rook's home square early, precisely to guard the square where the opposing rook pawn will arrive, and much of the opening's subtlety lies in when that gold steps up and when it stays put. King safety in Aigakari is minimal and late; kings typically shuffle one or two squares toward the center-left into thin, improvised shelters, because spending eight moves on a castle while the opponent's rook promotes is suicide. Modern professional practice, heavily influenced by engines since about 2017, has revived Aigakari and loosened its conventions: the old rule that the rook should retreat all the way home after the pawn trade has given way to floating placements in which the rook stops partway back on an open rank, and new plans with early central pawn pushes and rapid knight development have made the opening one of the most theoretically active areas in top play. For learners, Aigakari is the best opening for internalizing tempo: every move either creates a threat, answers one, or loses the race, and a single wasted move against a competent opponent converts directly into a lost game, a discipline that improves one's play in every other opening.

sections.heading: Side Pawn Capture: Yokofudori
sections.body: The Side Pawn Capture, yokofudori, is the sharpest of the double Static Rook openings and the closest thing shogi has to a mainline gambit complex. It arises from a rook-pawn race like the Double Wing Attack, but with the bishop diagonals open: after both sides exchange the pawns in front of their rooks, Black's rook, instead of retreating, slides sideways along the fourth rank from the enemy and captures the undefended pawn standing on the third file, the side pawn that gives the opening its name. Taking it wins clean material, a full pawn plus a pawn in hand, but spends several tempi with the most valuable attacking piece while the king still sits in the center, and the whole opening is the story of whether White can convert that lead in development into an attack before Black consolidates. The critical tries are famous and violent. In the immediate rook-confrontation lines, White floats the rook to the center or matches Black's grab by taking the corresponding side pawn, leading to open positions with both rooks airborne and drop tactics everywhere. The historic main tries send White's bishop out early to the aggressive central diagonal squares, aiming at the loose points behind Black's lines, and Black must know precise defensive sequences, because natural-looking moves lose by force to combinations that begin with a bishop or knight sacrifice at the edge of Black's camp. One notorious ultra-aggressive branch, the 4-5 bishop attack, was analyzed for years to near-forced conclusions and can decide the game within twenty-five moves; club players who take the side pawn without knowing it risk losing before their king ever moves. When White declines the immediate assault, both sides typically settle into the low, flexible structure named for the great champion Nakahara: each king takes a single sideways step toward safety, golds link in a low wall, and the middlegame begins with both rooks floating on open ranks, an unusually fluid arrangement by shogi standards in which minor slips cost the exchange or the game. The engine era has treated Side Pawn Capture kindly: computers confirmed that Black's extra pawn is real compensation for the exposed rook, sharpened White's attacking tries, and introduced new resources for both sides, so the opening remains a staple of professional play, favored by players who trust concrete calculation over structure. For students, the opening's value is diagnostic. If you enjoy memorizing forced sequences, calculating drops accurately, and defending with precision under fire, yokofudori will reward you; if you prefer to understand positions by shape and plan, you will likely be happier in the Yagura or in Ranging Rook, and you should at minimum learn the two or three trap lines well enough to decline the pawn safely when a booked-up opponent invites you to take it.

sections.heading: Fourth File Rook: Shikenbisha
sections.body: Fourth File Rook, shikenbisha, is the flagship of the Ranging Rook family, the system most amateurs learn first and the one whose name is nearly synonymous with furibisha. Black announces it by opening the bishop diagonal, defending the bishop's head with the silver, and swinging the rook from 2h to 6h, the fourth file counted from Black's left, then castling the king rightward into the Mino. The rook on 6h does quiet, multipurpose work: it supports the natural break of the sixth-file pawn, defends the bishop's flank laterally, and stands ready to redeploy left or right along its rank as files open elsewhere. The classical battle against a Static Rook opponent has a canonical shape. The Static Rook side builds a Boat castle and chooses between rapid attack and slow siege. Rapid attack plans strike within a dozen moves of castling, most famously by advancing the central pawn and hurling the left silver up the board at the fourth-file formation; named variations include the straight silver assaults and the angle-changing bishop exchanges, and against each of them the Fourth File Rook player has a well-mapped defensive scheme in which the rook, the defending silver, and a timely counter-push of the fourth-file pawn absorb the attack and leave White overextended. The slow plans are the modern main story: the Static Rook king burrows into the Anaguma, and the game becomes the signature strategic matchup of contemporary shogi, a fortress that cannot be quickly killed against a Mino that cannot be quickly reinforced. Against the Anaguma, pure Fourth File Rook suffered for years until Fujii Takeshi, in the mid-1990s, built the Fujii System, one of the most celebrated opening inventions in shogi history: Black delays or forgoes castling entirely, keeps the king on its starting square where it is paradoxically safe from the Anaguma player's standard attacking formations, and uses the saved tempi to launch a precise assault, with edge pawn, knight, and bishop, against the Anaguma's corner before it seals. The system demands exact knowledge, since an uncastled king invites tactics, but it changed professional fashion for a decade and remains the model of concept-driven opening design. Fourth File Rook also spawned radical modern descendants, systems in which the ranging player provokes early pawn exchanges on the rook's new file to activate the rook immediately rather than waiting behind closed lines. The opening's enduring appeal is economy of understanding: one castle, one set of defensive patterns, and one counterattacking philosophy handle nearly everything the opponent can try, which makes shikenbisha the most instructive single opening for a developing player to adopt for a year and the standard recommendation of Japanese teaching literature since the postwar era.

sections.heading: Third File Rook and the Ishida Attack
sections.body: Third File Rook, sankenbisha, moves the rook one file further than Fourth File Rook, to 7h for Black, placing it on the file where the Static Rook opponent's silver and pawn structure naturally stand, and this small difference gives the system a sharper, more provocative character. Where the Fourth File Rook waits, the Third File Rook threatens: the seventh-file pawn can advance with rook support at almost any moment, and if the Static Rook side develops carelessly, the ranging player rips the file open, exchanges pawns, and plants the rook or a dropped pawn deep in enemy territory before a castle is finished. The most famous expression of this energy is the Ishida style, named after Ishida Kengyō, a blind shogi master of the Edo period credited with the original fast attack. In the modern Masuda-refined form, the Quick Ishida, Black pushes the seventh-file pawn early, swings the rook behind it, and only then decides how much to invest in castling; if White grabs space or opens the bishop diagonal casually, Black sacrifices a pawn, floats the rook forward to an active central post, and generates threats that have felled unprepared professionals in under thirty moves. Masuda Yasuharu, one of the great postwar players, systematized these ideas in the 1970s and famously won with what he called the New Ishida, demonstrating that a Ranging Rook system could seize the initiative rather than merely counterpunch, and the line enjoyed a spectacular second youth from around 2010 when top players led by Kubo and later Fujii Sōta revived it with engine-checked improvements. The strategic behavior of Third File Rook against the standard anti-ranging plans differs from its quieter sibling in instructive ways. Against the Static Rook Anaguma, the third-file placement is genuinely annoying: the file the ranging rook pressures is the very file the Anaguma builder must cross with silver and gold to seal the corner, so the burrowing king often comes under fire in transit, and many Anaguma players switch to a different castle rather than face a well-played Ishida. Against rapid attacks, by contrast, the rook on the third file defends its own camp less well than a fourth-file rook does, the central squares behind it are thinner, and precise defense is required when White strikes at the center immediately. Third File Rook players accept this trade because their system carries its own initiative, and the opening attracts stylists who want Ranging Rook's structures with Static Rook's aggression. A characteristic motif worth knowing even if you never play the opening: in many Ishida lines the ranging player deliberately leaves the bishop diagonal closed while attacking, so that the position contains no bishop exchange for the defender to simplify into, and only opens the diagonal at the moment the resulting drop favors the attacker. That principle, open lines only when the exchanges favor you, is the whole philosophy of the system in one sentence, and it generalizes to every opening in the game.

sections.heading: Central Rook and the Gokigen System
sections.body: Central Rook, nakabisha, swings the rook to the fifth file, the exact center of the board, and aims it at the opponent's king position by the shortest path. It is the oldest recorded Ranging Rook strategy, appearing in Edo-period manuals, and in its classical form it is also the most direct: the central pawn advances to 5f and then 5e with rook support, the silver follows through the center, and the plan is simply to break open the middle of the board before the opponent's development can punish it. The modern game, however, belongs to a specific refinement that changed professional shogi at the turn of the millennium: the Gokigen Central Rook, the cheerful or good-mood Central Rook, popularized by Suzuki Daisuke around 2000 and named for its optimistic, fast-playing spirit. Its novelty is move order. The Gokigen player swings the rook to the center very early, before defending the bishop's head the way traditional Ranging Rook demands, and dares the opponent to punish the omission by capturing the bishop or by the direct rook-pawn advance; theory shows the punishment attempts fail or lead to wild, roughly balanced complications, and in exchange the Gokigen player gets an actively placed rook, a quick Mino castle, and central pawn breaks a full tempo faster than classical lines allow. Against it, Static Rook players developed a family of dedicated countermeasures that every Central Rook player must know. The most testing is rapid silver development toward the central files, in which the static side meets the central push head-on with silver and gold reinforcing the fifth-file pawn; another major try is the Super-Rapid attack in which the static side's rook pawn storms forward immediately, gambling that the Gokigen player's unfinished shape cannot absorb a direct hit; and the positional choice is, as ever, the Anaguma, though the central rook's pressure on the middle makes the burrowing slower and riskier than against Fourth File Rook. A separate branch of Central Rook theory embraces true double-edged play: the twisting Central Rook lines in which the ranging player answers a bishop exchange by recapturing toward the center and accepts a slightly airy king in return for a massive pawn center. Strategically, Central Rook teaches the value and cost of the center in a drop game. The central files are where promoted pieces are most powerful and where a breakthrough threatens both wings at once, but the center is also where the defender's counter-drops are most effective, because every open central square is a landing pad for enemy pieces as well as your own. Central Rook players therefore learn, faster than anyone, the discipline of opening the position only when their own castle is the sturdier one, and games between Central Rook and Static Rook remain among the most theoretically contested and double-edged in modern professional practice.

sections.heading: Opposing Rook and the Static-Ranging Arms Race
sections.body: Opposing Rook, mukaibisha, is the Ranging Rook system that swings the rook all the way across to face the opponent's rook file directly, to 8h for Black against White's rook on the eighth file. At first glance this looks like standing in front of a cannon, and that is precisely the point: the opposing rook waits behind its own pawn wall on the very file the Static Rook player most wants to open, so that when the static side finally achieves the thematic pawn exchange, the file opens onto a loaded gun pointing back. Classical Opposing Rook is thus the great counterattacking weapon against an overeager rook-pawn advance, and several trap-rich lines punish a Static Rook player who pushes the rook pawn to the fifth rank prematurely by opening the file and winning the exchange or the game outright. The system pairs naturally with an early bishop trade: with bishops in hand and the rook files facing, a single mistimed pawn push lets the Opposing Rook player drop a bishop into the resulting hole and fork camp and castle, which is why bishop-exchange Opposing Rook, and its aggressive modern cousin the direct Opposing Rook, in which the rook swings across before the diagonal is even settled, remain dangerous practical choices at every level. Beyond its concrete lines, Opposing Rook completes the strategic map of the Static-versus-Ranging arms race, which is worth understanding as a system because it explains why openings rise and fall. The static side's fundamental resources are the rapid attack, striking before the Mino castle is reinforced, and the deep fortress, the Anaguma, out-arming the Mino in a long game. The ranging side's answers are structural flexibility, upgrading Mino to High Mino to Silver Crown as the game demands, its own Anaguma in double ranging games, and system-level inventions like the Fujii System that attack the fortress while it is being built. Each era's fashion is a response to the previous counter: the Anaguma's rise in the 1980s drove classical Fourth File Rook into decline, the Fujii System revived it in the 1990s, engine preparation sharpened the static side's rapid attacks in the 2010s, and modern professional Ranging Rook increasingly means Third File Rook and Gokigen Central Rook, the two most initiative- seeking members of the family, with Opposing Rook as a surprise weapon. Amateur practice lags these fashions by decades, happily, because at club level every one of these systems is fully sound, and the player who understands the logic of the arms race, what each formation is for and what beats it, will outplay the player who has memorized twice as many concrete moves. If you adopt Ranging Rook, learn one primary system deeply, keep Opposing Rook in reserve for opponents who telegraph the rook-pawn rush, and study the static side's two master plans from both sides of the board, because you will face them forever.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Traps, and How Openings Go Wrong
sections.body: Opening disasters in shogi follow recognizable patterns, and a reader who internalizes the five most common ones will avoid most opening losses without memorizing anything further. The first and greatest is the unprotected bishop-head. The bishop's forward diagonal squares are defended, at the start, only by precise arrangement, and the moment the diagonal opens, a silver or the opposing bishop can descend on the square in front of your bishop with tempo; entire trap systems, including the notorious early bishop-exchange rook-swing tricks, exist to punish players who open the diagonal and then make one indifferent move. The countermeasure is a habit: whenever the bishop diagonal opens, ask what now attacks the head of my bishop and my 2b or 8h square before anything else. The second failure mode is castling into the attack, building the right castle against the wrong opponent: a Yagura against a Ranging Rook player, or a slow Anaguma against an opponent whose formation is already aimed at your corner. Castles are directional armor, and the opening classification exists precisely to tell you which direction the blow will come from. The third is the premature attack, launching with two pieces where three were needed, or attacking before your castle is closed; the position-level symptom is that your attack trades off and the opponent's hand fills with your pieces, which then land around your half-finished king. The fourth is pawn-drop blindness. Because no file may hold two of your unpromoted pawns, every pawn you push and every pawn you trade changes which files you can later seal or attack with drops; strong players count pawns in hand the way chess players count material, and a player who thoughtlessly trades away the pawn that will be needed to block a file has often lost the game an hour before it ends. The fifth is move-order carelessness in known positions: shogi theory is full of near-identical sequences in which one transposition is fine and the other loses a piece to a two-move drop combination, and the practical defense is not deeper memorization but the discipline of checking every check, capture, and drop the opponent has after each of your intended moves. When an opening has already gone wrong, the recovery principles are constant across all systems. Do not try to hold material at the cost of king safety; shogi punishes greed faster than chess because captured material returns as enemy reinforcements. Simplify toward positions where your castle is the sturdier one, even at the cost of a pawn or the exchange, since the race to the king is the only score that matters. If your castle is the weaker one, complicate instead, keep pieces on the board, and seek perpetual-check resources, which draw in shogi only through repetition rules and are often the defender's honest best outcome. And after the game, trace the loss backward to the first move that violated a family principle, because in shogi openings, unlike much of chess, the principles really do decide the games.

guides.title: Xiangqi: Chinese Chess Explained
guides.summary: A complete introduction to xiangqi, the Chinese form of chess: the board, every piece and its rules, checkmate and repetition law, opening systems, tactics, endgame theory, history, and how to study the game seriously.

sections.heading: What Xiangqi Is and Why It Matters
sections.body: Xiangqi, usually rendered in English as Chinese chess, is a two-player strategy game played on the intersections of a nine-by-ten grid of lines, and by most serious estimates it is one of the most widely played board games on Earth. Across China, Vietnam, and the Chinese diaspora, hundreds of millions of people know its rules, and it is a common sight in parks, teahouses, and street corners, where clusters of onlookers gather around a single board and offer loud, unsolicited advice. The name combines xiang, a character that can mean elephant or image, with qi, meaning board game; the same second syllable appears in weiqi, the game known in the West as Go. Xiangqi belongs to the same broad family as Western chess, shogi in Japan, and janggi in Korea, all of which are generally traced back to ancestors of the Indian game chaturanga, though the exact lines of descent are debated and Chinese scholars have long argued for substantial native invention. Whatever its precise origin, the game reached something close to its modern form during the Song dynasty, roughly the eleventh and twelfth centuries, and it has been played essentially unchanged for about nine hundred years. For a player who already knows Western chess, xiangqi is both familiar and disorienting. There are kings, rook-like chariots, knight-like horses, and pawn-like soldiers, and the goal is still checkmate. But the pieces stand on line intersections rather than squares, two fortified palaces confine the kings and their advisors, a river divides the board and changes what several pieces may do, and the cannon, a piece with no Western equivalent, captures by leaping over an intervening piece. The practical result is a game that is sharper and more open than Western chess from the very first moves: the files are open because soldiers do not stand shoulder to shoulder, the chariots come out early, and direct attacks on the king begin almost immediately. Draws are considerably less common at amateur level than in Western chess, partly because of the open character of the play and partly because the rules deliberately punish passive repetition. The game also carries a distinctive cultural weight. Its board commemorates a real war, the Chu-Han contention of 206 to 202 BC that ended with the founding of the Han dynasty, and its literature includes printed manuals more than three centuries older than any comparable Western chess book that survives in wide circulation. Learning xiangqi therefore rewards two kinds of curiosity at once: the tactical and strategic pleasure of a deep, fast, unforgiving chess variant, and a window into Chinese history, language, and everyday social life. This guide assumes no prior knowledge of any chess-family game, though comparisons to Western chess appear wherever they genuinely help, and it aims to take a reader from an empty board to competent, self-improving play.

sections.heading: The Board: Files, Ranks, River, and Palaces
sections.body: A xiangqi board is a grid of nine vertical lines, called files, crossed by ten horizontal lines, called ranks, producing ninety intersections. Pieces stand on the intersections, not inside the rectangles, exactly as stones do in Go, and they move along the drawn lines from point to point. This is the first habit a Western chess player must unlearn: there are no light and dark squares, no diagonals of color, and the geometry of the game is the geometry of the lines themselves. Between the fifth and sixth ranks runs a horizontal band with no vertical lines drawn through it. This is the river, and on a traditional board it carries the inscription chu he han jie, meaning the Chu River and the Han border, a reference to the truce line between the rival warlords Xiang Yu of Chu and Liu Bang of Han during the civil war of 206 to 202 BC. The river is not a wall; most pieces cross it freely, and a piece standing on the rank at its edge is simply on that rank. But it changes the powers of two piece types: elephants may never cross it, and soldiers gain a new power once they do. At each end of the board, centered on the back three ranks, is a three-by-three arrangement of nine points with two diagonal lines drawn corner to corner through its middle. This is the palace, sometimes called the fortress, and it permanently confines each side's general and both advisors. The diagonals of the palace are real lines of movement: advisors travel only along them, and a chariot or cannon aimed through the palace corners can exploit them in some mating patterns. Because the palace has only nine points and the general only ever occupies one of them, attacking play in xiangqi is unusually concrete; a mating attack is always an attack on a tiny, known region. Players conventionally sit at the short ends, and each numbers the files one through nine from their own right, which means the two players use different numbers for the same physical line; file one for Red is file nine for Black. This convention matters because standard game notation is written from the moving player's perspective. The central file, file five for both players, passes through the middle of each palace and is the single most important line on the board, since the generals begin on it and can never leave the three files of the palace. A full-size tournament board is typically printed on paper or cloth roughly forty by forty-five centimeters, and the pieces are flat wooden or plastic disks about three centimeters across, stacked easily and read from above. Nothing about the equipment is elaborate, which is one reason the game is played so casually and so widely: a paper board, thirty-two disks, and a flat surface are the entire material requirement.

sections.heading: The Pieces: Names, Characters, and Values
sections.body: Each side commands sixteen pieces of seven types: one general, two advisors, two elephants, two horses, two chariots, two cannons, and five soldiers. The pieces are flat disks marked with a Chinese character, and one side, conventionally called Red, plays against the other, called Black, though actual sets may use red against blue, green, or plain wood. A charming and initially confusing feature is that several piece types are written with different characters on the two sides even though the pieces move identically. Red's general is shuai while Black's is jiang; Red's advisors are shi written one way, Black's with a slightly different character pronounced the same; Red's elephants are xiang meaning minister while Black's are xiang meaning elephant; and Red's soldiers are bing while Black's are zu. Chariots, horses, and cannons also often differ by a radical. The doubling is partly literary flourish and partly a practical aid, since it lets a player identify ownership of a piece at a glance even when disks are unpainted. Western literature abbreviates the pieces with letters: K or G for the general, A for advisor, E or B for elephant, H or N for horse, R for chariot, C for cannon, and P for soldier. Understanding relative value is as important in xiangqi as in Western chess, and a widely taught scale, useful though never absolute, runs roughly as follows if a soldier before the river is worth one: a soldier that has crossed the river is worth about two, an advisor or an elephant about two, a horse about four, a cannon about four and a half, and a chariot about nine. The chariot is thus overwhelmingly the strongest piece, roughly as dominant as a queen is in Western chess, and games are frequently decided by who activates chariots faster. The cannon is slightly stronger than the horse in the opening and middlegame, when the board is crowded with potential screens for it to leap over, but it weakens as the board empties, while the horse strengthens in open positions because fewer pieces block its path; experienced players say cannons love a full board and horses love an empty one. Advisors and elephants have almost no attacking power, since neither can ever cross into the opponent's half, but their defensive worth is enormous, and many endgames are drawn or won purely on the question of whether the defender's advisor-and-elephant shell is intact. The starting position places, from each player's left along the back rank: chariot, horse, elephant, advisor, general, advisor, elephant, horse, chariot. The cannons stand on the third rank, each on the file just inside the horses, and the five soldiers stand on the fourth rank on alternating files, one on every odd file. Because the soldiers begin spaced apart with gaps between them, every file is half-open from the start, which is a structural reason the game is so immediately tactical.

sections.heading: The General and the Advisors
sections.body: The general is the heart of the game: the entire object of xiangqi is to checkmate the enemy general, and every rule about the palace exists to shape that hunt. The general moves one point at a time, forward, backward, left, or right, never diagonally, and it may never leave the nine points of its palace. Nine reachable points, four possible directions, no escape run to a far corner: the general is a nearly stationary target, and this single fact explains much of the game's character, because attacks do not need to chase the king across the board as they do in Western chess. To this confinement the rules add one famous and startling provision, usually called the flying general rule. The two generals may never stand on the same file with no piece of either color between them; a move that would create that naked face-off is illegal. The fiction is that either general could fly the length of the board and capture the other, and the rule is enforced as if that capture were real. In practice the rule means each general exerts a rook-like power along its file into the enemy camp whenever the file is otherwise empty, and strong players exploit this constantly: a general stepping sideways can pin an enemy piece to the opposing general, deliver a decisive supporting attack in an endgame, or deny the enemy general a flight point. Many mating combinations end not with a piece giving check but with the defending general finding that every escape point is covered by the attacker's distant general across an open file. The two advisors, sometimes translated as guards or mandarins, are the general's bodyguards. An advisor moves exactly one point diagonally, and only along the drawn diagonal lines of the palace, which restricts each advisor to five points: the palace center and its four corners. Advisors can never leave the palace, never give check, and never participate in an attack; their entire function is to shield the general, principally by occupying the palace center or blocking the diagonals against enemy chariots and horses. Because the advisor's five points all touch the palace center, a single advisor sitting on the center point blocks both palace diagonals at once, which is its most efficient defensive post. The standard defensive formation, with both advisors and both elephants intact, is proverbially difficult to break with a lone chariot, and a great deal of practical endgame technique consists of either preserving or dismantling this shell. A player who carelessly trades away advisors early often discovers twenty moves later that a routine enemy chariot invasion has become unanswerable. Conversely, the advisors can obstruct their own general; a surprising number of checkmates work because the general's flight point is occupied by its own bodyguard, so good defenders keep one eye on the escape geometry of the palace rather than reflexively centralizing an advisor at the first threat.

sections.heading: Elephants: The River-Bound Defenders
sections.body: The elephant moves exactly two points diagonally in a single move, no more and no fewer, landing two files and two ranks away from where it started. Two restrictions define its life. First, the move is blocked if the intermediate diagonal point, the single point one step diagonally along the way, is occupied by any piece of either color; Chinese players call this blocking point the elephant's eye, and to block it is to stuff the elephant's eye, a standard small tactic that can paralyze the defense at a critical moment. Second, the elephant may never cross the river. Since it starts on its own side and moves in fixed two-point diagonal hops, each elephant can only ever reach seven points on the entire board, all in its own camp: the two starting elephant points, the central point on its side of the river where the two elephants' paths cross, and four points on the edge and third rank. This tiny range makes the elephant purely defensive, and its Chinese name on the Red side, written with the character for minister rather than elephant, underlines its courtly, stay-at-home role. Defensively, however, the elephants matter enormously. The canonical setup posts one elephant on the central point of the third rank, where it simultaneously shields the palace, connects with its partner, and guards key soldier points; the two elephants defend each other when linked this way, since each stands on the other's movement path. Together with the two advisors they form the full shell that endgame theory treats as the standard defensive unit: the phrase full advisors and elephants describes a defender with all four minor defenders intact, and whole chapters of classical manuals are devoted to which attacking forces can and cannot crack that shell. An elephant also has one modest aggressive use: standing on the river's edge points it defends the crossing points of its own soldiers and controls the points an enemy horse would like to use to invade. The elephant's weaknesses are just as concrete. Because its eye can be stuffed, a single enemy soldier or horse planted on the right diagonal point can switch an elephant off entirely. Because both elephants want to link through the same central point, capturing one elephant often devalues the other. And because elephants cannot cross the river, they can never help a counterattack; a player who is losing the attacking race gains nothing from them. Beginners commonly make two opposite mistakes with elephants. The first is moving them too little, leaving the palace naked to a central cannon battery that a timely central elephant would have blunted. The second is moving them too much, spending early tempi shuffling defenders while the opponent seizes open files with chariots. The sound habit is to make one elephant move early to the central point in most openings, keep the pair connected, and thereafter touch them only when a threat demands it.

sections.heading: Horses: Power with a Hobble
sections.body: The horse moves one point orthogonally, along a file or rank, and then one point diagonally outward, continuing away from its starting point, ending two files and one rank away or two ranks and one file away, exactly the eight destinations of a Western chess knight. The crucial difference is that the xiangqi horse does not jump. If the adjacent orthogonal point that begins its move, the point one step along the file or rank in the direction of travel, is occupied by any piece of either color, that entire direction is forbidden. Chinese players say the horse's leg has been hobbled, and hobbling the horse is one of the most common tactical motifs in the game: a single soldier stepping to the right point can freeze a horse out of an attack, and many combinations begin by first tying a defending horse's leg so that it cannot recapture. Note carefully that the blocking point is the orthogonal one next to the horse, not the diagonal landing area; a horse on a crowded board may have all eight destinations empty and still be unable to move at all if its four adjacent points are occupied. In the opening, each horse typically develops one step toward the center, to the point in front of its neighboring cannon file, from which it defends the central soldier and eyes the river crossing. The formation with both horses developed this way is called the screen horses formation, because the horses stand like a screen in front of the central files, and it is the classical answer to the central cannon opening. A horse that reaches the enemy camp gains sharply in power, because near the enemy palace its forking range covers the general's confined quarters; specific invading posts even have names in Chinese praxis, such as the horse reaching the point diagonally in front of the enemy palace corner, from which a famous family of mates called the trough horse mates is delivered. Horses combine venomously with cannons: a standard winning pattern, literally named cannon behind the horse, places a horse giving check adjacent to the enemy general's file while a cannon lines up behind the horse, using it as the screen, so that capturing or blocking the horse walks into the cannon. In endgames the horse's value rises as the board empties and its legs are freed, and a bare horse can defeat a lone advisor or force mate against a bare general given the opposition of generals, results codified centuries ago in classical manuals. Its permanent weaknesses are the hobble, its slowness across the wide nine-file board, and its awkwardness at close quarters when defending its own palace, where its own advisors and general occupy the very points it needs. Handling horses well means constantly reading four little points around each horse, yours and the opponent's, and treating every soldier advance partly as a question about whose horse just gained or lost a leg.

sections.heading: Chariots and Cannons: The Heavy Artillery
sections.body: The chariot moves any number of vacant points along a file or rank and captures the first enemy piece in its path, exactly like a Western rook, and it is the strongest piece in xiangqi by a wide margin, worth about as much as a horse and cannon together. Because the soldiers begin on alternating files with gaps between them, files open far earlier than in Western chess, and chariot activity dominates the game from the first moves. A standard piece of proverbial advice tells players that a chariot left undeveloped for ten moves is a lost chariot; the practical rule is to connect and activate both chariots as fast as the position allows, seizing an open file or the powerful points on the river bank, from which a chariot controls both halves of the board. The chariot's favorite posts have names: the file directly in front of the enemy palace corner, the riverbank rank, and the enemy's second rank, called the bottom rank attack, where a chariot confines the general and combines with other pieces for back-rank style mates. The cannon is xiangqi's signature piece and has no counterpart in any other major chess variant. It moves exactly like a chariot when not capturing: any number of vacant points along a file or rank. But it captures differently: to take an enemy piece, the cannon must leap over exactly one intervening piece of either color, called the screen or the cannon mount, and land on the enemy piece beyond it, with all points between cannon and screen, and between screen and target, vacant. It cannot capture an adjacent piece with nothing to jump over, and it cannot jump two screens. This capture rule creates a paradoxical piece whose power depends on other pieces. On the crowded opening board, screens are everywhere, and the cannon is a terror; the single most popular first move in xiangqi, played for at least four centuries, moves a cannon to the central file, where it aims through its own soldier at the enemy central soldier and, behind that, at the general itself. As pieces are exchanged and the board empties, the cannon fades, and cannon-for-horse trades that favor the cannon in the opening favor the horse in the endgame. The cannon's dependence on screens produces rich tactics. A defending piece pinned as a screen dares not move, or the piece behind it falls; a cannon can check by hopping over the enemy's own advisor, making the defender's bodyguard the instrument of attack; and in the endgame an attacking cannon often retreats behind its own advisor, using its own bodyguard as a permanent mount to check the enemy palace, a technique so standard that endgame theory values cannon plus advisor far above cannon alone. Two cannons stacked on one file form the double cannon battery, where the front cannon serves as the rear cannon's screen; aimed at the central file against a general this battery delivers a family of quick mates that every beginner must learn to survive.

sections.heading: Soldiers: Small Steps, Growing Power
sections.body: Each side begins with five soldiers standing on the fourth rank on alternating files, so that a soldier occupies every other file and every file contains exactly one soldier of each color or none. Before crossing the river, a soldier may move only one point straight forward. It captures the same way it moves, directly forward onto an occupied point, which distinguishes it sharply from the Western pawn with its diagonal capture; there are no pawn chains in xiangqi, no locked structures, and two opposing soldiers standing face to face on adjacent points simply threaten to capture each other. A soldier can never move backward under any circumstances, and it can never move sideways while still on its own half of the board. The moment a soldier crosses the river onto the enemy's half, it gains the sideways step: from then on it may move, and capture, one point forward or one point left or right. This promotion by geography rather than by reaching a final rank is unique among the major chess variants, and it changes the soldier's worth dramatically; the traditional valuation doubles a soldier's value once it crosses, and a soldier that reaches the ranks beside the enemy palace, where its sideways step attacks palace points, is often worth as much as a minor piece. There is a corresponding decline at the far end. A soldier that marches all the way to the enemy's back rank gains nothing there and loses its forward move entirely, leaving it only the two sideways steps; players call it an old soldier, and though it can still shuffle along the last rank and occasionally deliver a mating touch, its force is largely spent. Good soldier play therefore aims soldiers at the fifth, sixth, and seventh points of their journey, not at the end of the board. Several conventions of soldier handling are worth learning early. The central soldier is the most valuable of the five, because it shields the central file where both generals live and because its advance opens the diagonal for the central cannon battery; pushing it prematurely, or losing it, exposes the palace's front door. The soldiers on the third and seventh files are the usual spearheads, since advancing one of them frees the adjacent horse's leg and opens a half-file for a chariot. Edge soldiers advance mostly to open a path for an attacking chariot along the flank or to trade themselves for an enemy edge soldier and create an outside passed file. Because there are only five soldiers and they cannot defend one another head-on, soldier shields evaporate quickly, and a player must decide early whether a given soldier is an attacker, to be pushed across the river as a battering ram, or a defender, to be left in place guarding horse legs and elephant eyes. Sacrificing a soldier to hobble a horse, stuff an elephant's eye, or open a file at the right moment is routine and often the cheapest good investment on the board.

sections.heading: Check, Checkmate, Stalemate, and Winning
sections.body: Red moves first, players alternate single moves, and passing is never allowed. A general is in check when the opponent could capture it on the next move, and the checked player must immediately parry the check by moving the general, capturing the checking piece, or interposing a piece; against a cannon check, uniquely, a defender can also parry by removing the screen the cannon jumps over, or by adding a second piece between cannon and general, since a cannon needs exactly one screen and two blockers are as safe as none. Announcing check aloud, saying jiang, is customary in casual play though not required in formal play. A player who cannot parry a check is checkmated and loses. Xiangqi departs from Western chess decisively on the question of stalemate: a player whose general is not in check but who has no legal move at all loses the game; there is no draw by stalemate. This rule keeps late endgames honest, since a bare general cannot shuffle into a corner and claim half a point, and it creates a real winning method in which the attacker deliberately strangles rather than mates. Perpetual check is likewise forbidden, in all rule sets: a player who checks repeatedly in a cycle of repeating positions must vary or lose, so there is no escape hatch of endless checks for a losing attacker. The related rule against perpetual chasing goes further and is the most distinctive feature of xiangqi law: with narrow exceptions, a piece may not endlessly attack the same unprotected enemy piece move after move through a repeating cycle. The details of chase law are genuinely intricate and differ among the Chinese national rules, the older Asian rules, and the World Xiangqi Federation rules used internationally; positions exist that experienced arbiters must adjudicate from published casebooks, and honest players simply avoid extended one-piece harassment. The practical summary a learner needs is this: repetition designed to force the game into a loop is generally illegal for the side doing the forcing, and if both sides repeat harmlessly without check or chase, three-fold repetition of the position leads to a draw. Draws also arise by agreement, and in tournament play by move-count rules when no capture or crossing occurs over a long sequence. Beyond checkmate and strangling, most decisive games end by resignation once material loss becomes hopeless, exactly as in Western chess; being a full chariot down without compensation is resignable between strong players. Timing rules in serious play use clocks much as chess does, commonly with a base time and an increment or a move quota, and touch-move applies in formal events: a touched piece that has a legal move must be moved. A final courtesy rule of the parks is worth knowing: onlookers advising the players, though universal, is traditionally deplored, and the proverb says a true gentleman watches chess without speaking.

sections.heading: The Repetition Laws in Practice
sections.body: Nothing in xiangqi confuses newcomers from the Western chess world more than the law of repetition, so it deserves unhurried treatment with concrete cases. The foundational principle is that the burden of varying falls on the player who is forcing the repetition, and forcing is defined by what the repeated moves threaten. A perpetual check is the clearest case: if the sequence of one player's moves in a repeating cycle consists entirely of checks, that player must deviate, and if they refuse, they lose. It does not matter that in Western chess the same sequence would rescue a half point; in xiangqi, checking forever is a losing strategy, full stop. The second case is the perpetual chase. Suppose your chariot attacks an enemy horse that is undefended, the horse steps aside, your chariot pursues and attacks it again, the horse returns, and the position repeats. Under all major rule sets this endless chase of an unprotected piece is illegal for the chasing side, which must vary or lose. The logic is the same as with perpetual check: a threat you can renew forever is a way of freezing the game, and xiangqi law refuses to let the game be frozen by the side making threats. Around this principle the rule sets differ in their fine print. Chinese national rules, the strictest and most elaborate, classify many mixed cycles, one check and one chase alternating, two pieces chasing in turn, chases of a piece that is protected only nominally, and resolve each with tables of precedent; the Asian rules used historically in much of Southeast Asia are somewhat more permissive; and the World Xiangqi Federation rules aim for a compromise that arbiters of different traditions can apply consistently. A few reliable simplifications cover almost everything an improving player will meet. Chasing a soldier that has not crossed the river is generally allowed, since such a soldier is deemed too minor to protect by law. A general or a soldier doing the chasing is generally exempt, on the theory that the weakest units may harass freely. Attacking a piece that is genuinely protected is not a chase at all, because the threat is not real; and threatening mate repeatedly, as opposed to check, is treated in most sets like a chase and is illegal to sustain forever. When both players repeat and neither side's moves are checks or chases, for example two chariots shadowing each other along a file with no capture threatened, the position is a dead repetition and is drawn after threefold occurrence. In online play the server enforces whichever rule set it implements and will simply forbid or adjudicate the repetition, which makes internet play a painless way to absorb the law by experience. Over the board, the etiquette is to state that the position has repeated, count the cycle aloud if needed, and consult an arbiter in formal play. The strategic moral runs deeper than legality: because repetition favors the defender, the attacker in xiangqi must always be building something, and an attack that can only repeat has, by definition, failed.

sections.heading: Opening Principles and the Central Cannon
sections.body: Xiangqi openings develop faster and clash sooner than Western chess openings, but the underlying principles are recognizably the same: develop the strong pieces quickly, fight for the center, do not move the same piece repeatedly without reason, and do not open lines toward your own general. The single most important opening move in the game's history is the central cannon: on the first move, one cannon slides to the central file, taking aim through the friendly central soldier at the enemy central soldier and, beyond it, the enemy general. This move, recorded as the main line in manuals from the Ming dynasty onward, immediately threatens to capture the central soldier with check-like pressure and forces Black to answer the center at once. Roughly half of all serious games still begin with it. Black's two classical replies define the game's oldest debate. The first is the screen horses defense: Black develops both horses toward the center so they jointly defend the central soldier, accepts a slightly passive but resilient structure, and counterattacks later against Red's advanced pieces; whole books, most famously the seventeenth-century manual Plum Flower Manual, are devoted to this single family. The second is the symmetrical reply: Black answers the central cannon with a central cannon of the same file or the opposite file, leading to the same-direction cannons and opposite-direction cannons systems respectively, both sharp and heavily analyzed. Beyond these, a player will quickly meet the elephant opening, in which the first move raises a central elephant, declining early conflict and preparing a solid shell, favored in modern professional play for its flexibility; the pawn opening, advancing the third or seventh file soldier to free a horse first; and the three-step tiger, a scheme in which a player develops a cannon to the flank and swings a chariot out along the opened edge file within three moves. Whatever the system, a few concrete habits separate sound opening play from flailing. Activate chariots by the fifth or sixth move; a chariot reaching an open file or the riverbank early is worth more than any subtle maneuver. Do not grab the central soldier with the central cannon prematurely, since the capture usually costs the cannon its safety and surrenders the initiative to a screen horse counterattack. Move one central elephant up early in most defensive schemes, keep the horse legs unhobbled when advancing soldiers, and advance the third or seventh soldier one step early, because that single step frees your horse and can never easily be exploited. Castling does not exist and is not needed, since the general starts in its fortress; the defensive analogue is completing the advisor-elephant shell before the middle game hits. Finally, respect tempo arithmetic. Because chariots and cannons come out so fast, being two developing moves behind in xiangqi is roughly as dangerous as being four behind in Western chess, and many miniature losses are nothing but three lazy early moves punished by a chariot invasion on move nine.

sections.heading: Middlegame Tactics and the Named Mates
sections.body: The middlegame in xiangqi is a tactical storm, and its recurring patterns have been named, cataloged, and drilled for centuries. The fundamental motifs will look familiar to any chess player: the fork, one piece attacking two targets, at which the horse and the crossed-river soldier excel; the pin, freezing a piece against the general or a chariot; the discovered attack, uncovered when a screen moves; and the sacrifice to strip the palace of defenders. But xiangqi adds motifs of its own born of cannon and palace geometry. The cannon pin holds a defender in place as a screen: if the screen moves, the piece behind it is captured, so the screen is paralyzed even though nothing directly attacks it. The double check with cannon and the piece that unmasks it is especially venomous, because interposition cannot answer two checks at once and the general has so few flight points. The elephant eye and horse leg motifs, stuffing the diagonal point or the orthogonal point to switch off a defender, begin countless combinations, and the flying general threat converts an open central file into a mating net from across the board. Every student learns a core set of named mates. Cannon behind the horse: a horse gives check while a cannon stands behind the horse on the same line, using it as a screen, so the check cannot be met by capturing the horse; the pattern wins innumerable endgames. The trough horse mate: a horse invades to the point beside the enemy palace's front corner, checking the general on its starting point while covering escape points, usually finished by a chariot on the back rank. The iron bolt mate: an attacking cannon posts on the central file using the enemy's own central advisor as its screen, while the attacker's general seizes the file across the board to pin everything; a chariot then slides to the palace's side and the door is bolted shut. The double cannon mate: two cannons stacked on the central file, front one screening for the rear, force mate against a palace whose central defenses are gone. The nine palace oblique mates use the palace diagonals: a chariot or soldier on the corner point cooperates with a distant cannon to cover the center. Learning these is not antiquarian study; strong players calculate by recognizing which named net the position is three moves away from, the way chess players see a back-rank mate before it exists. Two practical middlegame principles govern when tactics work. First, count attackers against the palace region rather than material in general: three attacking units against a shell missing one advisor usually means a decisive attack, while material grabbing on the far flank routinely loses to a faster mate. Second, exchange judiciously by phase: trade cannons when ahead in structure and the board is emptying, trade horses when the position stays crowded, and almost never trade an active chariot for a passive one, whatever the nominal values say.

sections.heading: Endgame Theory: What Wins and What Draws
sections.body: Xiangqi endgame theory is old, deep, and unusually settled, because the palace and the river shrink the space of possibilities enough that classical authors could work out exact results for the common material balances, and modern computer analysis has confirmed most of them. The results are organized around the defender's shell of advisors and elephants, and a learner should memorize the landmark cases the way a chess player memorizes king-and-pawn basics. A lone chariot against a defender with both advisors and both elephants intact is, with correct defense, a draw; the proverb says a single chariot struggles against full advisors and elephants, and the defensive method, keeping the shell connected and the general flexible, is the first technique every student drills. Remove one advisor and the chariot generally wins; the attack focuses on the side the missing advisor leaves soft. A chariot against a defender with elephants but no advisors wins, and against advisors but no elephants it also generally wins, which teaches the deeper point that the shell's value lies in its completeness.
