A lone horse defeats a single advisor but cannot beat two, and a horse against a bare general wins by driving the general to a corner and using the opposition of the two generals, since the flying general rule lets the attacker's own general take away the file the defender needs. A lone cannon with no helper cannot mate at all once its screens are gone, which is why endgame values flip; but cannon plus one advisor, the advisor serving as a portable screen, defeats two advisors, and cannon plus advisor against full shell is a famous drawn fortress. Soldier endings are exact: a single soldier that has crossed the river and not yet reached the back rank beats a bare general if its general assists, but an old soldier on the back rank only draws; a high soldier, one still with its forward step, wins against a single advisor and draws against more. Multi-piece endings follow a rough arithmetic that practitioners quote constantly: chariot beats horse plus one defender missing, horse plus cannon roughly equals chariot, two crossed soldiers roughly equal a minor piece, and an extra crossed soldier with equal pieces is very often decisive because soldiers never retreat and every step forward is irreversible progress toward the palace. Three defensive principles organize practical play. Keep the shell whole and connected; a defender down material but with four intact defenders should trade attackers, not defenders. Centralize the general only when the attacker's chariots are gone, since the palace center is safest against horse and cannon but deadliest against a chariot cross-check. And use your own general actively in won endings; because of the flying general power, the attacking general controlling a file is frequently the piece that delivers the point, a resource with no analogue in Western chess. Composed endgame studies, a celebrated genre with collections dating to the Ming dynasty, refine all of this into art, and solving a handful weekly is the fastest known way to sharpen calculation.

sections.heading: History: From Chaturanga Debates to the Song Dynasty Board
sections.body: The deep origin of xiangqi is genuinely contested, and an honest account gives the reader the competing claims rather than a tidy myth. The mainstream scholarly view ties all chess-family games to ancestors of chaturanga, the four-arm army game attested in northern India by roughly the sixth century AD, whose pieces, counselor, elephant, horse, chariot, foot soldier, map neatly onto both the Persian-Arab line that became Western chess and the Chinese line that became xiangqi. On this view the game entered China along the Silk Road trade routes during or before the Tang dynasty, and was then radically transformed: moved from squares to intersections, given the river and palace, and armed, uniquely, with the cannon. A rival tradition of Chinese scholarship argues for substantial or complete native origin, pointing to much older Chinese games whose names use the same characters, notably liubo, a race-and-capture game popular in the Han era, and to a story placing a game called xiangqi at the court of King Wu of Zhou; skeptics answer that shared names do not demonstrate shared rules, and that no pre-Tang source describes anything like the modern game. What the record does show clearly is this: a Tang dynasty text of the ninth century, the story collection Xuanguai lu, describes a dream battle whose recorded moves imply a board game with general, horse, chariot, and soldier moving in recognizable ways; Song dynasty sources of the eleventh and twelfth centuries describe and depict the modern thirty-two piece game, and surviving bronze and ceramic pieces from the Song are marked with the same characters used today. The cannon is the datable signature: the piece named pao appears in Song sources in the era when Chinese armies were fielding trebuchet artillery and early gunpowder weapons, and the character used for the piece shifted over time from the stone-hurling radical to the fire radical, tracking the technology. The board's famous inscription fixes its imagery to the Chu-Han war of 206 to 202 BC, when Xiang Yu and Liu Bang agreed a truce line at the Hong Canal before Liu Bang broke it and founded the Han dynasty; the game thus stages, forever, the most storied civil war in Chinese memory, which is also why the two sides' generals are written with different characters and why red, the Han color by convention, moves first. Printed strategy literature begins remarkably early. The Ming era produced the two classics still studied today: Secret in the Tangerine, published in 1632, a systematic opening and game collection whose title alludes to an old tale of immortals found playing chess inside a tangerine, and the Plum Flower Manual of the same century, the foundational text of the screen horses defense. Qing dynasty masters added great endgame collections, and by the twentieth century xiangqi had professional players, national championships in China from 1956, and an international federation organizing world titles from 1990 onward.

sections.heading: Xiangqi, Western Chess, and Its Cousins Compared
sections.body: Setting xiangqi beside its relatives clarifies what is essential in each. Against Western chess the deep structural differences are five. First, geometry: ninety points against sixty-four squares, play on intersections, and no diagonal color structure; the xiangqi board is wider, which slows knights and empowers rooks. Second, the palace: the Western king can run, castle, and hide behind a pawn wall, while the xiangqi general is caged in nine points, so attacks in xiangqi are aimed at a fixed address and defensive technique is about maintaining a shell rather than evacuating a monarch. Third, the soldier structure: Western pawns capture diagonally, form chains, and promote to queens, generating the closed structures and long strategic maneuvering characteristic of chess; xiangqi soldiers capture straight ahead, never lock, and merely gain a sideways step, so the game stays open and the strategic language of weak squares and pawn chains barely applies. Fourth, the pieces themselves: chess has the queen, a single overwhelming attacker, while xiangqi has the cannon, whose screen-dependent power creates tactics chess cannot express, and purely defensive pieces, advisors and elephants, which chess lacks entirely. Fifth, the rules of termination: stalemate wins in xiangqi and draws in chess, perpetual check loses in xiangqi and draws in chess, and these two choices alone make xiangqi markedly more decisive; draw rates in elite chess exceed half of games, while elite xiangqi, though Red's first-move advantage produces many draws at the very top, remains sharper below that level. Against shogi, the Japanese branch, the salient contrast is the drop rule: captured shogi pieces change sides and return to the board, so shogi material never depletes and attacks accelerate endlessly, while xiangqi, like chess, is a game of attrition, but with the palace focusing that attrition into mating races. Against janggi, the Korean branch, the kinship is visibly closer: janggi uses essentially the same board and pieces, but has no river, lets its elephants make a longer leg-blocked move anywhere on the board, lets the general and advisors use all palace lines, allows a cannon to move only by jumping and forbids it to jump or capture another cannon, and permits passing a turn; janggi soldiers start already able to move sideways. Vietnamese co tuong is not a cousin but the same game: Vietnam plays xiangqi under Vietnamese names, with a rich professional scene, and Vietnamese masters compete in the world championship on equal terms. For a player crossing over from chess, the reliable transfers are calculation discipline, tactical pattern hunger, and endgame patience; the habits to unlearn are queen-centered attacking instincts, pawn-chain strategy, and the assumption that repetition is a safe harbor. Crossing the other way, xiangqi players entering chess find their chariot handling and mating-net vision translate immediately, and their surprise is the tolerance chess extends to passive, closed, half-point play.

sections.heading: Notation, Study Tools, and the Path to Strength
sections.body: To study xiangqi you must read its notation, and the standard system is refreshingly compact. Each move names a piece, its current file counted from the mover's own right, one of three operations, and a destination number. The operations are: level, a purely sideways move along a rank, whose destination number is the new file; forward, a move toward the opponent, and backward, a move away, whose destination number is the new file for pieces that change file, horse, elephant, advisor, or the number of ranks traveled for pieces that stay on a file, chariot, cannon, soldier, general. In Western letters, C2=5 means the cannon on file two moves level to file five, the classic central cannon; H2+3 means the horse on file two advances ending on file three; R1+2 means the chariot on file one advances two ranks. When two identical pieces stand on one file, a front or rear marker replaces the file number. A few hours with annotated games makes the system automatic, and it repays the effort, because the game's literature is enormous. The classical canon, Secret in the Tangerine from 1632, the Plum Flower Manual, and the great Qing endgame anthologies, exists in modern editions and partial translations, and modern Chinese publishing produces opening monographs and yearbooks of professional games in numbers comparable to chess literature. For non-readers of Chinese, the practical study path today is digital. Strong engines, most notably the open-source Pikafish, an adaptation of the Stockfish architecture to xiangqi, play far above any human and analyze positions free of charge; major play servers and apps offer live opponents at every strength around the clock, enforce the repetition rules automatically, and carry libraries of tactics puzzles. A sound self-training program looks like this and can be stated briefly. Learn the piece moves until they are reflexes, then drill the basic mates against a bare palace, chariot mates, double cannon, cannon behind the horse, until you can execute them without thought. Play many fast games early, because pattern exposure matters more than deliberation at first, but review every loss for the single move where the game turned. Adopt one opening system for each color, the central cannon as Red and the screen horses as Black is the traditional and still excellent choice, and learn its first ten moves and typical middlegame plans rather than collecting variations. Solve endgame studies and tactics daily in small doses, ten minutes being genuinely enough to compound. The common failure modes of learners are stable across generations: hoarding material while the palace burns, moving chariots late, trading cannons into dead endgame positions or horses into crowded ones, forgetting the flying general until it decides a game, and treating the repetition law as a nuisance rather than a weapon. Watch instead for the improving player's markers, chariots active by move six, one elephant raised, horse legs free, and every check answered with a question: what does the attacker do next if the repetition rule forbids doing this again? When those habits are automatic, you are no longer a beginner.

guides.title: Xiangqi Openings and Cannon Tactics
guides.summary: A working education in the opening phase of xiangqi, the Chinese game of chess, built around the cannon, the piece that has no counterpart in the international game. Covers the board and rules, notation, the major opening systems and their ideas, the standard cannon tactics and mating patterns, trading judgement, endgame consequences, and the repetition rules that decide sharp games.

sections.heading: Why the cannon makes xiangqi its own game
sections.body:
Xiangqi, usually rendered in English as Chinese chess, is played on a grid of nine files and ten ranks, with the thirty-two pieces standing on the intersections rather than inside the squares. It is one of the most widely played board games in the world, with a competitive tradition in China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore and among Chinese communities everywhere, and a body of opening theory that is easily as deep as that of the international game. A player arriving from Western chess will recognise a great deal. There is a rook that slides along ranks and files, called the chariot. There is a knight that leaps in an L, called the horse. There are pawns, called soldiers, that shuffle forward one point at a time. There is a king, called the general, whose safety decides everything.

And then there is the cannon, and the cannon changes the character of the entire game. It moves exactly like the chariot when it is not capturing, sliding any distance along an empty rank or file. But it cannot capture anything it can merely see. To take a piece, a cannon must leap over exactly one intervening piece, of either colour, and land on the first occupied point beyond it. That intervening piece is called the screen, the mount, or in Chinese the cannon carriage. One screen is required; zero screens and two screens are equally useless.

This single rule inverts several instincts that a chess player carries in from elsewhere. Your opponent's pieces are your ammunition, so stripping the board bare disarms your own cannons. A piece placed on a line to block an enemy chariot may simultaneously arm an enemy cannon aimed down the same line, so that the defensive move and the fatal blunder are the same move. A cannon that appears to be doing nothing, sitting on a line with no screen at all, may in fact be exerting the most severe threat on the board, because the very act of interposing a defender on that line hands the cannon the screen it lacked and loses the general on the spot. Attack and obstruction, which in most games are opposites, become entangled.

Because the board is crowded at the start and empties as the game goes on, the cannon is at its most dangerous in the first twenty moves and steadily loses force thereafter. That is the deep reason xiangqi opening theory is so sharp, so concrete and so heavily catalogued: the strongest attacking configurations are available immediately and expire. A player who understands screens, and who can see which lines will still have screens on them three moves from now, has understood the essential thing about the game. The material that follows builds that understanding from the board upward, from the geometry through the standard opening systems to the tactical patterns that decide practical games.

sections.heading: The board, the river, the palace and the flying general
sections.body:
The playing surface is a grid of nine vertical lines, called files, and ten horizontal lines, called ranks, giving ninety intersections. Pieces occupy the intersections, including the ones on the outer edges, which is why a nine-by-ten grid of lines yields a ninety-point board rather than a seventy-two-square one. Across the middle, between the fifth and sixth ranks, runs a blank horizontal band called the river, conventionally inscribed with the phrases for the Chu River and the Han Border, a reference to the contest between Xiang Yu and Liu Bang around 203 BCE. The river is not a barrier for most pieces, but it is decisive for two of them.

At each end of the board, occupying three files by three ranks around the central file, is a square marked with two diagonals. This is the palace, sometimes called the fortress. It contains nine intersections. Two pieces, the general and its two advisors, may never leave it under any circumstance, so the general's entire life is spent on nine points, and the geometry of those nine points is the geometry of every mating attack in the game.

The elephants, or ministers, are the other river-bound pieces: they may never cross to the far bank. Each elephant therefore reaches only seven points on its own half, and the two elephants of one colour can never defend the same point, because one is confined to the odd-coloured diagonal system and one to the other. This is why elephants come in complementary pairs, why losing one elephant is a structural rather than a merely material loss, and why a great deal of attacking play consists of trading a minor piece for an elephant to open a diagonal that can never be closed again.

Soldiers cross the river and change nature when they do. Before the river a soldier may only advance one point straight ahead. After crossing, it may also move one point sideways, though never backwards and never diagonally. It never promotes. A soldier that reaches the enemy's back ranks alongside the palace is a genuine attacking piece, which is the sense behind the old saying that a small soldier across the river takes on a chariot.

Finally, and most strangely to a newcomer, the two generals may never face each other along an open file with no piece between them. This is the flying general rule, sometimes called the face-to-face generals or the white-faced general. In effect the general attacks along its own file like a chariot, so a player may not make a move that leaves the file between the generals empty, and a general may be used to deliver the winning threat from the other end of the board. It is a long-range, line-based rule in a game already dominated by line-based pieces, and it participates in an enormous number of tactics, particularly those involving a cannon or chariot vacating the central file at the right moment.

sections.heading: How each piece moves, and what it is worth
sections.body:
Each side has one general, two advisors, two elephants, two horses, two chariots, two cannons and five soldiers. The general moves one point orthogonally and stays in the palace. The advisors move one point diagonally and stay in the palace, which means each advisor touches only five of the nine palace points and the two advisors together, with the general, form the small defensive lattice that every attacker is trying to dismantle.

The elephant moves exactly two points diagonally, tracing the shape of the character for a field, and is blocked if the single intersection at the midpoint of that diagonal is occupied by any piece of either colour. Blocking that midpoint is called stuffing the elephant's eye, and it is a standard defensive and offensive resource. The horse moves one point orthogonally and then one point diagonally outward, the same geometry as a knight's L, but unlike a knight it does not jump: if the orthogonal point it steps through is occupied, the move is illegal. This is called hobbling the horse's leg. A horse on an open board commands eight destinations; a horse in a congested opening position may command two, and this difference is the single most important dynamic fact about the piece.

The chariot slides any distance along a rank or file, exactly like a rook, and is by a wide margin the strongest piece. The cannon slides identically but captures only by jumping exactly one screen. The soldier advances one point, gaining sideways movement after crossing the river.

Standard practical values, used by human players and roughly reproduced by engines, run about nine for the chariot, four and a half for the cannon, four for the horse, two apiece for advisors and elephants, one for a soldier before the river and about two for one after it. Those numbers are approximations and the two most useful things about them are the relationships rather than the absolute figures. First, the chariot is worth roughly two minor pieces, so trading a chariot for a horse and a cannon is close to even and is often correct when it removes a defender or opens a file. Second, and more importantly, the cannon-versus-horse relationship reverses over the course of a game. In the opening the board is dense with screens and the cannon is worth slightly more; by the late middlegame, with a dozen pieces gone, the horse has open ground and the cannon is starved of mounts, and the ordering flips.

Advisors and elephants are worth little in a vacuum and a great deal in defence, so their value is contextual rather than fixed. A side facing two chariots and a cannon would happily give a horse to restore a missing advisor; a side in a quiet symmetrical endgame might give an elephant to activate a soldier. The old rule of thumb is that a full set of advisors and elephants is worth about a chariot's worth of defensive resistance, which is why the standard endgame result of a lone chariot against a complete defensive set is a draw.

sections.heading: Reading the moves: the notation every book uses
sections.body:
Xiangqi notation is relative rather than absolute, and this trips up newcomers more than the rules do. There is no fixed grid of coordinates shared by both players. Instead, each player numbers the files one to nine starting from that player's own right-hand edge. Because the two players sit opposite one another, one side's file two is the other side's file eight, and the same physical line has two names depending on who is speaking. This feels perverse until you notice what it buys: every opening written for Red can be read unchanged by Black, because the description is symmetrical.

The most common system in English-language material is the World Xiangqi Federation notation, usually shortened to WXF. A move is written as four characters. First comes a letter for the piece: K for the general, A for advisor, E for elephant, H for horse, R for chariot, C for cannon, P for soldier. Second comes the number of the file the piece currently stands on, in the mover's own numbering. Third comes an operator: a plus sign for moving forward, a minus sign for moving backward, and an equals sign for moving sideways along a rank, described as traversing. Fourth comes a number whose meaning depends on the piece. For the chariot, cannon, general and soldier, which move in straight lines, a forward or backward move is followed by the number of ranks travelled, and a traversing move is followed by the destination file. For the horse, elephant and advisor, which move diagonally, the fourth character is always the destination file, because the rank change is implied by the piece's fixed geometry.

So C2=5 means the cannon standing on the mover's second file traverses to the fifth file, the central one. This is the Central Cannon, the most famous opening move in the game. H8+7 means the horse on the eighth file advances to the seventh file. R1=2 means the chariot on the first file slides across to the second. P7+1 means the soldier on the seventh file advances one rank. When two identical pieces stand on the same file, so that the file number alone is ambiguous, a plus or minus prefix identifies which one is meant, with the plus referring to the piece nearer the enemy: +R=4 means the more advanced of two stacked chariots traverses to the fourth file.

Chinese-language sources use an equivalent system with characters, in which Red conventionally writes file numbers with Chinese numerals and Black with Arabic ones, so that a printed game score shows at a glance which side is moving. The words for the operators are jin for advance, tui for retreat and ping for traverse. A reader who learns the seven piece letters and the three operators can follow any game score in any source, and can look up the named openings that follow, all of which are simply nicknames for particular sequences of these four-character tokens.

sections.heading: The cannon's mechanism: screens, ammunition and the arithmetic of the leap
sections.body:
Everything specific to xiangqi tactics follows from one sentence: a cannon captures by jumping exactly one occupied point along a rank or file and taking whatever stands on the next occupied point beyond. Work through the consequences slowly, because they are not obvious and strong play depends on holding all of them at once.

Consider a cannon aimed down an open file at the enemy general with nothing at all between them. The cannon cannot capture, since it has no screen. Yet this is one of the most feared configurations in the game, called the hollow cannon or empty-headed cannon. The reason is that the defender cannot block. Any piece interposed on that file immediately becomes the cannon's screen, and the cannon then captures the general straight through it. So a line that looks harmless is in fact permanently unblockable, and every other attacking piece the offensive player brings to bear on the general enjoys a defender who cannot use the ordinary resource of interposition. The general must run, capture the checking piece, or lose.

Now consider the reverse. A cannon with two pieces between it and its target is inert on that line. This means a defender can neutralise a cannon by adding a second body to the line rather than by removing the first, which is a defensive idea with no analogue in Western chess. It also means that a capture elsewhere on the board, or even a friendly piece stepping onto the line for entirely unrelated reasons, can silently switch a cannon on or off. Before every move, a disciplined player asks which lines have exactly one screen after the move under consideration.

The dependency on enemy material also gives the cannon its strange life cycle. In the opening position each side's cannons sit on the third rank of intersections, on the second and eighth files, and both of them already bear on the enemy back rank through crowded lines. As pieces come off, the number of available screens falls, and a cannon can find itself with no line on which it can capture anything at all. This is why the piece is worth marginally more than a horse at move ten and clearly less at move sixty, and why an attacker who has committed to a cannon-based initiative must convert it before the board thins.

One further arithmetic point is worth memorising. Two friendly cannons on the same line, one directly behind the other with nothing between them, form a battery in which the rear cannon uses the front cannon as its screen. The rear cannon therefore attacks the first piece beyond the front one. This stacked configuration, called double or heavy cannons, is the backbone of a family of forced mates, and it is the reason a defender must count not only how many screens sit on a line but which side of the screens the enemy artillery is on.

sections.heading: The Central Cannon: the oldest and sharpest first move
sections.body:
The move C2=5, swinging a cannon to the central file on move one, is called the Central Cannon, or zhongpao. It has been the main line of xiangqi for at least four centuries and remains the most played first move at every level. Its logic is immediate and brutal. The cannon now bears down the central file. The enemy's central soldier stands on that file and is defended only by the soldier's own position, and behind it, further down the file, sits the enemy general. Using the enemy central soldier as a screen, the Central Cannon attacks the point directly behind it; more importantly, it threatens to reach a configuration in which the central file is cleared of everything except one screen at the right moment.

The threat is not usually a one-move capture. It is a threat of tempo. Because the cannon already eyes the heart of the enemy position, Red can develop the horse to the third file, bring the chariot out along the second file, and generate a coordinated attack on the central and adjacent files within about six moves, all while Black is obliged to spend moves neutralising the central pressure. The classic manual Secrets Within the Tangerine, compiled by Zhu Jinzhen and printed in 1632, is essentially a monument to this idea; its analysis of the Central Cannon attack was so influential that for a century the opening was regarded as close to winning by force.

Structurally, the Central Cannon commits Red to a plan rather than merely occupying a good point. Typical follow-ups have their own names, and learning them is how the opening becomes navigable. Advancing the chariot past the river gives the crossing-river chariot systems, the most aggressive treatment, in which Red trades speed for the risk of an exposed piece. Keeping the chariot on the rank just below the river gives the patrolling-river chariot, a slower build that watches the whole middle of the board. Bringing both horses up the centre behind the advanced central soldier gives the coiled horses, a battering-ram formation designed to break through on the central file by sheer weight. Placing the second cannon on the seventh file produces the five-seven cannons, and on the sixth file the five-six cannons, each with a large independent body of theory.

What unites all of them is that Red is spending the first-move advantage on a direct attack against a specific target, the enemy general's file, and accepting that if the attack is parried the resulting position will be slightly loose. The historical record is a long argument about whether that trade is sound. The modern verdict, informed by engines strong enough to have surpassed the best human players in roughly the 2010s, is that the Central Cannon is excellent but not winning, and that the defensive systems developed since the seventeenth century hold if played precisely.

sections.heading: Screen Horses: the classical answer and why it works
sections.body:
To see why the standard defence is what it is, count the pieces on the central file after Red plays C2=5. Going up the file from Red's side there is the cannon on the third rank, Red's own central soldier on the fourth rank, then two empty points in the middle of the board where the river runs, then Black's central soldier on the seventh rank, and behind that, eventually, Black's general. Red's cannon has exactly one screen, Red's own soldier, and the first occupied point beyond that screen is Black's central soldier. So the Central Cannon does not merely aim at the enemy position in some vague sense: it attacks a specific undefended piece on move one.

Worse for Black, if that capture happens the Red cannon lands on the point Black's soldier occupied, deep in Black's half and staring at the general down an empty stretch of file. That is the hollow cannon configuration, and Black cannot answer it by interposing, because any interposed piece becomes the cannon's screen. The general would have to run and the position would be close to lost. So Black's first move is essentially forced to address the threat.

The move that does it most economically is H8+7, bringing a horse forward one file so that it stands on the third rank of Black's half, from where it covers the central soldier. Now if Red captures, Black simply recaptures with the horse, and Red has traded a good cannon for a soldier and a large loss of time. Playing the mirror-image move as well, H2+3, so that both horses stand flanking the centre and both guard the central soldier, produces the formation called Screen Horses, from the resemblance of the two horses side by side to a folding screen.

The formation is more than a defensive patch. The two horses defend each other's approach squares, they support the eventual advance of the third- and seventh-file soldiers, and they leave both chariot files clear so that Black can contest the open lines Red is trying to seize. The cost is that the horses are slightly passive and that the points in front of them, particularly on the third and seventh files, become the targets of Red's second cannon. That is exactly the argument of the five-seven cannons system, where Red's other cannon swings to the seventh file to pressure the horse's supporting soldier.

Historically the defence is associated with the manual known as the Plum Blossom Manual, attributed to Wang Zaiyue and circulated from the late seventeenth century onward, which set out to demonstrate that Screen Horses holds against the Central Cannon attacks that Secrets Within the Tangerine had presented as overwhelming. The argument between those two books is, in a real sense, still the central argument of xiangqi opening theory, and Screen Horses in its many modern refinements remains the most played answer to the most played first move.

sections.heading: Same-direction and opposite-direction cannons
sections.body:
Instead of defending the central soldier, Black may answer a Central Cannon with a Central Cannon of his own, and the resulting fight is one of the most double-edged in the game. There are two versions, distinguished by which of Black's cannons makes the journey.

In the same-direction system, called shunpao, Black moves the cannon that was already facing Red's cannon down the same physical file, so that both central cannons originate from the same wing of the board. In the opposite-direction system, called liepao, Black brings the other cannon across, so the two central cannons come from opposite wings. The distinction sounds cosmetic and is not: it determines which chariot files open first, which flank is congested, and therefore which side gets to attack.

In both cases Black declines to defend the central soldier, which means Red may simply take it. Beginners take it almost every time. The capture is not refuted by force, but it is regarded as premature at any serious level, for two connected reasons. First, the capturing cannon lands on a point where Black's horse can attack it within a move or two, so Red spends further tempi shuffling a piece he has already moved twice while Black develops chariots. Second, once Red's cannon eventually leaves the central file, Black's own central cannon is looking down that file at Red's general, using Red's own central soldier as its screen. The soldier Red won is small compensation for handing the opponent an unblockable line into the palace.

Play therefore usually proceeds with both sides developing horses and racing to activate chariots, and the resulting positions are famously sharp because the two central cannons are mutually inert on the file while remaining ready to reactivate the moment a screen appears or disappears. Same-direction games tend to become a straight race in which the side that opens a chariot file first dictates events; the older literature is full of aphorisms about how a single tempo decides these positions. Opposite-direction games are structurally lopsided, since Black's queenside and kingside develop at very different speeds, and they include the half-way variation in which Black delays committing the central cannon until Red has shown his hand.

Both systems are less popular today than Screen Horses, and the reason is instructive. They are counterattacking systems that accept an inferior structure in exchange for immediate activity, and modern preparation, backed by engines, is very good at defusing immediate activity. They remain excellent practical weapons at club level and are still seen at the top when a player needs a win with Black, precisely because they make a draw hard for both sides. That last point matters more in xiangqi than in most games, because the draw rate in elite play is high enough that some team competitions score a drawn game asymmetrically in Black's favour to discourage short peace treaties.

sections.heading: The Sandwiched Horse and the other replies to the Central Cannon
sections.body:
Between the solidity of Screen Horses and the sharpness of the mirrored cannons sits a family of defences that reshape the same material into different structures, and a serious player should recognise all of them even if only one becomes part of a personal repertoire.

The most important is the Sandwiched Horse, known in Chinese as fangongma and in older sources as the cannon-sandwiched screen. Black develops both horses to the same flanking points used in Screen Horses, but relocates one cannon to the fourth or sixth file so that it stands between the two horses, tucked beside the palace. The gain is defensive coordination: the repositioned cannon guards the point in front of one horse, blunts the standard attack against the third or seventh file, and can swing to the central file later to contest it. The cost is a tempo and a certain passivity, and a specific structural weakness on the wing the cannon left, which is where informed opponents aim. The defence was rehabilitated and popularised in the second half of the twentieth century, notably by players of Hu Ronghua's generation, and it is now fully respectable.

The Single Horse defence develops one horse toward the edge rather than toward the centre, leaving an asymmetrical structure with a clearer path for one chariot. It is the oldest of the systems, common in the classical manuals, and rarer today because the edge horse is slow to re-enter play, but it still appears as a surprise weapon and it teaches the fundamental point that a horse's value is almost entirely a function of how many of its eight destinations are actually reachable.

Beyond these come the various flank cannon replies. Black may answer with an advisor's-corner cannon, placing a cannon on the fourth or sixth file to eye a diagonal route toward Red's palace. He may play a cannon to the edge file to free the chariot behind it, a plan quick enough to have earned the nickname three-step tiger, since the chariot reaches an active post in three moves. He may play the elephant to the central point, which both connects the defence and plugs the central file with a screen that makes Red's cannon harmless there.

The choice among these is not arbitrary and is worth stating plainly. Against a Central Cannon, Black is choosing where to accept his structural concession, because he must accept one somewhere. Screen Horses concedes the third- and seventh-file soldiers as targets. The Sandwiched Horse concedes a wing. The mirrored cannons concede the central soldier and the safety of the structure in exchange for counterplay. There is no reply that is simply solid and simply active. Understanding which concession suits your own style, and which resulting middlegames you actually enjoy playing, is more useful than memorising twenty moves of any single line.

sections.heading: Quiet first moves: elephant, soldier, horse and flank cannons
sections.body:
Not every game begins with a cannon lunging at the centre, and the quiet first moves have grown enormously in importance over the last half century. The reason is competitive rather than aesthetic. The Central Cannon leads to positions that have been analysed for four hundred years and are now analysed by engines to a depth no human can match; a player who wants to reach a fresh middlegame with the first-move advantage intact has good reason to look elsewhere.

The Elephant Opening, E3+5 or E7+5, brings an elephant to the central point of its own third rank. It develops nothing aggressive and takes no risk. What it does is place a permanent screen on the central file, which means an enemy Central Cannon aimed down that file has two pieces in the way rather than one and is neutralised there. It also connects the elephants, so that each defends the other, which is the most durable defensive structure the game offers. The move keeps every option open: Red can follow with a Central Cannon next move if Black's reply invites it, or with horses and chariots. At professional level over recent decades it has been one of the two or three most common first moves, and it is the standard choice of players who want a long game.

The Soldier Opening, P3+1 or P7+1, advancing one of the flanking soldiers a single point, carries the wonderful name of the Immortal Pointing the Way. It commits almost nothing while doing something genuinely useful: it opens a route for the horse behind it to develop toward the centre without being hobbled, and it stakes a small claim to space. Its great virtue is transpositional flexibility, since almost any system can be reached from it, and its great vice is that Black has an equally wide choice and can steer toward structures Red did not want.

The Horse Opening, H2+3, develops a piece immediately and prepares a chariot lane. The Crossing-the-Palace Cannon, C2=6, swings a cannon over the top of its own palace to the far side, aiming diagonally at the enemy position along a line the opponent may be slow to defend. The Advisor's-Corner Cannon, C2=4, is a smaller version of the same idea. The Edge Cannon pushes a cannon to the outermost file, chiefly to free the chariot behind it for a rapid swing along the back rank.

None of these is objectively better than the Central Cannon. What they change is the shape of the fight. A Central Cannon sets a concrete problem that Black must solve correctly on move one; an elephant or soldier move sets no problem at all but keeps a small, durable edge in hand and asks Black to commit first. Which of those you prefer says more about temperament than about theory, and both approaches are represented among the strongest players in the game's history.

sections.heading: Development principles: the chariot is king
sections.body:
Underneath the named systems sit a handful of principles that decide far more club games than any memorised line, and the first of them concerns the chariot. The traditional saying holds that one chariot chills ten pieces, meaning a single activated chariot exerts more practical pressure than a crowd of undeveloped material. In the initial position both chariots are buried in the corners with no open line. Almost every sound opening plan is, at bottom, a scheme for getting them out fast.

There are exactly three ways to free a chariot, and recognising which one an opening is using clarifies the whole sequence. You can move the horse in front of it, which is why horse development so often precedes chariot development. You can move the cannon off the third rank so the chariot can swing sideways along that rank, which is why so many openings begin by relocating a cannon that then does nothing for ten moves. Or you can advance the edge soldier and use the outermost file, the slowest route but sometimes the only one available. Counting how many moves each side needs to activate both chariots is a crude but remarkably reliable way to evaluate an unfamiliar opening position.

The second principle is tempo, expressed in the classical maxim that it is better to lose a piece than to lose the initiative. This is hyperbole, but the sentiment is sound in a game where a coordinated attack against a nine-point palace can be decisive within six or seven moves. Grabbing a soldier with a developed piece, and then having to retreat that piece under attack, is the archetypal way club players lose the opening. As a working rule, a capture that costs two tempi in the opening is worth making only if the material is at least a minor piece or the capture destroys the enemy's structure.

Third, do not move the same piece twice without a concrete reason, and be especially wary of moving a cannon three times. Fourth, keep the elephants connected where possible, because a pair of mutually defending elephants is dramatically harder to break down than two loose ones, and an attack that begins by trading a horse for an unsupported elephant is a standard and often winning idea. Fifth, remember that soldier moves are irreversible. Advancing the third- or seventh-file soldier frees a horse, but it also permanently weakens the point behind it and gives the enemy's cannon a target on that file. This is precisely the tension the five-seven cannons system exploits against Screen Horses.

Finally, keep the general's file in mind at all times, both because of the flying general rule and because the central file is where the heaviest artillery ends up. Many opening disasters are not the result of a missed tactic but of a routine developing move that quietly emptied the central file at the wrong moment.

sections.heading: Cannon tactics: hollow cannons, stacked batteries and the back-rank sweep
sections.body:
The tactical vocabulary of xiangqi is largely a vocabulary of cannon configurations, and a player who knows perhaps a dozen of them by name and by shape will see combinations that are otherwise invisible.

The first and most important is the hollow cannon, sometimes translated as the empty-headed cannon: a cannon on the central file with nothing at all between it and the enemy general. It gives no check, since a cannon needs a screen to capture. Its power is prohibitive rather than active. The defender cannot interpose on that file, because an interposed piece would become the screen and lose the general immediately. So every other check the attacker delivers must be answered by moving the general or capturing the checker, and the general's five or so available palace points shrink accordingly. A hollow cannon plus a chariot arriving on the back rank is a standard winning combination, known as the iron bolt, because the cannon bars the door while the chariot forces the lock.

The second is the stacked or heavy cannon battery: two friendly cannons on the same line with nothing between them. The rear cannon uses the front cannon as its screen, so the rear cannon attacks the first piece beyond the front one. If that piece is the enemy general, the rear cannon gives check, and the check cannot be blocked by any piece placed between the two cannons, because that would only shield the front cannon rather than the general. The defender must move the general or capture the front cannon. When the front cannon stands adjacent to the general and is defended, and the general's escape points are covered or occupied by its own advisors, this is mate. It is one of the cleanest forced finishes in the game.

The third is the back-rank sweep, which the classical literature calls the cannon grinding the cinnabar sand. A cannon that reaches the enemy's own back rank, with the enemy's chariots and advisors still cluttering that rank, becomes lethal precisely because those pieces are the ammunition. Every defender the opponent keeps at home is a screen the attacker can use, so a passive defensive set-up can turn from a wall into a firing range in a single move.

Two further ideas complete the basic set. A cannon can create a pin of a peculiar kind: a piece standing as the screen between a cannon and the general is not pinned in the Western sense, since moving it does not expose the general to capture, but it is anti-pinned, because as long as it stays put the cannon is loaded. Removing your own screen is therefore a defensive resource, and adding a second body to the line is another. And the flying general rule interacts with every one of these patterns, because clearing the central file to unleash your own general is functionally identical to unleashing a chariot, and combinations that win by discovered general are common enough to have their own name in the manuals.

sections.heading: Mating nets: the standard finishes worth memorising
sections.body:
Because the general is confined to nine points, xiangqi mates are highly patterned, and perhaps eight or ten configurations account for the large majority of decisive games. Learning them as shapes, rather than calculating them afresh each time, is the single fastest way to gain playing strength.

The cannon behind the horse is the most famous. The horse stands two points directly in front of the enemy general on the general's own file, from where it covers the two points to either side of the general on the back rank. A friendly cannon sits further back on that same file with the horse as its screen, so the cannon bears directly on the general. The general cannot step sideways, because the horse covers those points. It cannot move up or down the file, because the cannon still attacks wherever it lands. It cannot capture either attacker. The one escape is to interpose a piece on the single point between horse and general, which is exactly why an attacker building this pattern spends material freely to remove the advisors that could reach that point.

The smothered palace is the opposite idea: the general is killed by its own defenders. With both advisors sitting on the back-rank corners of the palace, the general in the middle has no lateral escape at all, and a cannon checking down the central file with any screen delivers mate. Every player who has clung to a full defensive formation under pressure has lost a game to this. The practical lesson is that advisors are not unambiguously good; an advisor on the wrong point is a wall around your own general.

The heaven and earth cannon combines two cannons at right angles, one hollow on the central file and one raking the enemy's back rank, so that the palace is attacked along both axes at once and the defenders that block one line arm the other. The iron bolt is the hollow cannon plus a chariot invading the central file, where the cannon guarantees that the chariot's check cannot be blocked. The horse in the trough is a horse that reaches the point immediately beside the enemy back rank on the third or seventh file, giving a check that is peculiarly hard to answer because the horse is both close and awkward to attack.

Finally there is the discovered general. Because the two generals may not face each other on an open file, an attacker whose general already sits on the enemy general's file wins the moment the last piece between them moves away, and a great many combinations end with a chariot or cannon leaving the central file with tempo. Defenders lose to this constantly, because the losing move looks like an ordinary developing move. Before any move that empties the central file, check whether the generals are on it, and before accepting any exchange in the middle of the board, ask what the file will look like after the recaptures.

sections.heading: Trading judgement: when a cannon is worth more than a horse
sections.body:
The most consequential judgement calls in a practical game are exchanges, and in xiangqi they are harder than in most games because piece values genuinely move as the position changes. The rough figures of four and a half for a cannon and four for a horse describe the opening. They describe nothing else.

The reason is ammunition. A cannon's power is proportional to the number of lines on which it has exactly one screen, and that number falls as the board empties. A horse's power is proportional to how many of its eight destinations are unhobbled, and that number rises as the board empties. Somewhere in the middlegame the two curves cross. As a practical heuristic, with more than about twenty pieces still on the board the cannon is the better piece; with fewer than about fourteen the horse usually is; in between it depends on structure. A player who is going to win must think about which side of that crossing point the game is heading toward, and steer.

There is one large exception, and it is the most useful piece of trading knowledge in the game. Against an intact defensive formation of two advisors and two elephants, the cannon is often superior to the horse even in a simplified position, because the enemy's own defenders are the screens. A cannon on the central file with the defender's advisor as a mount attacks straight into the palace; a horse must physically walk to a checking point and can be blocked at every step. This is why the standard technique for grinding down a fortified position involves a cannon, and why a defender facing a chariot and cannon should think hard about whether to keep advisors at home at all.

The corollary is that stripping the enemy defence is not always progress. Trading a horse to remove both elephants is one of the classic strategic sacrifices, since elephants can never be replaced and their absence permanently opens the diagonals into the palace. It is roughly sound when the attacker retains a chariot plus one other attacker and can generate threats within a few moves; it is bad when the attacker cannot, because the material deficit persists and the exposed palace becomes irrelevant once the queenside artillery is traded off. Cannon for two elephants is the same trade a half point more expensive and is judged the same way.

Two further rules of thumb are worth carrying. The side under attack wants to trade chariots, and the side attacking should avoid it, more strongly than the equivalent rule in Western chess, because a single chariot is such a large fraction of any attack's force. And when you are ahead in material, trade attackers rather than defenders; when behind, keep the position congested, since congestion is precisely what makes cannons dangerous and horses useless, and a cluttered board is the best friend of the player who needs complications.

sections.heading: Endgames: what happens when the ammunition runs out
sections.body:
Xiangqi endgames are unusually rich in exact, memorisable results, and they behave differently from any other chess variant because of two facts: the general never leaves nine points, and the cannon stops working when the board empties.

Start with the starkest consequence. A lone cannon cannot force mate against a bare general, ever. To capture the general the cannon needs exactly one screen on the line, and with only two pieces on the board there is nothing to use. A cannon supported by a single advisor is a completely different animal, because the advisor can be parked as a permanent gun mount, letting the cannon check into the palace from a distance. The technique of using your own advisor as a carriage is the first thing to learn about cannon endings, and it explains why a player heading for a cannon ending should be reluctant to give up advisors even when they seem passive.

The horse is the mirror image. A lone horse also cannot force mate against a bare general, but a horse with almost any support wins comfortably, because its checking geometry against a general trapped in a three-by-three box is excellent and it needs no screen at all. Broadly, in simplified endings with few pieces the horse outperforms the cannon; with several defenders still standing, the cannon does better, because the defenders themselves are mounts.

Several standard results are worth knowing by name even at club level. A lone chariot beats a bare general and beats a general with advisors alone, but against a complete defensive set of two advisors and two elephants the accepted verdict is a draw, since the defender can build a fortress the chariot cannot penetrate without help. This is the origin of the old line that a single chariot cannot break a full defence. A cannon with two advisors is generally held to hold the draw against a lone chariot, again by fortress. Results of this kind are compiled in exhaustive tables in the classical and modern literature, and although a few marginal cases remain disputed and some have been revised by computer analysis, the main body of the theory is settled.

Soldiers matter far more in the endgame than their nominal value suggests, because a soldier that crosses the river gains sideways movement and a soldier that reaches the enemy's palace region can participate directly in mate. The saying that a small soldier across the river takes on a chariot is an exaggeration, but a passed soldier on the central file, supported by anything, is often decisive. And the flying general rule turns the general itself into an active endgame piece, since threatening to open the file between the generals is a real threat that can win a tempo or force a defender to a worse square. Endgame play in this game is not a quiet phase; it is where the geometry becomes most exact.

sections.heading: Repetition, perpetual check, and the mistakes that lose games
sections.body:
The rules on repetition are the largest single difference between xiangqi and Western chess, and ignorance of them costs points every week in club play. In international chess a perpetual check is a draw. In xiangqi it is a loss for the side giving the checks. Under the codified Chinese rules, and with only small variations under Asian federation rules, repeated positions are adjudicated by classifying each side's moves. A move may be a check, a threat to mate, a chase, meaning a direct threat to capture a specific piece, or idle. If one side repeats using only checks and the other does not, the checking side must vary or forfeit the game. Perpetual chasing of a piece is treated the same way, with carefully specified exceptions, notably that chasing a soldier that has not crossed the river, or chasing with a general or a soldier, is generally permitted. If both sides are doing something prohibited, the result is a draw.

The practical consequences are sharp. A player who has sacrificed material for an attack cannot bail out with a perpetual, so the attack must actually work. A defender who can force his opponent into a position where only checks maintain the balance may be winning rather than drawing. And a player who does not know the rules will sometimes play a beautiful perpetual and then discover he has lost. Learn the four categories, and when in doubt, break the repetition yourself with an idle move rather than gambling on the arbiter's reading.

The recurring practical mistakes cluster into a short list. Grabbing the enemy central soldier with the Central Cannon on move two, then spending three moves rescuing the cannon. Moving the same cannon three or four times in the first ten moves while the chariots sit in the corners. Answering a check by interposing on the file of a hollow cannon, which loses instantly. Making a routine developing move that empties the file between the generals. Stuffing your own elephant's eye or hobbling your own horse's leg with a defensive move and only noticing two moves later. Trading down into a cannon ending having already given away both advisors, so the cannon has no mount. Clinging to both advisors on the back-rank corners until the general is smothered by them.

The most efficient study path reverses the order in which most people learn. Begin with the mating nets, because they are finite and they decide games. Then learn the basic endgame results, because they tell you which exchanges are safe. Then take one opening as Red and two replies as Black, learn the ideas rather than the move lists, and only afterwards read deeply in the classical manuals, which reward a reader who already knows what the positions are trying to do. Solving composed endgame problems, a genre with a long tradition in Chinese collections dating back to the sixteenth century, sharpens calculation faster than any amount of casual play.

guides.title: Janggi: Korean Chess and Its Strategy
guides.summary: A complete introduction to Janggi, the Korean chess variant: the board and palace, how every piece moves, the pre-game setup choice, the point-scoring rules that decide most games, and the opening, middlegame and endgame strategy that follows from them.

sections.heading: What Janggi Is and Why It Rewards Serious Study
sections.body:
Janggi is the Korean member of the great chess family, played on a nine-by-ten grid of lines with sixteen pieces a side, and it is the everyday board game of Korea in roughly the way that chess is of Russia or shogi is of Japan. It descends from Chinese xiangqi, which in turn descends from the Indian chaturanga that also produced European chess, so a player arriving from any of those games will recognise the skeleton immediately: a king that must be protected, sliding line pieces, leaping cavalry, a rank of foot soldiers. What makes Janggi worth learning rather than treating as a footnote is that its handful of divergences from xiangqi are not cosmetic. They change the character of the game so thoroughly that xiangqi theory transfers poorly, and they produce a game with a distinct feel: slower to ignite, sharper once it does, and decided far more often by arithmetic than by mate.

Three of those divergences matter most. First, there is no river, so the elephants roam the whole board and the soldiers, though they never retreat, cross freely from move one. Second, the cannon jumps a screen piece to move as well as to capture, which makes it a strange, conditional, terrain-dependent attacker whose power appears and evaporates as the board empties. Third, and most consequential, each piece carries a numerical value and a game that reaches no checkmate is decided by adding those values up. A Janggi player is therefore always doing two things at once: hunting for mate, and keeping a running ledger. It is entirely normal to reach a position where neither side can force a win, agree that fact, and simply count. That single rule reshapes everything upstream of it, because a two-point soldier is not a rounding error to be sacrificed casually for vague initiative; it may be the whole game.

The pieces themselves are octagonal discs of graded size, larger for the stronger units, with the two armies labelled in Chinese characters: the green or blue side is Han and the red side is Cho, named for the Chu–Han contention of the third century BC that also names the xiangqi armies. Korean sets write the Han pieces in a flowing cursive script and the Cho pieces in a squarer one, which is a genuine legibility aid once you learn it. The game is documented in Korea from the Goryeo period onward and has been played more or less continuously since; rules were only tightened into a single competitive standard in the twentieth century by the national association, which is why older books and casual players in a park may still be using conventions that a tournament hall has retired.

sections.heading: The Board, the Palace, and the Starting Array
sections.body:
The Janggi board is a lattice of nine vertical lines and ten horizontal lines, and pieces stand on the intersections rather than in the squares, so there are ninety playable points. Files are numbered one to nine across the board and ranks one to ten up it, with each player counting from their own side. Unlike xiangqi there is no river across the middle; the board is one continuous territory, and this is the single most visible physical difference between the two games.

At each end sits the palace, a three-by-three block of nine points occupying the middle three files and the three ranks nearest that player's edge. The palace is marked with two drawn diagonals forming an X from corner to corner through its centre point. Those drawn diagonals are real lines for movement purposes: a piece that moves along lines may travel them, and a piece that does not may not. The general and the two guards are permanently confined to these nine points and can never leave, which means that the whole endgame of Janggi is a nine-point problem, and that a great deal of technique consists of learning which of those nine points are safe against which attackers.

The starting array is fixed except for one choice. On the back rank, reading from the left edge, stand chariot, horse, elephant, guard, an empty point, guard, elephant, horse, chariot. The general does not stand on the back rank; it begins on the centre point of the palace, one rank forward, which is why the middle of the back rank is vacant. The two cannons stand on the third rank, on the second and eighth files, and the five soldiers stand on the fourth rank on the odd files: one, three, five, seven and nine. The two armies mirror each other exactly.

The one choice is the horse-and-elephant arrangement. Before play begins, each player may independently swap the horse and elephant on either wing, or both, giving four possible arrangements. This is not a minor cosmetic option; it is the closest thing Janggi has to opening repertoire, and it is committed before a single move is made. A curiosity worth noticing at once is that in the initial position neither cannon can move at all. A cannon needs exactly one piece to jump, and along its own file the first piece it meets is the enemy cannon, which cannons are forbidden to jump; along its own rank the only other occupant is its partner cannon, equally forbidden. The opening therefore always begins by manoeuvring something else, and much of the first ten moves is about building the screens that will let the cannons wake up.

sections.heading: The Chariot and the Horse: Line Power and Leg Blocking
sections.body:
The chariot is the strongest piece on the board and is valued at thirteen points, more than the next two pieces combined. It moves any distance along a rank or a file, stopping at the first occupied point, capturing an enemy piece there and being blocked by a friendly one. This is exactly the rook of international chess with one addition: inside either palace, a chariot standing on a palace point may also travel along the drawn diagonals. So a chariot on a palace corner may slide through the palace centre to the opposite corner if both intervening points are clear, and a chariot that reaches an enemy palace corner is often already threatening the general along a line that does not exist anywhere else on the board. Learning to see those two extra diagonals is one of the first real skill jumps for a player coming from chess.

Because the board is open, with no river and no pawn structure in the European sense, chariots become active early and stay active. A rough practical rule that most strong players endorse is that a chariot which is passive for ten moves is worth perhaps half of one that is not, and that trading your active chariot for the opponent's passive one is usually good even at nominal parity. The classical warning in Korean is against the chariot that never leaves home; a whole game can be lost with thirteen points of material sitting on its starting point.

The horse is valued at five and moves one point orthogonally and then one point diagonally outward, ending on a point two away in one axis and one in the other — the knight's L of international chess. The crucial difference is that it does not leap. The orthogonal first step is called the leg, and if the point at the end of that step is occupied by anything at all, friend or enemy, the move is illegal. A horse therefore has anywhere from eight legal destinations down to none, and blocking an enemy horse's leg with a single soldier is a standard, cheap, extremely effective defensive device.

This blocking rule gives Janggi horses a personality quite unlike chess knights. In a crowded opening a horse is nearly inert; as the board empties it becomes formidable, and in a bare endgame it is a genuine mating threat. It also means that horses are strongly affected by the setup choice made before move one, because a horse placed on the wing next to the chariot has different escape routes and different legs than one placed inside next to the guard. Horses defend each other well when placed so that each covers the other's escape squares, a formation valuable enough to have its own name.

sections.heading: The Cannon: The Piece That Defines the Game
sections.body:
The cannon, worth seven points, is the piece that makes Janggi Janggi, and its rule is the one that trips up every visiting xiangqi player. In xiangqi a cannon slides like a rook to move and jumps a screen only to capture. In Janggi it jumps to do both. A Janggi cannon may move along a rank or file only by passing over exactly one occupied point — the screen, which may be a friendly or enemy piece — and then continuing along that line over any number of empty points, coming to rest on an empty point or capturing the enemy piece it lands on. No screen, no move. Two screens on the line, no move. This makes the cannon a conditional piece whose mobility is a function of how cluttered the board is, and it is why cannons are strongest in the middlegame and often nearly useless in a bare endgame, when there is nothing left to jump.

Two further restrictions are absolute and must be memorised. A cannon may never jump over another cannon, of either colour, and a cannon may never capture a cannon. A cannon on a line therefore behaves as a wall to enemy cannons, and a pair of opposed cannons on the same file simply cannot touch each other. This is why, in the starting position, no cannon has a legal move. It also produces the standard defensive trick of parking a cannon on a file specifically to make it unusable by the opponent's cannon, a resource with no analogue in chess.

Inside a palace, the cannon may also use the drawn diagonals: a cannon on a palace corner may jump a piece standing on the palace centre and land on the opposite corner. Since the general starts on the palace centre, and since guards often occupy it later, this diagonal jump is a recurring mating pattern and a recurring reason to keep the palace centre empty.

Two standing positions deserve names because Korean players use them constantly. A cannon placed on the front-centre point of one's own palace, directly in front of where the general sits, is the myeonpo or face cannon: a superb defensive post that covers the general's approach lines and simultaneously points down the centre file. A cannon that ends up on the palace centre point itself is the gungjungpo, and it is regarded as bad, because it blocks the general's own movement and the guards' coordination while being awkward to extract. Beginners fall into gungjungpo constantly; the cure is to notice, before jumping, whether the landing point is the one square your own king most needs.

The practical consequence is that a cannon must be thought of as a piece with a supply chain rather than a piece with a range. Before relying on it, ask whether there is exactly one occupant on the line, whether you control that occupant, and whether the line survives the trades you are planning. A cannon whose only screen can simply walk away is not attacking anything.

sections.heading: The Elephant: Long Reach, Awkward Geometry
sections.body:
The Janggi elephant is worth three points and moves one point orthogonally followed by two points diagonally outward in the same general direction, so its net displacement is two points along one axis and three along the other. Drawn on the board it is a long, hooked stride that reaches much further than a horse. Like the horse it does not leap: it is blocked if the first orthogonal step is occupied, and blocked again if the first of the two diagonal steps is occupied. Only the final landing point may hold a piece, and only if that piece is an enemy. An elephant therefore has up to eight destinations and, in a crowded position, frequently has one or none.

The vital divergence from xiangqi is that a Janggi elephant is not confined to its own half. There is no river, and no rule restricting elephants to home territory, so an elephant can and does cross into the enemy camp and attack the enemy palace directly. This transforms it from the purely defensive minister of xiangqi into a genuine, if clumsy, attacking piece. It also makes it dangerous to your own side, because an elephant deep in enemy territory is often trapped: its long stride means it can rarely retrace its steps in one move, and a single well-placed blocker can strand it permanently.

Elephants are the hardest piece for newcomers to see. The reliable trick is to stop counting the move as one-plus-two and instead learn the eight destination points as a shape, then check the two intermediate points for blockers. Many players draw the eight points once on paper and never need to again. A second useful habit is to notice that an elephant always changes the colour-parity of its position in a way that repeats on a cycle, so an elephant can only ever reach a subset of the ninety points from any given start; if you need it on a particular point and cannot get there in two moves, check whether it can ever get there at all before spending time on it.

Because an elephant is worth three and a horse five, the elephant-for-horse trade is nominally good for the elephant's owner by two points, and offering that trade is a standard opening motif. But the raw numbers mislead in one common structure: an elephant aimed at the enemy palace with clear intermediate points can be worth far more than three, while an elephant with all eight destinations blocked is worth nearly nothing until the position opens. Strong players therefore treat elephant value as unusually position-dependent, and one of the recognisable marks of an experienced Janggi player is a willingness to spend two or three tempi early simply to give an elephant a clean diagonal.

sections.heading: Soldiers, Guards, and the General
sections.body:
Each side begins with five soldiers on the fourth rank, on the odd-numbered files, and each is worth two points. A soldier moves one point forward or one point sideways, never backward, and it captures the same way it moves — there is no separate diagonal capture as in international chess. There is no promotion of any kind. A soldier that reaches the far rank is not transformed; it simply loses the ability to move forward and can only shuffle sideways for the rest of the game, which is one reason experienced players do not push soldiers thoughtlessly.

The one exception is the enemy palace. A soldier standing on a palace point may also move along the drawn palace diagonals, but only in a direction that carries it forward or sideways, never back. This makes a soldier that has infiltrated an enemy palace corner a real threat to the general rather than a nuisance, and infiltrating a soldier is a standard winning plan in simplified positions. Two soldiers standing side by side on the same rank defend each other and are collectively far harder to remove than two scattered ones; the Korean term for joining them up is worth knowing because the formation shows up in almost every game.

The two guards, three points each, are confined to the nine points of the palace and move one point along any drawn line: orthogonally along the palace grid, and diagonally where the X is drawn. From the palace centre a guard therefore has up to eight destinations; from a corner it has three; from an edge midpoint it has three. They never leave. Their entire job is to stand on the points from which the general could otherwise be checked, and a common way to lose a materially equal Janggi game is to let both guards be traded off, after which the general is naked.

The general moves exactly like a guard — one point along a drawn line, confined to the palace — and may not move onto a point where it would be captured. It has no value in the scoring, because a game in which a general is captured is over anyway. The general is not merely a liability, though: with the palace diagonals available it can shuffle usefully to block lines, and moving the general off the palace centre to unblock a friendly cannon's diagonal jump is a routine manoeuvre.

One further rule about generals is genuinely contested. In traditional play, when the two generals come to face each other along an open file with no piece between them, the position is called bikjang and functions as a draw offer: the player creating it is proposing a draw, which the opponent accepts by leaving it or refuses by interposing. Most modern tournament rule sets have abolished bikjang entirely, treating facing generals as an ordinary legal position. Agree which convention applies before you sit down, because it changes whole endgames.

sections.heading: Choosing a Setup: Gwima, Wonangma, Yanggwima and Myeonsang
sections.body:
Before the first move, each player independently arranges the horse and elephant on each wing, choosing which of the two sits next to the chariot on the outside and which sits next to the guard on the inside. Four arrangements are possible, and all four have names, histories and reputations. This pre-game decision is the closest analogue Janggi has to choosing an opening system in chess, with the difference that both sides commit before any moves are played and the commitment is permanent.

The overwhelmingly most common arrangement is gwima, the corner horse, in which one wing has the horse on the outside next to the chariot and the other wing has the elephant outside. It is asymmetric, and that asymmetry is the point: one wing becomes the natural attacking side and the other the natural defensive side, giving the player a clear plan from move one. The great majority of serious games at every level are gwima on at least one side, and most published Janggi theory is gwima theory. Because it is asymmetric, a gwima-versus-gwima game further divides depending on whether the two players' strong wings face each other or are on opposite sides of the board, and those two matchups play quite differently.

Wonangma, the mandarin-duck horses, places both horses on the inside so that they stand near each other and mutually cover each other's escape and blocking points, with both elephants on the outside next to the chariots. The horses are hard to attack and coordinate beautifully; the cost is that both elephants sit on the wings where their long strides are most easily blocked and least aimed at the enemy palace. Yanggwima, both corner horses, is the mirror choice with both horses outside and both elephants inside, giving fast wing play and central elephants. Myeonsang, the face elephant, is the arrangement in which an elephant ends up covering the approach to one's own general's front, a solid defensive choice with a reputation for being difficult to break down and slightly passive.

The practical advice for a new player is unambiguous: learn gwima first and play it almost exclusively for the first several hundred games. It has the deepest published theory, it produces clear plans, and it is what every opponent will expect and be prepared for, which means your mistakes get punished and therefore corrected. The temptation to play wonangma because the horses look pretty should be resisted until you understand why the elephants suffer for it.

Conventions differ on who declares first. Common practice is that the arrangement is announced rather than concealed, and rule sets typically arrange the order of declaration so that the side with the first-move advantage must commit before its opponent. Check the house rule, because a player who gets to see the opponent's arrangement before choosing their own holds a small but genuine edge.

sections.heading: Scoring, the Deom, Passing and How Games Actually End
sections.body:
Janggi's scoring rule is the single most important thing to understand about the game, because most games between evenly matched players end by it rather than by checkmate. Every piece has a fixed point value: chariot thirteen, cannon seven, horse five, elephant three, guard three, soldier two, and the general nothing. Each side therefore begins with two chariots, two cannons, two horses, two elephants, two guards and five soldiers, totalling twenty-six plus fourteen plus ten plus six plus six plus ten, which is seventy-two points.

Because the side that moves first has an advantage, the other side is compensated with a fixed bonus called the deom, conventionally one and a half points. In standard modern practice the red Cho side moves first and the green Han side carries the deom, so Han's starting total is seventy-three and a half against Cho's seventy-two. The half point is not decorative. Since every piece value is a whole number, the half point makes an exact tie arithmetically impossible, which means a scored game always has a winner. This is a deliberate and rather elegant piece of rule design: Janggi does not need a draw result for material-equal positions, because the deom breaks every tie.
