A game ends in one of a few ways. Checkmate, called oetong, ends it immediately, as does capture of a general in casual play. If a position is agreed to be dead — neither side can force mate, and both are simply shuffling — the players stop and count, and the higher total wins. Repetition of position typically forces the side causing it to vary; perpetual check is forbidden outright, and a player who checks endlessly without progress will be required to change or forfeit the claim.

The other rule that distinguishes Janggi sharply from chess is that a player may pass. Surrendering your turn is a legal move in most rule sets, subject only to the restriction that you may not pass while in check. The immediate consequence is that stalemate does not exist in Janggi: a player with no legal move simply passes, and the game continues. The strategic consequence is subtler and more interesting. In an endgame where any move worsens your position — chess's zugzwang — Janggi simply lets you decline, which removes an entire class of winning technique that chess and shogi players rely on. Some tournament rule sets restrict repeated passing to prevent stalling; check before you play.

The practical upshot for a student is that you should count constantly. Before every non-forced capture or trade, ask what the point difference will be afterward and whether you still have enough force to hunt for mate. A player who is four points ahead and simplifies correctly has, in a real sense, already won, and the discipline of counting is worth more early rating points than any amount of tactical flair.

sections.heading: Opening Principles and Standard Formations
sections.body:
Janggi openings look strange to a chess player because there is no centre to occupy in the chess sense and no pawn structure to build. What there is instead is a set of connectivity problems: the cannons cannot move until screens exist, the elephants cannot move until their intermediate points clear, the horses cannot move if their legs are blocked, and the palace needs a defensive shape before the enemy chariots arrive. The opening is essentially the process of solving those four problems faster than your opponent solves theirs.

The first practical principle is to build the face cannon early. Getting a cannon to the front-centre point of your own palace, the myeonpo, does three jobs simultaneously: it covers the central approach to your general, it establishes a long line down the centre file, and it puts a piece where it can later jump the enemy's own screens. Most gwima systems reach this formation within the first handful of moves, and a player who has not made a plan for their myeonpo by move ten is usually already worse. The mirror principle is to keep the palace centre point itself clear, so that neither your own general is boxed in nor an enemy cannon gains a diagonal jump through it.

The second principle is soldier coordination rather than soldier advance. Because soldiers cannot retreat and cannot promote, every push is permanent and slightly weakening. The productive early soldier moves are sideways ones that join soldiers into mutually defending pairs and, incidentally, create cannon screens on useful ranks. Advancing a soldier merely to gain space is a beginner's move that usually costs two points a dozen moves later.

The third principle is chariot activation on the strong wing. In a gwima setup the wing where the horse sits outside is generally the active wing, and getting a chariot onto an open file there, ideally with a cannon behind or in front of it, is the standard plan. Because there is no river to slow the advance, a chariot can reach the enemy third rank very quickly, and the arrival of the first enemy chariot on your side of the board is the moment the opening ends.

The fourth principle is that elephants should be given a road early or written off. An elephant with all its intermediate points blocked is dead weight, and because its stride is so long it takes several moves to reroute. Deciding on move three or four where each elephant is going, and making the one or two clearing moves needed, is time well spent.

Finally, resist early exchanges. Every trade simplifies toward the scored endgame, and in the opening you rarely know yet whether you want that. The exception is the elephant-for-horse offer, which trades three points for five and is usually worth taking even at a small cost in time, provided the resulting structure does not leave your palace bare.

sections.heading: The Middlegame: Exchange Values and Palace Pressure
sections.body:
The Janggi middlegame is a negotiation between two ledgers. One is material: the running point total that will decide the game if nobody mates. The other is attacking potential: how many pieces bear on the enemy palace and how many defenders remain. The two ledgers pull against each other, because every simplifying trade improves clarity for whoever is ahead on points and destroys attacking chances for whoever is not, and the whole art of the middlegame is knowing which ledger you are playing for.

The nominal values — thirteen, seven, five, three, three, two — are a starting point, not a verdict. Several systematic corrections are worth internalising. A cannon's value collapses as the board empties, because it needs screens; a cannon in an endgame with six pieces left may be worth less than a horse despite being nominally two points more. Conversely a horse's value rises as the board empties, because its leg stops being blocked. An elephant aimed at an open diagonal toward the enemy palace can be worth double its nominal three, while a blocked one is nearly worthless. And guards, nominally three each, are worth far more than three once your general is being hunted, because they are the only pieces that can stand on the palace points the enemy needs.

Pressure on the palace works differently from a chess king hunt because the target cannot run. The general is confined to nine points and can only step one at a time, so an attack does not need to chase; it needs to cover points. A practical way to evaluate an attack is simply to count how many of the nine palace points are currently attacked, how many are occupied by defenders, and how many moves it takes to add one more attacker. When every point the general can reach is covered and it is in check, the game is over.

The palace diagonals are the recurring theme. A chariot that reaches a palace corner attacks along the diagonal through the centre; a cannon on a palace corner jumps a centre occupant to the far corner; a soldier that reaches a palace point gains diagonal moves toward the general. Because all three of these depend on the palace centre point, whether it is empty or occupied and by what is often the single most important feature of a Janggi middlegame position. Defenders repeatedly face the dilemma that filling the centre blocks chariot lines but supplies a cannon screen.

Guards deserve a paragraph of their own because mishandling them is the most common way strong-looking positions collapse. A guard that leaves its natural post to grab material is called an out-of-place guard, and the resulting palace is often indefensible against two coordinated attackers. As a rule of thumb, do not move a guard off the palace's defensive shape for anything worth less than seven points, and never trade both guards while the opponent retains a chariot.

sections.heading: Tactical Motifs: Batteries, Screens, and Discovered Attacks
sections.body:
Janggi tactics revolve around the fact that the cannon's power is borrowed. It depends on a screen it does not own, and that screen may be a friendly piece, an enemy piece, or a piece that is about to move. This produces a family of tactics with no chess analogue, and learning to see them is most of what separates a competent Janggi player from a beginner who knows the rules.

The foundational pattern is the double attack created by a moving screen. If a friendly piece is serving as a screen for one of your cannons, moving it does not merely develop that piece; it switches the cannon off. Conversely, if a friendly piece moves onto a line to become a screen, the cannon switches on and may instantly attack something distant. Every quiet-looking move in Janggi should therefore be checked for what it turns on or off along all four directions from every cannon on the board, yours and your opponent's. The commonest catastrophic blunder in amateur Janggi is capturing a piece that was, unnoticed, the only thing preventing an enemy cannon from reaching your palace.

The second pattern is the screen removal. Because a cannon needs exactly one intervening piece, adding a second one is as good as removing the first: a line with two occupants is dead to cannons. Interposing a cheap soldier on a line that an enemy cannon is using is often a complete defence, and it costs two points at most. This is why a defender under cannon pressure counts occupants rather than looking for blocks in the chess sense.

The third pattern is the cannon-behind-cannon impossibility. Since cannons cannot jump or capture cannons, placing your cannon on a file simply switches off the enemy cannon on that file. It is a purely positional resource that costs nothing and is regularly decisive in defence of the palace.

Horse forks work much as knight forks do, with the extra condition that the horse must have a free leg both before and after; a fork that relies on a horse whose leg an opponent can block with one move is not a fork. Chariot skewers along the palace diagonals are especially strong because the general cannot step off a line quickly. Discovered checks using the general itself are legal and occasionally decisive, since moving the general off the palace centre can open a cannon's diagonal jump.

Finally, a defensive motif every player should own: because passing is legal, many apparent zugzwang traps evaporate, but perpetual check is forbidden, so a defender who can force repetition by checking cannot rely on it. The legitimate drawing resource is repetition without check, which under most rule sets leads to the position being scored — and if you are ahead on points, that is a win, not a draw. Knowing your point total tells you whether repetition is a resource or a disaster.

sections.heading: Endgame Technique and Minimum Mating Force
sections.body:
Endgames in Janggi are dominated by two facts: the target is confined to nine points, and if nobody mates, the arithmetic decides. Together these produce a distinctive practical question that arises in almost every game — not simply "am I winning?" but "can I force mate with what I have left, and if not, am I ahead on points?" Answering the first half correctly is the core of endgame technique, and answering it wrongly in either direction loses games. A player who trades into a materially winning endgame that they then cannot convert still wins on points; a player who trades away the material edge chasing a mate they cannot force loses.

The practical thresholds are worth memorising. A lone chariot, with no other attackers, generally cannot force mate against a general defended by two guards inside its palace, because the guards can be arranged to cover the critical points and the chariot cannot both check and cover simultaneously. A chariot plus almost any second attacker — another chariot, a horse, a cannon with a usable screen, or an infiltrated soldier — usually can. Two horses can mate a bare general but struggle badly against two guards, because guards block legs. A cannon alone is nearly useless in a bare endgame for the obvious reason that there is nothing left to jump; a cannon plus a soldier is dangerous precisely because the soldier supplies the screen. This last combination is the single most valuable endgame pattern to learn, because it turns a two-point piece into the enabling condition for a seven-point one.

Guards are the endgame currency. Stripping one guard is worth far more than its nominal three points if you retain mating material, and correspondingly a defender who is behind on points should usually refuse guard trades even at a nominal loss, because a general with two guards is often simply unmatable with the force the opponent has left. This is a real and repeated source of upsets: a player five points down who keeps both guards, keeps the palace shape, and forces the position to be scored will lose the count, so the defender's true goal is not to survive but to win back points while surviving.

Soldier endgames repay study. Soldiers cannot retreat, cannot promote, and lose their forward move at the far rank, so a soldier's useful life is finite and its position is irreversible. The technique is to advance them in mutually defending pairs and to aim at the palace corners, because a soldier on a palace point gains diagonal moves and becomes a genuine mating piece.

The final technique is simply counting accurately and stopping. When you are ahead on points and no mate is available, the correct plan is to trade everything, keep both guards, and force the scored ending. It is unglamorous and it wins.

sections.heading: Notation, Recording Games, and Studying Efficiently
sections.body:
Korean Janggi notation is coordinate-based and, once the numbering convention is clear, easy to read. Files are numbered one through nine and ranks one through ten, with the tenth rank conventionally written as zero so that every point is a two-digit number: the file digit followed by the rank digit. A move is then written as the origin point, the piece character, and the destination point — five characters in all, such as an origin of one-two, the character for horse, and a destination of three-three. Because each point has a unique two-digit label there is no ambiguity and no need for disambiguation markers of the kind chess notation requires. Rank numbering runs from each player's own edge, so the same physical point has different labels for the two sides; published game scores state which side's numbering is in use.

Recording your own games is the single highest-return study habit available to a Janggi improver, and it is more valuable here than in chess for a specific reason: the scoring rule means many of your losses will be quiet, gradual point losses rather than dramatic blunders, and those are almost impossible to remember accurately without a score sheet. Reviewing a game with the point total written in the margin every ten moves reveals patterns that no amount of post-mortem discussion will.

For structured study, the most efficient order is roughly this. First, drill the elephant's eight destination points and the two blocking conditions until they are automatic, because elephant blindness costs more beginner games than anything else. Second, drill cannon lines: on any position, name every cannon's legal moves out loud, including the ones that exist only because of an enemy screen. Third, learn the gwima setup and one plan within it, deeply, rather than sampling all four setups shallowly. Fourth, memorise the six piece values and practise counting the total in under fifteen seconds from a position, because a player who cannot count quickly will make the wrong strategic decision at the exact moment it matters.

Computer opposition exists and is strong, and playing engines is useful for tactics but can mislead on strategy, because engines are extremely good at the point-counting endgame in ways that do not transfer to human play. Human game collections from Korean professional play are the better strategic resource where you can find them, though the literature in languages other than Korean remains thin — an honest limitation for a student outside Korea, and one worth planning around by leaning on annotated positions and engine analysis rather than expecting a translated opening manual.

Finally, play slow games. The temptation online is toward fast blitz, but the counting discipline that Janggi rewards simply cannot be built at speed, and a player who only plays fast games tends to plateau at the level where they can see tactics but never learns to evaluate.

sections.heading: Janggi Compared with Xiangqi and International Chess
sections.body:
Setting Janggi beside its two famous relatives makes its design choices visible. Against xiangqi, the differences are few but load-bearing. There is no river, so elephants cross freely and soldiers advance from move one without a crossing rank that changes their powers. The elephant moves two-and-three rather than two-and-two, giving it a longer, hookier stride and a second blocking point. The general begins on the palace centre rather than the back rank, and may move on the palace diagonals, which xiangqi generals may not. The cannon jumps to move as well as to capture, rather than sliding to move, which is the deepest change of all. And the whole scoring apparatus — piece values, the deom, decision by count — is a Janggi invention with no xiangqi equivalent. A strong xiangqi player transplanted into Janggi will play the opening reasonably and then misjudge cannon activity and every trade, because their instincts about when a cannon is strong and whether an equal-looking trade is good are both wrong.

Against international chess the gap is wider. Janggi has no castling, no en passant, no promotion, no bishops, and no stalemate; it has a king that cannot leave a nine-point box, a piece whose movement requires borrowing an intervening screen, and a legal pass. The absence of promotion in particular removes the entire endgame architecture that chess players rely on — there is nothing to queen, so a material edge does not automatically convert, and the compensating mechanism is the point count. The legal pass removes zugzwang, which removes another large family of chess endgame technique. Conversely, the confined king makes mating patterns far more geometric and, once learned, more reliably calculable than chess king hunts.

The strategic temperament of the three games differs accordingly. Chess rewards long-term structural planning around a pawn skeleton that Janggi does not possess. Xiangqi rewards fast, direct attacks along open files with cannons behind chariots. Janggi rewards patience and accounting: slow build-up, careful counting, and a willingness to enter a scored ending a point and a half ahead. Korean players sometimes describe it as the most arithmetic of the three, and that characterisation is fair.

For a player deciding which to learn, the honest assessment is that Janggi has the shallowest published theory of the three outside Korea, which is simultaneously a drawback and an attraction: less to memorise, more to discover, and a genuinely lower barrier to reaching a level where your own analysis matters. It is also, for whatever it is worth, the easiest of the three to play badly but enjoyably, because the scoring rule means a losing position rarely collapses instantly.

One transfer does work cleanly in both directions, and it is worth stating because it saves months. Board vision — the trained habit of scanning every line from every piece before committing a move — is a general skill and carries over intact from any of the three games. What does not carry over is evaluation, the sense of what a position is worth, and a player crossing between these games should expect their evaluation to be misleading rather than merely absent.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes, Failure Modes, and How to Recover
sections.body:
The failure modes of amateur Janggi are consistent enough to list, and most of them are correctable in a single sitting once named. The largest by a wide margin is failing to count. Players raised on chess treat material as a rough guide and initiative as the real currency, and in Janggi that instinct is simply wrong, because the count is not a guide to the result — very often it is the result. The cure is mechanical: after every capture, state the current totals. A player who does this for fifty games will never go back.

The second failure is capturing a piece that was holding a cannon line shut. Because a cannon needs exactly one screen, removing a screen switches an enemy cannon on, and the natural greedy capture is frequently the move that loses. Before any capture, check every enemy cannon on the same rank and file as the captured point and ask what its screen count becomes. This one habit prevents a large fraction of amateur losses.

The third is guard mismanagement — sending a guard out to grab material, trading both guards, or filling the palace centre with a guard at the wrong moment and handing the opponent a cannon jump. A useful discipline is to decide early where your two guards will stand for the whole game and to require a very good reason to change it.

The fourth is elephant blindness: not seeing an enemy elephant's stride, or committing your own elephant to a square from which it can never return. Elephants are the most commonly hung piece in the game, on both sides of the board.

The fifth is over-advancing soldiers. They cannot come back. A soldier pushed to gain a tempo is a permanent structural decision, and five badly pushed soldiers is ten points of material that will slowly become unusable.

When a game goes wrong, the recovery plan depends on which ledger is broken. If you are behind on points but the position is complicated, do not trade — keep pieces on, keep the cannons screened, and aim at the palace, because your only path is mate or a swindle. If you are behind on points and the position is simple, your goal is to win points back cheaply: hunt guards and soldiers, avoid trades that preserve the deficit, and accept some risk. If you are ahead on points, do the opposite in every respect — trade relentlessly, keep both guards, avoid complications, and steer for the scored ending. Many amateurs know these plans and still play the wrong one because they never checked which situation they were in, which returns to the first failure on the list.

sections.heading: Etiquette, Competition, Handicaps, and the Modern Game
sections.body:
Janggi in Korea is a public game as much as a competitive one. It is played in parks, in tea houses, at family gatherings during holidays, and by two people on a folded paper board on a train, and the culture around it is correspondingly relaxed about kibitzing and commentary in a way that a chess tournament hall is not. In casual settings spectators comment freely and the players do not usually mind, though the same behaviour at a rated event is as unwelcome as anywhere else. Pieces are traditionally slapped down with a distinct clack, and doing so is not rudeness but part of the game's texture.

Competitive play is organised nationally, with professional and amateur ranks, published tournament rules, and televised matches. Modern tournament rules tighten several things that casual play leaves loose: they fix the deom, specify handling of repetition and perpetual check, usually abolish the bikjang draw, may restrict repeated passing to prevent stalling, and impose clocks. The single most useful thing a visiting player can do is to ask, before the first move, four questions: does bikjang apply, is passing unrestricted, what is the deom, and how is repetition handled. Those four answers determine a surprising amount of correct strategy.

Handicaps have a long tradition and are how mixed-strength play stays interesting. The natural handicap in a scored game is simply an adjustment to the deom — giving the weaker player an agreed number of extra points at the count — which is elegant because it is continuous and finely adjustable in a way that chess's remove-a-piece handicaps are not. Material handicaps also exist, typically removing an elephant or a horse from the stronger side, and are used at wider gaps.

The modern game faces the same demographic question as many traditional board games: its heartland audience skews older, and younger Korean players have many competing options. Against that, online play and engines have widened access considerably, and the game has a small but real following outside Korea. Engines now play Janggi at a level well beyond strong humans, which has been useful for endgame technique and has begun to shift opening evaluations, particularly around the relative merits of the four setups — though the sample of high-level engine games remains small enough that any confident claim about, say, wonangma being refuted should be treated sceptically.

For a reader learning alone with no opponent, the practical route is to get a board or a paper grid, set up the array, and spend an hour simply moving each piece type around the empty board until the elephant's stride and the cannon's screen requirement are automatic. Everything else in the game is built on those two, and both are learnable in a single session.
